entries.zh: 是以《書》稱：「葉時月正日，同律度量衡。」
entries.en: Hence the Documents states: "Align the seasons, months, and corrected day with unified pitch pipes, measures, and weights."
entries.literal: Therefore the Book of Documents says: "The seasons, the months, the corrected day, and the pitch pipes, measures, and weights are all in accord.

entries.zh: 又曰：「予欲聞六律、五聲、八音、七始詠，以出納五言。」
entries.en: It also says: "I desire to hear the six pitch standards, five tones, eight timbres, and seven beginnings sung, to produce and receive the five-word verses."
entries.literal: It also says: "I wish to hear the six pitch standards, the five notes, the eight timbres, and the seven beginnings chanted, so as to bring forth and receive the five words."

entries.zh: 此皆候金常而列管，憑璿璣以運鈞，統三極之元，紀七衡之響，可以作樂崇德，殷薦上帝。
entries.en: These all depend on metal bells to set the pipes, on the armillary instrument to drive the steelyard, to unify the three cosmic poles and mark the seven celestial harmonies—making music to ennoble virtue and richly offering worship to Heaven.
entries.literal: All these await the constant of metal to array the pipes, rely on the armillary sphere to turn the steelyard, unify the origin of the three ultimates, and record the resonance of the seven armillary rings—they can be used to make music and exalt virtue, and abundantly to offer to the Supreme Lord.

entries.zh: 故能動天地，感鬼神，和人心，移風俗，考得失，徵成敗者也。
entries.en: Music thus moves Heaven and Earth, stirs spirits, harmonizes hearts, changes customs, and reveals success or failure.
entries.literal: Therefore they can move Heaven and Earth, touch spirits and ghosts, harmonize human hearts, transform customs, examine gain and loss, and verify success and failure.

entries.zh: 粵在夏、商，無聞改作。
entries.en: Under Xia and Shang, no alterations to the system are recorded.
entries.literal: In Xia and Shang, nothing is recorded of changes or new creations.

entries.zh: 其于《周禮》，曲同則「掌六律六同之和，以辨天地四方陰陽之聲，以為樂器。」
entries.en: The Rites of Zhou's section on pitch concordance says: "He oversees the harmony of the six pitch standards and six concordances, distinguishing the sounds of Heaven, Earth, the four directions, and yin and yang, for use in instruments."
entries.literal: In the Rites of Zhou, in the section on pitch concordance, it states: "He manages the harmony of the six pitch standards and six concordances, to distinguish the sounds of Heaven and Earth, the four directions, yin and yang, and to make them into musical instruments.

entries.zh: 景王鑄鐘，問律於泠州鳩，對曰：「夫律者，所以立鈞出度。」
entries.en: When King Jing of Zhou cast bells, he asked Leng Zhoujiu about pitch; the reply was: "Pitch standards establish the steelyard and derive all measures."
entries.literal: When King Jing cast bells, he inquired about pitch from Leng Zhoujiu, who replied: "Pitch standards are what establish the steelyard and produce measures."

entries.zh: 鈞有五，則權衡規矩準繩鹹備。
entries.en: With five parts to the steelyard, scales, weights, compasses, squares, plumb lines, and measuring cords all follow.
entries.literal: When the steelyard has five parts, then scales, steelyard-weights, compasses, squares, plumb lines, and measuring cords are all complete.

entries.zh: 故《詩》曰：「尹氏太師，執國之鈞，天子是裨，俾眾不迷」是也。
entries.en: As the Odes put it: "Grand Master Yin holds the nation's steelyard, assists the Son of Heaven, and keeps the people from losing their way."
entries.literal: Thus the Odes say: "The Grand Master Yin, holding the state's steelyard, assists the Son of Heaven and keeps the multitude from going astray"—this is the meaning.

entries.zh: 太史公《律書》云：「王者制事立物，法度軌則，一稟於六律，為萬事之本。
entries.en: Sima Qian's Treatise on Pitch Standards states: "The king, in ordering affairs and setting standards, derives all laws and measures from the six pitch standards—the foundation of everything.
entries.literal: Grand Historian Sima Qian's Treatise on Pitch Standards says: "The king, in establishing affairs and setting things in order, with laws, measures, and rules, takes the six pitch standards as the single source—the root of the ten thousand affairs.

entries.zh: 其于兵械，尤所重焉。
entries.en: They are held in particular esteem for military equipment.
entries.literal: In military weapons, they are especially valued.

entries.zh: 故云：「望敵知吉凶，聞聲效勝負。
entries.en: Hence the saying: "Look at the enemy and know fortune or misfortune; listen to sounds and foretell victory or defeat.
entries.literal: Therefore it is said: "Gazing at the enemy reveals good or ill fortune; hearing sounds predicts victory or defeat."

entries.zh: 百王不易之道也。」
entries.en: This is the unchanging principle of all dynasties."
entries.literal: This is the Way that the hundred kings have never changed.

entries.en: End of quotation.
entries.literal: Close quotation mark.

entries.zh: 齊後主有寵姬馮小憐，慧而有色，能彈琵琶，尤工歌儛。
entries.en: Northern Qi's last emperor had a favored consort Feng Xiaolian—clever and beautiful, skilled on the pipa and especially in song and dance.
entries.literal: Northern Qi Houzhu had a favored consort Feng Xiaolian, clever and beautiful, able to play the pipa, especially skilled in song and dance.

entries.zh: 後主惑之，拜為淑妃。
entries.en: The emperor was captivated and made her Shufei.
entries.literal: Houzhu was deluded by her and made her Shufei.

entries.zh: 選彩女數千，為之羽從，一女之飾，動費千金。
entries.en: Several thousand attendants were selected for her retinue; a single woman's adornments cost a thousand gold pieces.
entries.literal: Several thousand colored women were selected as her retinue; one woman's adornment cost a thousand gold.

entries.zh: 帝從禽於三堆，而周師大至，邊吏告急，相望於道。
entries.en: The emperor was hunting at Sandui when Zhou armies arrived; urgent reports lined the roads.
entries.literal: The emperor was hunting at Sandui when Zhou armies arrived in force; border officials reported urgent news one after another on the road.

entries.zh: 帝欲班師，小憐意不已，更請合圍。
entries.en: The emperor wished to withdraw, but Xiaolian insisted on continuing the hunt.
entries.literal: The emperor wished to withdraw the army; Xiaolian was unwilling and asked to continue the encirclement.

entries.zh: 帝從之。
entries.en: The emperor complied.
entries.literal: The emperor followed her.

entries.zh: 由是遲留，而晉州遂陷。
entries.en: Because of this delay, Jinzhou fell.
entries.literal: Because of this delay, Jinzhou then fell.

entries.zh: 後與周師相遇于晉州之下，坐小憐而失機者數矣，因而國滅。
entries.en: Later, meeting Zhou armies below Jinzhou, he lost opportunity repeatedly because of Xiaolian—and the state was destroyed.
entries.literal: Later meeting Zhou armies below Jinzhou, because of Xiaolian he lost opportunity several times, and thus the state perished.

entries.zh: 齊之士庶，至今咎之。
entries.en: Qi gentry and commoners blame her to this day.
entries.literal: The gentry and common people of Qi blame her to this day.

entries.zh: 牛禍梁武陵王紀祭城隍神，將烹牛，忽有赤蛇繞牛口，牛禍也。
entries.en: Cow omen: Prince Wuling Xiao Ji was sacrificing to the city god; as an ox was about to be cooked, a red snake coiled around its mouth.
entries.literal: Cow portent—Prince of Wuling Ji of Liang was sacrificing to the city god; about to cook an ox, suddenly a red snake coiled around the ox's mouth—cow portent.

entries.zh: 象類言之，又為龍蛇之孽。
entries.en: In symbolic terms, it was also a dragon-and-snake calamity.
entries.literal: Speaking in terms of elephant categories, it is also dragon-and-snake calamity.

entries.zh: 魯宣公三年，郊牛之口傷，時以為天不享。
entries.en: In Lu Duke Xuan's year 3, the suburban ox's mouth was injured; at the time Heaven was thought to reject the offering.
entries.literal: In the third year of Duke Xuan of Lu, the suburban ox's mouth was injured; at the time it was thought Heaven did not accept the offering.

entries.zh: 棄宣公也。
entries.en: Duke Xuan was abandoned by Heaven.
entries.literal: Duke Xuan was abandoned.

entries.zh: 《五行傳》曰：「逆君道傷，故有龍蛇之孽。」
entries.en: The Wuxing Commentary says: "When the ruler's way is violated, dragon-and-snake calamities arise."
entries.literal: The Wuxing Zhuan says: 'When the ruler's way is violated and injured, therefore there are dragon-and-snake calamities."

entries.zh: 是時紀雖以赴援為名，而實妄自尊亢。
entries.en: Though nominally going to aid, Ji in fact arrogantly exalted himself.
entries.literal: At that time Ji, though nominally going to aid, in fact arrogantly exalted himself.

entries.zh: 思心之咎，神不享，君道傷之應。
entries.en: The fault of a confused mind; the spirits rejected him—the ruler's way was injured.
entries.literal: The fault of the reflective mind; the spirits do not accept; the response of the ruler's way being injured.

entries.zh: 果為元帝所敗。
entries.en: He was ultimately defeated by Emperor Yuan.
entries.literal: In the end he was defeated by Emperor Yuan.

entries.zh: 陳後主時，有張貴妃、孔貴嬪，並有國色，稱為妖豔。
entries.en: During Houzhu's reign Consorts Zhang and Kong, both renowned for beauty, were called bewitchingly lovely.
entries.literal: During Chen Houzhu's reign there were Consort Zhang and Consort Kong, both of national beauty, called bewitchingly lovely.

entries.zh: 後主惑之，寵冠宮掖，每充侍從，詩酒為娛。
entries.en: Houzhu was captivated; they held supreme favor in the palace, always at his side, devoted to poetry and wine.
entries.literal: Houzhu was deluded by them; their favor topped the palace; they always attended him; poetry and wine were their pleasure.

entries.zh: 一入後庭，數旬不出，荒淫侈靡，莫知紀極。
entries.en: Once they entered the inner palace, they did not emerge for weeks; debauchery and extravagance knew no bounds.
entries.literal: Once entering the rear palace, for several ten-day periods they did not emerge; debauchery and extravagance beyond measure.

entries.zh: 府庫空竭，頭會箕斂，天下怨叛，將士離心。
entries.en: The treasury emptied; taxes piled high; the realm rebelled; officers and soldiers lost heart.
entries.literal: Treasury emptied; taxes piled high; the realm rebelled; officers and soldiers lost heart.

entries.zh: 敵人鼓行而進，莫有死戰之士。
entries.en: The enemy marched in formation; none would fight to the death.
entries.literal: The enemy marched in formation; none would fight to the death.

entries.zh: 女德之咎也。
entries.en: This was the fault of female influence.
entries.literal: The fault of female virtue.

entries.zh: 及敗亡之際，後主與此姬俱投于井，隋師執張貴妃而戮之，以謝江東。
entries.en: At the moment of defeat, Houzhu and these consorts threw themselves into a well; Sui forces seized Consort Zhang and executed her to appease Jiangdong.
entries.literal: At the moment of defeat and ruin, Houzhu and these consorts together threw themselves into a well; Sui armies seized Consort Zhang and executed her to appease Jiangdong.

entries.zh: 《洪範五行傳》曰：「華者，猶榮華容色之象也。
entries.en: The Wuxing Commentary says: "Flower symbolizes splendor and beauty.
entries.literal: The Hongfan Wuxing Zhuan says: 'Flower is the image of splendor and countenance.

entries.zh: 以色亂國，故謂華孽。」
entries.en: Using beauty to disorder the state—this is called flower calamity."
entries.literal: Using beauty to disorder the state—therefore called flower calamity.'

entries.zh: 序《洪範五行傳》曰：「視之不明，是謂不知。
entries.en: The preface to the Wuxing Commentary on the Great Plan says: "When sight is dim, it is called ignorance.
entries.literal: The preface to the Hongfan Wuxing Zhuan says: 'When vision is not clear, this is called not knowing.

entries.zh: 厥咎舒，厥罰常燠，厥極疾。
entries.en: The fault is slackness; the penalty is unrelenting heat; the ultimate consequence is disease.
entries.literal: Its fault is laxity; its punishment is constant heat; its extreme is illness.

entries.zh: 時則有草妖，時則有羽蟲之孽。
entries.en: In such seasons grass-spirits appear, and calamities wrought by winged creatures arise.
entries.literal: At such times there are grass demons; at such times there are calamities of winged insects.

entries.zh: 故有羊禍，故有目疾，有赤眚赤祥。
entries.en: Hence come sheep omens, eye afflictions, and baleful red signs.
entries.literal: Therefore there are sheep portents; therefore there are eye ailments, red disasters and red omens.

entries.zh: 惟水沴火。」
entries.en: Water alone overcomes fire."
entries.literal: Only water harms fire.'"

entries.zh: 常燠後齊天保八年三月，大熱，人或暍死。
entries.en: As for "constant heat": in the third month of Northern Qi's Tianbao year 8, the heat was extreme, and people died of sunstroke.
entries.literal: Constant heat'—afterward, in the third month of the eighth year of Tianbao of Northern Qi, there was great heat, and some people died of heatstroke.

entries.zh: 劉向《五行傳》曰：「視不明，用近習，賢者不進，不肖不退，百職廢壞，庶事不從，其過在政教舒緩。」
entries.en: Liu Xiang's Wuxing Commentary says: "When a ruler's sight is clouded, he relies on those near at hand; the worthy are not promoted, the unworthy are not dismissed; every office falls into ruin and nothing is properly managed—the fault lies in slack governance and instruction."
entries.literal: Liu Xiang's Wuxing Zhuan says: 'When vision is not clear, employing close favorites, the worthy are not advanced, the unworthy are not removed, the hundred offices are ruined, and the myriad affairs are not followed—the fault lies in lax government and teaching.'"

entries.zh: 時帝狂躁、荒淫無度之應。
entries.en: This was Heaven's response to an emperor's frenzy, recklessness, and boundless debauchery.
entries.literal: At that time it was the response of the emperor's frenzy, wildness, and boundless debauchery.

entries.zh: 草妖高祖時，上黨有人，宅後每夜有人呼聲，求之不得。
entries.en: Grass-spirit omen: During Emperor Gaozu's reign, a man in Shangdang heard voices calling every night behind his house, yet however he searched, he could find no one.
entries.literal: Grass demon—during Gaozu's reign, in Shangdang there was a man whose behind his house every night there were voices calling; he searched but could not find them.

entries.zh: 去宅一里所，但見人參一本，枝葉峻茂。
entries.en: About a li from his home he found only a single ginseng plant, its branches and leaves towering and lush.
entries.literal: One li from the house, he only saw one ginseng plant, its branches and leaves luxuriant.

entries.zh: 因掘去之，其根五尺餘，具體人狀，呼聲遂絕。
entries.en: When he dug it up, the root was more than five chi long and shaped like a human being—and the calling voices stopped.
entries.literal: He dug it out; its root was more than five chi, fully in human form, and the calling voices then ceased.

entries.zh: 蓋草妖也。
entries.en: It was evidently a grass-spirit omen.
entries.literal: This was probably a grass demon.

entries.zh: 視不明之咎。
entries.en: This was the penalty for clouded royal sight.
entries.literal: The fault of unclear vision.

entries.zh: 時晉王陰有奪宗之計，諂事親要，以求聲譽譖皇太子，高祖惑之。
entries.en: At the time the Prince of Jin secretly plotted to seize the succession, fawning on the emperor's intimates and trading on his reputation to slander the crown prince—and Gaozu was taken in.
entries.literal: At that time Prince of Jin secretly harbored a plan to seize the succession, flattered those close to the emperor, sought reputation, and slandered the crown prince; Gaozu was deluded by this.

entries.zh: 人參不當言，有物憑之。
entries.en: Ginseng ought not to speak; some entity had possessed it.
entries.literal: Ginseng should not speak; some thing possessed it.

entries.zh: 上黨，黨與也。
entries.en: Shangdang: dang means "faction."
entries.literal: Shangdang—dang means faction.

entries.zh: 親要之人，乃党晉王而譖太子。
entries.en: The emperor's intimates formed a faction backing the Prince of Jin and defaming the crown prince.
entries.literal: Those close to the emperor were a faction for the Prince of Jin and slandered the crown prince.

entries.zh: 高祖不悟，聽邪言，廢無辜，有罪用，因此而亂也。
entries.en: Gaozu failed to see the truth, heeded slander, deposed the innocent and empowered the guilty—and disorder followed.
entries.literal: Gaozu did not understand, listened to evil words, deposed the innocent, employed the guilty, and thereby came disorder.

entries.zh: 羽蟲之孽梁中大同元年，邵陵王綸在南徐州，坐廳事。
entries.en: Winged-creature calamity: In Liang's Datong year 1, Prince Shaoling Xiao Lun was sitting in his reception hall in Southern Xuzhou.
entries.literal: Calamity of winged insects—in the first year of Datong of Liang, Prince of Shaoling Lun was at Southern Xuzhou, seated in the reception hall.

entries.zh: 有野鳥如鳶數百，飛屋樑上，彈射不中。
entries.en: Several hundred wild birds resembling kites alighted on the roof beams; neither bow nor sling could bring them down.
entries.literal: There were several hundred wild birds like kites that flew onto the roof beams; shooting and slinging could not hit them.

entries.zh: 俄頃失所在。
entries.en: Moments later they disappeared.
entries.literal: In a moment they vanished.

entries.zh: 京房《易飛候》曰：「野鳥入君室，其邑虛，君亡之他方。」
entries.en: Jing Fang's Yifeihou says: "When wild birds enter the ruler's hall, the city will be emptied and the lord will flee elsewhere."
entries.literal: Jing Fang's Yifeihou says: 'When wild birds enter the ruler's chamber, the city will be emptied, and the ruler will flee to another region.'"

entries.zh: 後綸為湘東王所襲，竟致奔亡，為西魏所殺。
entries.en: Later Lun was attacked by the Prince of Xiangdong, fled in defeat, and was killed by Western Wei.
entries.literal: Afterward Lun was attacked by the Prince of Xiangdong, and in the end fled and was killed by Western Wei.

entries.zh: 然后妃之制，夏、殷以前略矣。
entries.en: As for the institution governing empresses and consorts, before the Xia and Yin dynasties it existed only in rough outline.
entries.literal: As for the institution of empresses and consorts, before Xia and Yin it was only sketched in outline.

entries.zh: 周公定禮，內職始備列焉。
entries.en: When the Duke of Zhou established the rites, the inner palace offices were first set out in full array.
entries.literal: When the Duke of Zhou fixed the rites, the inner offices first took full array.

entries.zh: 秦、漢以下，代有沿革，品秩差次，前史載之詳矣。
entries.en: From Qin and Han onward, each dynasty revised the system, and the gradations of rank differed from age to age; the earlier histories record all this in detail.
entries.literal: From Qin and Han downward, each age had its reforms; ranks and grades differed in order—the former histories record these in detail.

entries.zh: 齊、梁以降，歷魏暨周，廢置益損，參差不一。
entries.en: From Qi and Liang through Wei and into Zhou, offices were abolished and restored, expanded and cut back, in ways that were uneven and inconsistent.
entries.literal: From Qi and Liang downward, through Wei and on to Zhou, abolitions and establishments increased and diminished, uneven and not uniform.

entries.zh: 周宣嗣位，不率典章，衣褘翟、稱中宮者，凡有五。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou succeeded to the throne, he did not follow the canonical regulations: five women in all wore the empress's hui and di robes and were styled ladies of the Central Palace.
entries.literal: When Xuan of Zhou succeeded to the throne, he did not follow the statutes; those who wore the hui and di robes and were called Central Palace numbered five in all.

entries.zh: 夫人以下，略無定數。
entries.en: Below the rank of Lady, there was scarcely any fixed quota at all.
entries.literal: Below the rank of Lady, there was scarcely any fixed number.

entries.zh: 高祖思革前弊，大矯其違，唯皇后正位，傍無私寵，婦官稱號，未詳備焉。
entries.en: Emperor Wen wished to reform the abuses of earlier ages and to correct their excesses in full. Only the empress held the legitimate position, with no private favorites beside her, while the titles for palace women had not yet been worked out in complete detail.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor wished to reform the abuses of earlier times and greatly correct their deviations; only the empress held the orthodox position, with no private favorites at her side, while titles for palace women were not yet fully detailed.

entries.zh: 開皇二年，著內官之式，略依周禮，省減其數。
entries.en: In the second year of Kaihuang (582), he promulgated the regulations for inner palace officials, following the Rites of Zhou in broad outline and reducing the number of posts.
entries.literal: In the second year of Kaihuang, he set down the pattern for inner officials, following in outline the Rites of Zhou and reducing their number.

entries.zh: 嬪三員，掌教四德，視正三品。
entries.en: Three Pin, who supervised instruction in the four virtues, were ranked equal to regular third grade.
entries.literal: Three Pin, who supervised instruction in the four virtues, ranked equal to regular third grade.

entries.zh: 世婦九員，掌賓客祭祀，視正五品。
entries.en: Nine Shifu, who managed guests and sacrifices, were ranked equal to regular fifth grade.
entries.literal: Nine Shifu, who managed guests and sacrifices, ranked equal to regular fifth grade.

entries.zh: 女御三十八員，掌女工絲枲，視正七品。
entries.en: Thirty-eight Nuyu, who supervised women's work in silk and hemp, were ranked equal to regular seventh grade.
entries.literal: Thirty-eight Nuyu, who managed women's work in silk and hemp, ranked equal to regular seventh grade.

entries.zh: 又採漢、晉舊儀，置六尚、六司、六典，遞相統攝，以掌宮掖之政。
entries.en: He also drew on the old regulations of Han and Jin and established the Six Chiefs, Six Directors, and Six Registrars, each level supervising the next, to govern affairs within the palace.
entries.literal: He also drew on the old regulations of Han and Jin, establishing the Six Chiefs, Six Directors, and Six Registrars, each supervising the next in turn, to administer the affairs of the inner palace.

entries.zh: 一曰尚宮，掌導引皇后及閨閤廩賜。
entries.en: The first was the Chief of the Palace, who guided the empress and managed granary distributions within the inner quarters.
entries.literal: The first was Chief of the Palace, who managed guiding the empress and the granary gifts of the inner quarters.

entries.zh: 管司令三人，掌圖籍法式，糾察宣奏；
entries.en: Under her were three Directors of Orders, who managed maps, registers, statutes, and patterns and who inspected and forwarded memorials;
entries.literal: under whom were three Directors of Orders, who managed maps, registers, statutes, and patterns, and who inspected and announced memorials;

entries.zh: 典琮三人，掌琮璽器玩。
entries.en: and three Registrars of the Jade Tablet, who managed jade tablets, seals, vessels, and precious objects.
entries.literal: and three Registrars of the Jade Tablet, who managed jade tablets, seals, vessels, and curios.

entries.zh: 二曰尚儀，掌禮儀教學。
entries.en: The second was the Chief of Ceremonies, who managed ritual and instruction.
entries.literal: The second was Chief of Ceremonies, who managed ritual and instruction.

entries.zh: 管司樂三人，掌音律之事；
entries.en: Under her were three Directors of Music, who managed matters of pitch and regulation;
entries.literal: under whom were three Directors of Music, who managed matters of pitch and regulation;

entries.zh: 典贊三人，掌導引內外命婦朝見。
entries.en: and three Registrars of Presentation, who guided titled ladies of the inner and outer courts in their audiences.
entries.literal: and three Registrars of Presentation, who managed guiding inner and outer titled ladies in audience.

entries.zh: 三曰尚服，掌服章寶藏。
entries.en: The third was the Chief of Vestments, who managed garments, insignia, and the treasure store.
entries.literal: The third was Chief of Vestments, who managed garments, insignia, and the treasure store.

entries.zh: 管司飾三人，掌簪珥花嚴；
entries.en: Under her were three Directors of Adornment, who managed hairpins, earrings, flowers, and formal dress;
entries.literal: under whom were three Directors of Adornment, who managed hairpins, earrings, flowers, and formal dress;

entries.zh: 典櫛三人，掌巾櫛膏沐。
entries.en: and three Registrars of the Comb, who managed towels, combs, oils, and bathing.
entries.literal: and three Registrars of the Comb, who managed towels, combs, oils, and bathing.

entries.zh: 四曰尚食，掌進膳先嘗。
entries.en: The fourth was the Chief of Provisions, who managed the presentation of food and tasted it before the emperor.
entries.literal: The fourth was Chief of Provisions, who managed presenting food and tasting it first.

entries.zh: 管司醫三人，掌方藥卜筮；
entries.en: Under her were three Directors of Medicine, who managed prescriptions, drugs, divination, and milfoil;
entries.literal: under whom were three Directors of Medicine, who managed prescriptions, drugs, divination, and milfoil;

entries.zh: 典器三人，掌樽彝器皿。
entries.en: and three Registrars of Vessels, who managed goblets, sacrificial bronzes, and serving vessels.
entries.literal: and three Registrars of Vessels, who managed goblets, sacrificial bronzes, and utensils.

entries.zh: 五曰尚寢，掌幃帳牀褥。
entries.en: The fifth was the Chief of the Bedchamber, who managed curtains, canopies, beds, and bedding.
entries.literal: The fifth was Chief of the Bedchamber, who managed curtains, canopies, beds, and bedding.

entries.zh: 管司筵三人，掌鋪設灑掃；
entries.en: Under her were three Directors of Mats, who managed furnishings, sprinkling, and sweeping;
entries.literal: under whom were three Directors of Mats, who managed spreading furnishings and sprinkling and sweeping;

entries.zh: 典執三人，掌扇傘燈燭。
entries.en: and three Registrars of Attendants, who managed fans, parasols, lamps, and candles.
entries.literal: and three Registrars of Attendants, who managed fans, parasols, lamps, and candles.

entries.zh: 六曰尚工，掌營造百役。
entries.en: The sixth was the Chief of Works, who managed construction and the hundred crafts.
entries.literal: The sixth was Chief of Works, who managed construction and the hundred tasks.

entries.zh: 管司製三人，掌衣服裁縫；
entries.en: Under her were three Directors of Tailoring, who managed garments, cutting, and sewing;
entries.literal: under whom were three Directors of Tailoring, who managed garments, cutting, and sewing;

entries.zh: 典會三人，掌財帛出入。
entries.en: and three Registrars of Accounts, who managed the receipt and disbursement of valuables and silks.
entries.literal: and three Registrars of Accounts, who managed the receipt and disbursement of valuables and silks.

entries.zh: 六尚各三員，視從九品，六司視勳品，六典視流外二品。
entries.en: Each of the Six Chiefs numbered three posts and was ranked equal to subordinate ninth grade; the Six Directors were ranked as merit grades; the Six Registrars were ranked as outside-the-register second grade.
entries.literal: Each of the Six Chiefs had three posts, ranked equal to subordinate ninth grade; the Six Directors were ranked equal to merit grades; the Six Registrars were ranked equal to outside-the-register second grade.

entries.zh: 初，文獻皇后功參歷試，外預朝政，內擅宮闈，懷嫉妬之心，虛嬪妾之位，不設三妃，防其上逼。
entries.en: At first Empress Wenxian had shared in her husband's rise to power. She took part in court politics and dominated the inner palace. Jealous by nature, she left the posts of concubines empty, did not establish the Three Consorts, and guarded against any rival who might press upon her from above.
entries.literal: At first Empress Wenxian's merit shared in the trials of the age; outwardly she took part in court government, inwardly she monopolized the inner palace. Harboring a jealous heart, she left the posts of concubines vacant and did not establish the Three Consorts, guarding against being pressed from above.

entries.zh: 自嬪以下，置六十員。
entries.en: From the rank of Pin downward, only sixty posts were established in all.
entries.literal: From Pin downward, sixty posts were established.

entries.zh: 加又抑損服章，降其品秩。
entries.en: She further reduced the insignia on their garments and lowered their ranks.
entries.literal: Moreover she further reduced insignia on garments and lowered their grades.

entries.zh: 至文獻崩後，始置貴人三員，增嬪至九員，世婦二十七員，御女八十一員。
entries.en: Only after Empress Wenxian's death were three Noble Ladies first established; the Pin were increased to nine, the Shifu to twenty-seven, and the Imperial Women to eighty-one.
entries.literal: Only after Wenxian's death were three Noble Ladies first established; Pin were increased to nine, Shifu to twenty-seven, and Imperial Women to eighty-one.

entries.zh: 貴人等關掌宮闈之務，六尚已下，皆分隸焉。
entries.en: The Noble Ladies and their subordinates supervised affairs within the palace, and from the Six Chiefs downward all were placed under them.
entries.literal: The Noble Ladies and others supervised the affairs of the inner palace; from the Six Chiefs downward, all were placed under them in separate subordination.

entries.zh: 文獻獨孤皇后，河南洛陽人，周大司馬、河內公信之女也。
entries.en: Empress Wenxian of the Dugu clan was a native of Luoyang in Henan, daughter of Dugu Xin, Grand Marshal of Zhou and Duke of Hanoi.
entries.literal: Empress Wenxian of the Dugu clan was a native of Luoyang in Henan, daughter of Xin, Grand Marshal of Zhou and Duke of Hanoi.

entries.zh: 信見高祖有奇表，故以后妻焉，時年十四。
entries.en: When Dugu Xin saw that the future Emperor Wen had an extraordinary appearance, he gave him his daughter in marriage; she was then fourteen.
entries.literal: Xin saw that the Founding Emperor had an extraordinary appearance and therefore gave him his daughter as wife; she was then fourteen.

entries.zh: 高祖與后相得，誓無異生之子。
entries.en: Emperor Wen and the empress were deeply devoted to each other and swore that they would have no sons by any other woman.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor and the empress were well matched; they swore there would be no sons born to another.

entries.zh: 后初亦柔順恭孝，不失婦道。
entries.en: At first the empress was gentle, compliant, respectful, and filial and did not fall short in the duties of a wife.
entries.literal: At first the empress was also gentle, compliant, respectful, and filial, not failing in the way of a wife.

entries.zh: 后姊為周明帝后，長女為周宣帝后，貴戚之盛，莫與為比，而后每謙卑自守，世以為賢。
entries.en: Her elder sister was empress to Emperor Ming of Northern Zhou, and her eldest daughter became empress to Emperor Xuan; no consort kin in the realm was more exalted. Yet the empress always kept herself humble and restrained, and the world regarded her as worthy.
entries.literal: The empress's elder sister was empress to Ming of Zhou, and her eldest daughter was empress to Xuan of Zhou; no kin by marriage was more exalted, yet the empress always kept herself humble and restrained, and the age considered her worthy.

entries.zh: 及周宣帝崩，高祖居禁中，總百揆，后使人謂高祖曰：「大事已然，騎獸之勢，必不得下，勉之！」
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou died, Emperor Wen remained within the palace and took charge of all government affairs. The empress sent word to him: "The decisive moment has come. Once you are mounted on a beast, you cannot dismount—press forward!"
entries.literal: When Xuan of Zhou died, the Founding Emperor dwelt in the forbidden precincts and oversaw all affairs of state. The empress sent someone to tell him: "The great matter is already settled. Once you are mounted on a beast, you cannot come down—press on!"

entries.zh: 高祖受禪，立為皇后。
entries.en: When he accepted the abdication and took the throne, he installed her as empress.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor received the abdication and established her as empress.

entries.zh: 突厥嘗與中國交市，有明珠一篋，價值八百萬，幽州總管陰壽白后市之。
entries.en: The Turks once traded with China, and a casket of luminous pearls worth eight million came on the market. Yin Shou, regional commander of Youzhou, reported to the empress that she might buy them.
entries.literal: The Turks once traded with China; there was a casket of bright pearls worth eight million, and Yin Shou, regional commander of Youzhou, reported to the empress that she might purchase them.

entries.zh: 后曰：「非我所須也。
entries.en: The empress said, "These are not what I need.
entries.literal: The empress said: "These are not what I need.

entries.zh: 當今戎狄屢寇，將士罷勞，未若以八百萬分賞有功者。」
entries.en: The barbarians raid us again and again, and our officers and soldiers are worn out with labor. Would it not be better to divide the eight million and reward those who have served with merit?"
entries.literal: Nowadays the barbarians raid repeatedly and the officers and soldiers are weary and worn. Would it not be better to divide the eight million and reward those who have merit?"

entries.zh: 百僚聞而畢賀。
entries.en: When the officials heard this, all congratulated her.
entries.literal: When the hundred officials heard this, all congratulated her.

entries.zh: 高祖甚寵憚之。
entries.en: Emperor Wen both cherished and stood in awe of her.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor greatly favored and feared her.

entries.zh: 上每臨朝，后輒與上方輦而進，至閣乃止。
entries.en: Whenever the emperor went to court, the empress rode in the same carriage with him and went as far as the gate-tower before stopping.
entries.literal: Whenever the emperor attended court, the empress would ride in the same carriage with him and advance together, stopping only when they reached the gate-tower.

entries.zh: 使宦官伺上，政有所失，隨則匡諫，多所弘益。
entries.en: She had eunuchs watch him in court, and whenever his governance went astray she would remonstrate with him at once. Much good came of this.
entries.literal: She had eunuchs watch the emperor; whenever his governance went astray, she would immediately correct and remonstrate with him, and much was thereby enlarged and benefited.

entries.zh: 候上退朝而同反燕寢，相顧欣然。
entries.en: She waited for him to leave court and returned with him to the private apartments, where they would look at each other with quiet delight.
entries.literal: She waited for the emperor to leave court and returned with him to the private apartments, gazing at each other with pleasure.

entries.zh: 后早失二親，常懷感慕，見公卿有父母者，每為致禮焉。
entries.en: The empress had lost both parents early in life and always cherished their memory. Whenever she saw a high minister who still had living parents, she would extend special courtesy to him.
entries.literal: The empress had early lost both parents and always cherished feelings of longing and admiration; when she saw high ministers who still had parents, she would each time extend courtesy to them on that account.

entries.zh: 有司奏以周禮百官之妻，命於王后，憲章在昔，請依古制。
entries.en: The responsible offices memorialized that, according to the Rites of Zhou, the wives of officials received their appointments from the queen, and that precedent from antiquity supported this; they asked to follow the ancient system.
entries.literal: The responsible offices memorialized that according to the Rites of Zhou the wives of the hundred officials received their appointments from the queen, and that the statutes of old stood on record; they asked to follow the ancient system.

entries.zh: 后曰：「以婦人與政，或從此漸，不可開其源也。」
entries.en: The empress said, "If women are allowed to share in government, the practice may spread from this beginning. The source of such a change must not be opened."
entries.literal: The empress said: "To let women share in government may begin gradually from this—one must not open the source of it."

entries.zh: 不許。
entries.en: She did not permit it.
entries.literal: She did not permit it.

entries.zh: 后每謂諸公主曰：「周家公主，類無婦德，失禮於舅姑，離薄人骨肉，此不順事，爾等當誡之。」
entries.en: The empress often told the princesses, "The princesses of the Zhou house for the most part lacked wifely virtue. They were disrespectful to their parents-in-law and drove wedges between close kin. These are unfitting acts, and you must take warning from them."
entries.literal: The empress often told the princesses: "The princesses of the Zhou house for the most part lacked wifely virtue, were disrespectful to parents-in-law, and estranged and pitted kin against kin. These are unfitting acts—you must take warning from them."

entries.zh: 大都督崔長仁，后之中外兄弟也，犯法當斬。
entries.en: Grand Commander Cui Changren, a brother of the empress on both her father's and mother's sides, broke the law and was sentenced to execution.
entries.literal: Grand Commander Cui Changren, a brother of the empress on both her father's and mother's sides, violated the law and should be beheaded.

entries.zh: 高祖以后之故，欲免其罪。
entries.en: Because of the empress, Emperor Wen wished to spare him.
entries.literal: Because of the empress, the Founding Emperor wished to spare him punishment.

entries.zh: 后曰：「國家之事，焉可顧私！」
entries.en: The empress said, "This is a matter of state. How can one show favor to a relative!"
entries.literal: The empress said: "Matters of the state—how can one look to private ties!"

entries.zh: 長仁竟坐死。
entries.en: In the end Changren was put to death.
entries.literal: Changren in the end was punished with death.

entries.zh: 后異母弟陀，以猫鬼巫蠱，咒詛於后，坐當死。
entries.en: The empress's younger half-brother Tuo used cat-demon witchcraft to curse her and was sentenced to death.
entries.literal: The empress's younger half-brother Tuo, by means of cat-demon witchcraft and sorcery, cursed and imprecated against the empress, and for this offense was liable to death.

entries.zh: 后三日不食，為之請命曰：「陀若蠧政害民者，妾不敢言。
entries.en: For three days the empress ate nothing and pleaded for his life, saying, "If Tuo had harmed the government or injured the people, I would not dare speak for him.
entries.literal: For three days the empress ate nothing and pleaded for his life, saying: "If Tuo were one who harmed government and injured the people, your servant would not dare speak.

entries.zh: 今坐為妾身，敢請其命。」
entries.en: But he is punished only on my account, and I venture to ask for his life."
entries.literal: Now he is punished on account of your servant's person—I venture to ask for his life."

entries.zh: 陀於是減死一等。
entries.en: Tuo's sentence was reduced one degree from death.
entries.literal: Tuo was thereby reduced one degree from death.

entries.zh: 后每與上言及政事，往往意合，宮中稱為二聖。
entries.en: Whenever the empress discussed government with the emperor, their views often agreed, and within the palace they were called the Two Sages.
entries.literal: Whenever the empress spoke with the emperor about government affairs, their intentions often agreed, and within the palace they were called the Two Sages.

entries.zh: 仁壽二年八月甲子，月暈四重，己巳，太白犯軒轅。
entries.en: In the second year of Renshou, on the jiazi day of the eighth month, the moon showed fourfold halos; on the jisi day, Venus encroached upon the Xuanyuan constellation.
entries.literal: In the second year of Renshou, on the jiazi day of the eighth month, the moon had halos within halos fourfold; on the jisi day, the Great White star encroached upon Xuanyuan.

entries.zh: 其夜，后崩於永安宮，時年五十。
entries.en: That night the empress died at Yong'an Palace at the age of fifty.
entries.literal: That night the empress died at Yong'an Palace; she was then fifty.

entries.zh: 葬於太陵。
entries.en: She was buried at Tailing.
entries.literal: She was buried at Tailing.

entries.zh: 其後，宣華夫人陳氏、容華夫人蔡氏俱有寵，上頗惑之，由是發疾。
entries.en: Afterward both Lady Xuanhua of the Chen clan and Lady Ronghua of the Cai clan won his favor. He was much taken with them, and from this he fell ill.
entries.literal: Afterward Lady Xuanhua of the Chen clan and Lady Ronghua of the Cai clan both received favor; the emperor was rather bewildered by them, and from this illness arose.

entries.zh: 及危篤，謂侍者曰「使皇后在，吾不及此」云。
entries.en: When he was critically ill, he told his attendants, "Had the empress still been alive, I would not have come to this."
entries.literal: When he was critically ill, he told his attendants, "Had the empress still been alive, I would not have come to this," he said.

entries.zh: 后頗仁愛，每聞大理決囚，未嘗不流涕。
entries.en: The empress was compassionate by nature. Whenever she heard that the Court of Review had passed sentence on prisoners, she wept without fail.
entries.literal: The empress was quite benevolent; whenever she heard that the Court of Review had passed sentence on prisoners, she never failed to shed tears.

entries.zh: 然性尤妬忌，後宮莫敢進御。
entries.en: Yet she was fiercely jealous, and no woman in the inner palace dared share the emperor's bed.
entries.literal: Yet her nature was especially jealous, and none in the inner palace dared approach the emperor's bed.

entries.zh: 尉遲迥女孫有美色，先在宮中。
entries.en: A granddaughter of Yuchi Jiong was exceptionally beautiful and was already in the palace.
entries.literal: A granddaughter of Yuchi Jiong had beautiful looks and was already in the palace.

entries.zh: 上於仁壽宮見而悅之，因此得幸。
entries.en: The emperor saw her at Renshou Palace and was pleased with her, and through this she gained his favor.
entries.literal: The emperor saw her at Renshou Palace and was pleased with her; through this she gained his favor.

entries.zh: 后伺上聽朝，陰殺之。
entries.en: The empress waited until the emperor was at court and secretly had her killed.
entries.literal: The empress waited until the emperor was attending court and secretly killed her.

entries.zh: 上由是大怒，單騎從苑中而出，不由徑路，入山谷間二十餘里。
entries.en: The emperor was furious. Alone on horseback he rode out of the park, left the main path, and plunged more than twenty li into the mountain valleys.
entries.literal: The emperor was thereby greatly enraged. Alone on horseback he rode out of the park, not by the main path, and entered the mountain valleys for more than twenty li.

entries.zh: 高熲、楊素等追及上，扣馬苦諫。
entries.en: Gao Jiong, Yang Su, and others overtook him, seized his horse's bridle, and remonstrated with him in desperate earnest.
entries.literal: Gao Feng, Yang Su, and others overtook the emperor, seized his horse's bridle, and remonstrated with bitter earnestness.

entries.zh: 上太息曰：「吾貴為天子，而不得自由！」
entries.en: The emperor sighed deeply and said, "I am exalted as Son of Heaven, yet I am not free!"
entries.literal: The emperor sighed deeply and said: "I am exalted as Son of Heaven, yet I cannot be free!"

entries.zh: 高熲曰：「陛下豈以一婦人而輕天下！」
entries.en: Gao Jiong said, "Your Majesty, would you slight the realm under Heaven for the sake of one woman!"
entries.literal: Gao Feng said: "Your Majesty, would you for a single woman slight the realm under Heaven!"

entries.zh: 上意少解，駐馬良久，中夜方始還宮。
entries.en: The emperor's anger eased a little. He halted his horse for a long while and did not return to the palace until midnight.
entries.literal: The emperor's mind was somewhat eased; he halted his horse for a long while and only at midnight did he return to the palace.

entries.zh: 后俟上於閣內。
entries.en: The empress waited for him inside the gate-tower.
entries.literal: The empress waited for the emperor inside the gate-tower.

entries.zh: 及上至，后流涕拜謝，熲、素等和解之。
entries.en: When he arrived, the empress wept and bowed in apology. Jiong, Su, and the others brought about a reconciliation.
entries.literal: When the emperor arrived, the empress wept and bowed in apology; Feng, Su, and the others reconciled them.

entries.zh: 上置酒極歡，后自此意頗衰折。
entries.en: The emperor set out wine and they made merry together, but from that time the empress's authority was noticeably diminished.
entries.literal: The emperor set out wine and they were extremely merry; from this time the empress's will was rather diminished and broken.

entries.zh: 初，后以高熲是父之家客，甚見親禮。
entries.en: At first, because Gao Jiong had been a retainer in her father's household, the empress treated him with great intimacy and respect.
entries.literal: At first, because Gao Feng had been a household guest of her father's house, the empress treated him with great intimacy and courtesy.

entries.zh: 至是，聞熲謂己為一婦人，因此銜恨。
entries.en: Now, hearing that Jiong had called her a mere woman, she bore a deep grudge against him.
entries.literal: At this time, hearing that Feng had called her a mere woman, she therefore harbored resentment.

entries.zh: 又以熲夫人死，其妾生男，益不善之，漸加譖毀，上亦每事唯后言是用。
entries.en: When Jiong's principal wife died and his concubine bore a son, she thought even less of him and gradually slandered him to the emperor. The emperor, for his part, followed her word in almost every matter.
entries.literal: Moreover, when Feng's principal wife died and his concubine bore a son, she thought even less well of him and gradually added slander and defamation; the emperor too in every matter followed only what the empress said.

entries.zh: 后見諸王及朝士有妾孕者，必勸上斥之。
entries.en: Whenever she saw a prince or court official whose concubine was pregnant, she urged the emperor to dismiss him.
entries.literal: Whenever the empress saw princes or court gentlemen whose concubines were pregnant, she would urge the emperor to dismiss them.

entries.zh: 時皇太子多內寵，妃元氏暴薨，后意太子愛妾雲氏害之。
entries.en: At that time the crown prince kept many concubines. His consort of the Yuan clan died suddenly, and the empress suspected that the prince's beloved concubine, Lady Yun, had caused her death.
entries.literal: At that time the crown prince had many inner favorites; the consort of the Yuan clan died suddenly, and the empress suspected that the crown prince's beloved concubine of the Yun clan had harmed her.

entries.zh: 由是諷上黜高熲，竟廢太子立晉王廣，皆后之謀也。
entries.en: Through this she urged the emperor to dismiss Gao Jiong, and in the end the crown prince was deposed and Prince Guang of Jin was made heir. All of this was the empress's doing.
entries.literal: Thereby she indirectly urged the emperor to dismiss Gao Feng, and in the end the crown prince was deposed and Prince of Jin Guang was established—all this was the empress's design.

entries.zh: 初，上寢疾於仁壽宮也，夫人與皇太子同侍疾。
entries.en: At first, when the emperor lay ill at Renshou Palace, Lady Xuanhua and the crown prince attended him together.
entries.literal: At first, when the emperor lay ill at Renshou Palace, the lady and the crown prince together attended his sickness.

entries.zh: 平旦出更衣，為太子所逼，夫人拒之得免，歸於上所。
entries.en: At daybreak she went out to change her clothes and was accosted by the crown prince. She resisted and escaped, then returned to the emperor's bedside.
entries.literal: At daybreak she went out to change her clothes and was pressed by the crown prince; the lady resisted and escaped, then returned to the emperor's side.

entries.zh: 上怪其神色有異，問其故。
entries.en: The emperor noticed her altered expression and asked the reason.
entries.literal: The emperor wondered at her altered expression and asked the reason.

entries.zh: 夫人泫然曰：「太子無禮。」
entries.en: With tears in her eyes she said, "The crown prince behaved without propriety."
entries.literal: The lady said with tears: "The crown prince was without propriety."

entries.zh: 上恚曰：「畜生何足付大事，獨孤誠誤我！」
entries.en: The emperor said in anger, "That beast is not fit to be entrusted with great affairs. Dugu truly misled me!"
entries.literal: The emperor said in anger: "That beast is not fit to be entrusted with great affairs—Dugu truly misled me!"

entries.zh: 意謂獻皇后也。
entries.en: He meant Empress Dugu.
entries.literal: He meant Empress Xian.

entries.zh: 因呼兵部尚書柳述、黃門侍郎元巖曰：「召我兒！」
entries.en: He then called Minister of War Liu Shu and Palace Attendant Yuan Yan and said, "Summon my son!"
entries.literal: Thereupon he called Minister of War Liu Xu and Palace Attendant Yuan Yan and said: "Summon my son!"

entries.zh: 述等將呼太子，上曰：「勇也。」
entries.en: Xu and the others were about to summon the crown prince, but the emperor said, "Yong."
entries.literal: Xu and the others were about to summon the crown prince; the emperor said: "Yong."

entries.zh: 述、巖出閤為勑書訖，示左僕射楊素。
entries.en: Xu and Yan left the gate-tower, drafted the imperial order, and showed it to Left Director Yang Su.
entries.literal: Xu and Yan went out of the gate-tower, completed the imperial order, and showed it to Left Director Yang Su.

entries.zh: 素以其事白太子，太子遣張衡入寢殿，遂令夫人及後宮同侍疾者，並出就別室。
entries.en: Su reported the matter to the crown prince. The crown prince sent Zhang Heng into the sleeping hall and ordered Lady Xuanhua and all the women of the inner palace who were attending the emperor to leave for separate rooms.
entries.literal: Su reported the matter to the crown prince; the crown prince sent Zhang Heng into the sleeping hall and then ordered the lady and all in the inner palace who were attending the sickness to go out to separate rooms.

entries.zh: 俄聞上崩，而未發喪也。
entries.en: Soon they heard that the emperor had died, but the death had not yet been announced.
entries.literal: Soon they heard that the emperor had died, but mourning had not yet been proclaimed.

entries.zh: 夫人與諸後宮相顧曰：「事變矣！」
entries.en: Lady Xuanhua and the other palace women looked at one another and said, "Things have changed!"
entries.literal: The lady and the women of the inner palace looked at one another and said: "Things have changed!"

entries.zh: 皆色動股慄。
entries.en: All turned pale and trembled in their limbs.
entries.literal: All changed color and their thighs trembled.

entries.zh: 晡後，太子遣使者齎金合子，帖紙於際，親署封字，以賜夫人。
entries.en: In the afternoon the crown prince sent an envoy bearing a golden casket sealed with paper at the seam and inscribed in his own hand, to present it to Lady Xuanhua.
entries.literal: After the hour of shen, the crown prince sent an envoy bearing a golden casket, with paper pasted at the seam and the seal characters written in his own hand, to bestow it upon the lady.

entries.zh: 夫人見之惶懼，以為鴆毒，不敢發。
entries.en: When she saw it she was terrified, thinking it contained poison, and did not dare open it.
entries.literal: When the lady saw it she was fearful and afraid, thinking it poison, and did not dare open it.

entries.zh: 使者促之，於是乃發，見合中有同心結數枚。
entries.en: The envoy urged her, and only then did she open it and find several matching-knot ornaments inside.
entries.literal: The envoy urged her, and only then did she open it and see several matching-knot ornaments inside the casket.

entries.zh: 諸宮人咸悅，相謂曰：「得免死矣！」
entries.en: All the palace women rejoiced and said to one another, "We have escaped death!"
entries.literal: All the palace women were pleased and said to one another: "We have escaped death!"

entries.zh: 陳氏恚而却坐，不肯致謝。
entries.en: Lady Chen was angry, drew back, and refused to offer thanks.
entries.literal: The Chen lady was angry and drew back to sit, refusing to offer thanks.

entries.zh: 諸宮人共逼之，乃拜使者。
entries.en: The other palace women pressed her until she bowed to the envoy.
entries.literal: The palace women together pressed her, and only then did she bow to the envoy.

entries.zh: 其夜，太子烝焉。
entries.en: That night the crown prince violated her.
entries.literal: That night the crown prince took her in the forbidden union.

entries.zh: 煬帝蕭皇后，梁明帝巋之女也。
entries.en: Empress Xiao of Emperor Yang was a daughter of Emperor Ming of Liang, Xiao Kui.
entries.literal: Empress Xiao of Emperor Yang was a daughter of Emperor Ming of Liang, Kui.

entries.zh: 江南風俗，二月生子者不舉。
entries.en: In the Jiangnan region, custom held that children born in the second month were not to be raised.
entries.literal: In the customs of the south of the Yangzi, children born in the second month were not raised.

entries.zh: 后以二月生，由是季父岌收而養之。
entries.en: The future empress was born in the second month, and for this reason her uncle Ji took her in and raised her.
entries.literal: The empress was born in the second month; for this reason her father's younger brother Ji took her in and raised her.

entries.zh: 未幾，岌夫妻俱死，轉養舅氏張軻家。
entries.en: Before long both Ji and his wife died, and she was sent to be raised in the household of her uncle Zhang Ke.
entries.literal: Before long both Ji and his wife died, and she was transferred to be raised in the household of her mother's brother Zhang Ke.

entries.zh: 然軻甚貧窶，后躬親勞苦。
entries.en: Zhang Ke was very poor, and the future empress labored with her own hands.
entries.literal: Yet Ke was very poor and destitute, and the empress personally bore toil and hardship.

entries.zh: 煬帝為晉王時，高祖將為王選妃於梁，遍占諸女，諸女皆不吉。
entries.en: When the future Emperor Yang was Prince of Jin, Emperor Wen sought a bride for him in Liang. He cast lots for every daughter of the house, and every result was inauspicious.
entries.literal: When Emperor Yang was Prince of Jin, the Founding Emperor was about to choose a consort for the prince in Liang; he divined for all the daughters, and all were inauspicious.

entries.zh: 巋迎后於舅氏，令使者占之，曰：「吉。」
entries.en: Xiao Kui brought her from her uncle's house and had the envoy cast lots for her. The result was auspicious.
entries.literal: Kui brought the empress from her mother's brother's house and had the envoy divine for her; he said: "Auspicious."

entries.zh: 於是遂策為王妃。
entries.en: She was then chosen as the prince's consort.
entries.literal: Thereupon she was established as the prince's consort.

entries.zh: 后性婉順，有智識，好學解屬文，頗知占候。
entries.en: The empress was gentle and compliant by nature, intelligent and well educated, skilled in literary composition, and versed in divination and astronomy.
entries.literal: The empress's nature was gentle and compliant; she had wisdom and knowledge, loved learning and understood literary composition, and was quite versed in divination and observation of the heavens.

entries.zh: 高祖大善之，帝甚寵敬焉。
entries.en: Emperor Wen thought very highly of her, and her husband cherished and respected her deeply.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor greatly approved of her, and the emperor cherished and respected her deeply.

entries.zh: 及帝嗣位，詔曰：「朕祗承丕緒，憲章在昔，爰建長秋，用承饗薦。
entries.en: When he succeeded to the throne, an edict declared, "We respectfully receive the great succession. Following the statutes of old, We establish the office of the empress to preside over the sacrifices.
entries.literal: When the emperor succeeded to the throne, an edict said: "We respectfully receive the great succession; the statutes of old stand on record. We therefore establish the Eternal Autumn to undertake the offerings of sacrifice.

entries.zh: 妃蕭氏，夙禀成訓，婦道克修，宜正位軒闈，式弘柔教，可立為皇后。」
entries.en: Consort Xiao has from childhood received proper instruction and fully cultivated the duties of a wife. She is fit to take the empress's place in the inner court and to extend gentle teaching throughout the realm. Let her be established as empress."
entries.literal: Consort of the Xiao clan, from of old endowed with completed instruction, has fully cultivated the way of a wife—she should take the orthodox position in the inner gate and broadly extend gentle teaching; she may be established as empress."

entries.zh: 煬帝時，后妃嬪御，無釐婦職，唯端容麗飾，陪從醼遊而已。
entries.en: Under Emperor Yang, empresses, consorts, and palace women no longer performed the duties of wives; they merely dressed their faces, arrayed themselves in finery, and accompanied the emperor at banquets and excursions.
entries.literal: In the time of Emperor Yang, empresses, consorts, Pin, and attendants did not put in order women's duties; they only composed their appearance with fine adornment and accompanied banquets and excursions.

entries.zh: 帝又參詳典故，自製嘉名，著之於令。
entries.en: The emperor also studied ancient precedents, devised elegant titles of his own, and set them down in edict.
entries.literal: The emperor also consulted and examined ancient precedents, devised fine names himself, and set them down in edict.

entries.zh: 貴妃、淑妃、德妃，是為三夫人，品正第一。
entries.en: Imperial Consort, Pure Consort, and Virtuous Consort—these were the Three Ladies, of orthodox first rank.
entries.literal: Imperial Consort, Pure Consort, and Virtuous Consort—these were the Three Ladies, of orthodox first rank.

entries.zh: 順儀、順容、順華、修儀、修容、修華、充儀、充容、充華，是為九嬪，品正第二。
entries.en: Compliant Form, Compliant Countenance, Compliant Splendor, Cultivated Form, Cultivated Countenance, Cultivated Splendor, Fulfilling Form, Fulfilling Countenance, and Fulfilling Splendor—these were the Nine Pin, of orthodox second rank.
entries.literal: Compliant Form, Compliant Countenance, Compliant Splendor, Cultivated Form, Cultivated Countenance, Cultivated Splendor, Fulfilling Form, Fulfilling Countenance, and Fulfilling Splendor—these were the Nine Pin, of orthodox second rank.

entries.zh: 婕妤一十二員，品正第三，美人、才人一十五員，品正第四，是為世婦。
entries.en: Twelve Ladies of Handsome Fairness of orthodox third rank; fifteen Beauties and fifteen Talented Ladies of orthodox fourth rank—these constituted the Shifu.
entries.literal: Twelve Ladies of Handsome Fairness, of orthodox third rank; fifteen Beauties and fifteen Talented Ladies, of orthodox fourth rank—these were the Shifu.

entries.zh: 寶林二十四員，品正第五；
entries.en: Twenty-four Treasured Forest attendants of orthodox fifth rank;
entries.literal: Twenty-four Treasured Forest attendants, of orthodox fifth rank;

entries.zh: 御女二十四員，品正第六；
entries.en: twenty-four Imperial Women of orthodox sixth rank;
entries.literal: twenty-four Imperial Women, of orthodox sixth rank;

entries.zh: 采女三十七員，品正第七，是為女御。
entries.en: and thirty-seven Selected Women of orthodox seventh rank—these were the Nuyu.
entries.literal: thirty-seven Selected Women, of orthodox seventh rank—these were the Nuyu.

entries.zh: 總一百二十，以叙於宴寢。
entries.en: In all there were one hundred twenty, ranked in order for banquets and the bedchamber.
entries.literal: In all one hundred twenty, arranged in order for banquets and bedchambers.

entries.zh: 又有承衣刀人，皆趨侍左右，並無員數，視六品已下。
entries.en: There were also robe-bearers and blade-women, all of whom hurried to wait upon him at his side; they had no fixed quota and were ranked below sixth grade.
entries.literal: There were also robe-bearers and blade-women, all hurrying to attend at left and right, with no fixed quota, ranked below sixth grade.

entries.zh: 宣華夫人陳氏，陳宣帝之女也。
entries.en: Lady Xuanhua of the Chen clan was a daughter of Emperor Xuan of Chen.
entries.literal: Lady Xuanhua of the Chen clan was a daughter of Emperor Xuan of Chen.

entries.zh: 性聰慧，姿貌無雙。
entries.en: She was intelligent by nature and without peer in beauty.
entries.literal: By nature she was intelligent and clever, and in looks without peer.

entries.zh: 及陳滅，配掖庭，後選入宮為嬪。
entries.en: When Chen fell, she was assigned to the palace women, and later she was selected to enter the inner palace as a Pin.
entries.literal: When Chen was destroyed, she was assigned to the palace women; later she was selected to enter the palace as a Pin.

entries.zh: 時獨孤皇后性妬，後宮罕得進御，唯陳氏有寵。
entries.en: At that time Empress Dugu was fiercely jealous, and few women in the inner palace shared the emperor's bed. Only Lady Chen enjoyed his favor.
entries.literal: At that time Empress Dugu was jealous by nature, and those in the inner palace rarely gained access to the emperor; only the Chen lady had favor.

entries.zh: 晉王廣之在藩也，陰有奪宗之計，規為內助，每致禮焉。
entries.en: When Prince Guang of Jin was in his fief, he secretly plotted to seize the succession and sought her help within the palace. He often sent her gifts.
entries.literal: When Prince of Jin Guang was in his fief, he secretly had a plan to seize the succession and schemed to make her an inner helper; he often sent her gifts.

entries.zh: 進金蛇、金駝等物，以取媚於陳氏。
entries.en: He sent her golden snakes, golden camels, and other gifts to win her favor.
entries.literal: He presented golden snakes, golden camels, and other objects to win the Chen lady's favor.

entries.zh: 皇太子廢立之際，頗有力焉。
entries.en: At the time of the crown prince's deposition and replacement, she exerted considerable influence.
entries.literal: At the time of the crown prince's deposition and establishment, she contributed considerable force.

entries.zh: 及文獻皇后崩，進位為貴人，專房擅寵，主斷內事，六宮莫與為比。
entries.en: When Empress Wenxian died, Lady Chen was promoted to Noble Lady. She monopolized the emperor's favor, controlled affairs within the palace, and none of the six palaces could compare with her.
entries.literal: When Empress Wenxian died, she was advanced to the rank of Noble Lady, monopolized the bedchamber and held favor alone, decided inner affairs, and none of the six palaces could compare with her.

entries.zh: 及上大漸，遺詔拜為宣華夫人。
entries.en: When the emperor's illness grew grave, his final edict invested her as Lady Xuanhua.
entries.literal: When the emperor's illness grew grave, his final edict invested her as Lady Xuanhua.

entries.zh: 及煬帝嗣位之後，出居仙都宮。
entries.en: After Emperor Yang succeeded to the throne, she was sent to live at Xiandu Palace.
entries.literal: After Emperor Yang succeeded to the throne, she went out to dwell at Xiandu Palace.

entries.zh: 尋召入，歲餘而終，時年二十九。
entries.en: Soon she was summoned back to the palace, and a little more than a year later she died at the age of twenty-nine.
entries.literal: Soon she was summoned back in; a little more than a year later she died, aged twenty-nine.

entries.zh: 帝深悼之，為製神傷賦。
entries.en: The emperor mourned her deeply and composed the Rhapsody of Spirit's Wounding in her memory.
entries.literal: The emperor mourned her deeply and composed the Rhapsody of Spirit's Wounding for her.

entries.zh: 及帝幸江都，臣下離貳，有宮人白后曰：「外聞人人欲反。」
entries.en: When the emperor went to Jiangdu, his officials grew disloyal, and a palace woman told the empress, "Outside, everyone says the people wish to rebel."
entries.literal: When the emperor favored Jiangdu, his ministers and subordinates were divided in loyalty, and a palace woman reported to the empress: "Outside one hears that everyone wishes to rebel."

entries.zh: 后曰：「任汝奏之。」
entries.en: The empress said, "Then report it as you wish."
entries.literal: The empress said: "As you wish—report it."

entries.zh: 宮人言於帝，帝大怒曰：「非所宜言！」
entries.en: The palace woman told the emperor. He flew into a rage and said, "That is not what should be spoken!"
entries.literal: The palace woman told the emperor; the emperor said in great anger: "This is not what should be spoken!"

entries.zh: 遂斬之。
entries.en: He had her beheaded at once.
entries.literal: He then beheaded her.

entries.zh: 後人復白后曰：「宿衞者往往偶語謀反。」
entries.en: Later someone again told the empress, "The night guards are often heard whispering together about rebellion."
entries.literal: Later someone again reported to the empress: "Those on night guard often speak together in pairs, plotting rebellion."

entries.zh: 后曰：「天下事一朝至此，勢已然，無可救也。
entries.en: The empress said, "Affairs under heaven have come to this in a single morning. The momentum is already set, and nothing can save us.
entries.literal: The empress said: "Affairs under heaven have in a morning come to this—the momentum is already set, and nothing can save them.

entries.zh: 何用言之，徒令帝憂煩耳。」
entries.en: What use is there in speaking of it? It would only add to the emperor's grief."
entries.literal: What use is there in speaking of it? It would only make the emperor worried and troubled."

entries.zh: 自是無復言者。
entries.en: From that time on, no one spoke of it again.
entries.literal: From this time there was no one who spoke again.

entries.zh: 容華夫人蔡氏，丹陽人也。
entries.en: Lady Ronghua of the Cai clan was a native of Danyang.
entries.literal: Lady Ronghua of the Cai clan was a native of Danyang.

entries.zh: 陳滅之後，以選入宮，為世婦。
entries.en: After the fall of Chen she was selected for the palace and became a Shifu.
entries.literal: After Chen was destroyed, she was selected to enter the palace and became a Shifu.

entries.zh: 容儀婉嫕，上甚悅之。
entries.en: Her bearing was gentle and lovely, and the emperor was greatly pleased with her.
entries.literal: Her bearing and appearance were gentle and lovely, and the emperor was greatly pleased with her.

entries.zh: 以文獻皇后故，希得進幸。
entries.en: Because of Empress Wenxian, she rarely shared the emperor's bed.
entries.literal: Because of Empress Wenxian, she rarely gained access to the emperor's bed.

entries.zh: 及后崩，漸見寵遇，拜為貴人，參斷宮掖之務，與陳氏相亞。
entries.en: After the empress died, she gradually won favor, was appointed Noble Lady, took part in governing affairs within the palace, and stood second only to Lady Chen.
entries.literal: When the empress died, she gradually received favor and was appointed Noble Lady, took part in deciding affairs of the inner palace, and was second only to the Chen lady.

entries.zh: 上寢疾，加號容華夫人。
entries.en: When the emperor fell ill, she was given the additional title Lady Ronghua.
entries.literal: When the emperor lay ill, she was given the additional title Lady Ronghua.

entries.zh: 上崩後，自請言事，亦為煬帝所烝。
entries.en: After the emperor's death she volunteered to report a matter and was likewise violated by Emperor Yang.
entries.literal: After the emperor died, she herself asked to report a matter and was likewise taken in the forbidden union by Emperor Yang.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：二后，帝未登庸，早儷宸極，恩隆好合，始終不渝。
entries.en: The historian says: Both empresses became imperial consorts while their husbands were still princes, and the bond between them was deep and unchanging from first to last.
entries.literal: The historian says: The two empresses, before the emperors had ascended to office, early became consorts of the imperial apex; their grace was lofty and their union good, unchanging from beginning to end.

entries.zh: 文獻德異鳲鳩，心非均一，擅寵移嫡，傾覆宗社，惜哉！
entries.en: Wenxian's virtue fell short of that praised in the Ospreys; her heart was not even-handed. She monopolized favor, displaced the rightful heir, and brought ruin upon the dynasty—alas!
entries.literal: Wenxian's virtue differed from the osprey; her heart was not evenly one. Monopolizing favor, she shifted the heir and overturned the ancestral altars—alas!

entries.zh: 書曰：「牝雞之晨，惟家之索。」
entries.en: The Documents say, "When the hen crows at dawn, the household is brought to ruin."
entries.literal: The Documents say: "When the hen crows at dawn, the house is brought to ruin."

entries.zh: 高祖之不能敦睦九族，抑有由矣。
entries.en: That Emperor Wen could not keep his kinsmen in harmony likewise had its cause.
entries.literal: That the Founding Emperor could not make his nine kindreds harmonious and close likewise had its reason.

entries.zh: 蕭后初歸藩邸，有輔佐君子之心。
entries.en: When Empress Xiao first entered the prince's household, she had the heart of one who would assist a worthy ruler.
entries.literal: When Empress Xiao first came to the prince's residence, she had a heart to assist the gentleman.

entries.zh: 煬帝得不以道，便謂人無忠信。
entries.en: Emperor Yang gained the throne by improper means and thereafter believed that no one could be loyal or trustworthy.
entries.literal: Emperor Yang gained the throne not by the proper way and thereupon supposed that people had no loyalty or faith.

entries.zh: 父子之間，尚懷猜阻，夫婦之際，其何有焉！
entries.en: Between father and son he still harbored suspicion and distrust—what bond could remain between husband and wife!
entries.literal: Between father and son he still harbored suspicion and obstruction—what could there be between husband and wife!

entries.zh: 暨乎國破家亡，竄身無地，飄流異域，良足悲矣！
entries.en: When at last the state was ruined and her house destroyed, she had nowhere to hide and drifted in a foreign land—a fate truly pitiable enough to break the heart!
entries.literal: When at last the state was broken and the house destroyed, she had no place to hide her person and drifted in a foreign land—truly enough to grieve one!

entries.zh: 夫陰陽肇分，乾坤定位，君臣之道斯著，夫婦之義存焉。
entries.en: When yin and yang first separated and heaven and earth took their fixed places, the bond between ruler and minister came into view, and the duties of husband and wife were set in place.
entries.literal: When yin and yang first divided, heaven and earth took their places; the way of ruler and minister was thereby made manifest, and the meaning of husband and wife was established.

entries.zh: 陰陽和則裁成萬物，家道正則化行天下，由近及遠，自家刑國，配天作合，不亦大乎！
entries.en: When yin and yang are in harmony, the myriad things take shape; when the household is rightly ordered, its influence reaches the whole realm. From the family to the state, from what is near to what is far—union with heaven in marriage—is this not a matter of the greatest weight?
entries.literal: When yin and yang are in harmony, the myriad things are fashioned; when the way of the household is correct, transformation spreads through the realm—from near to far, from family to state, matching heaven in union—is this not great!

entries.zh: 興亡是繫，不亦重乎！
entries.en: Upon it the rise and fall of dynasties depend—is this not grave indeed!
entries.literal: Rise and fall depend upon it—is this not weighty!

entries.zh: 是以先王慎之，正其本而嚴其防。
entries.en: That is why the ancient kings treated the matter with care, setting the foundation aright and guarding the barriers with strictness.
entries.literal: Therefore the former kings were cautious regarding it, rectifying the root and making strict the defenses.

entries.zh: 後之繼體，靡克聿修，甘心柔曼之容，罔念幽閑之操。
entries.en: Later rulers who inherited the throne seldom carried on the tradition; they were content with soft, alluring beauty and gave no thought to quiet, modest virtue.
entries.literal: Later heirs to the throne mostly could not continue the tradition, content with soft and alluring looks, heedless of quiet and modest conduct.

entries.zh: 成敗攸屬，安危斯在。
entries.en: Victory and defeat hang upon it; safety and danger rest upon it as well.
entries.literal: Success and failure depend upon it; security and peril lie therein.

entries.zh: 故皇、英降而虞道隆，任、姒歸而姬宗盛，妹、妲致夏、殷之釁，褒、趙結周、漢之禍。
entries.en: When E Huang and Nüying came down to Shun, the way of Yu flourished; when Ren and Si entered the Zhou house, the Ji clan rose to greatness. Mei Xi and Daji brought ruin upon Xia and Yin; Bao Si and Zhao Feiyan brought disaster upon Zhou and Han.
entries.literal: Thus when Huang and Ying descended, the way of Yu flourished; when Ren and Si came home, the Ji clan prospered; Mei and Da brought the calamities of Xia and Yin, Bao and Zhao sealed the disasters of Zhou and Han.

entries.zh: 爰歷晉、宋，實繁有徒。
entries.en: Down through Jin and Song, examples of this kind were truly numerous.
entries.literal: Continuing through Jin and Song, there were indeed many such cases.

entries.zh: 皆位以寵升，榮非德進，恣行淫僻，莫顧禮儀，為梟為鴟，敗不旋踵。
entries.en: They all advanced through imperial favor rather than merit, abandoned themselves to licentious and perverse conduct, and cared nothing for ritual propriety. Like owls and kites among birds, they met ruin almost at once.
entries.literal: All rose in rank through favor, their glory gained not through virtue; they indulged in wanton and perverse conduct, heedless of ritual propriety—becoming owls and kites, their ruin came without turning the heel.

entries.zh: 後之伉儷宸極，正位居中，罕蹈平易之塗，多遵覆車之轍。
entries.en: Later empresses who shared the imperial throne and sat in the central place seldom took the easy road; far more often they followed the tracks of overturned carts.
entries.literal: Later consorts of the imperial apex, occupying the central position, rarely trod the level path and mostly followed the tracks of overturned carts.

entries.zh: 睢鳩之德，千載寂寥；
entries.en: The virtue praised in the Ospreys lay silent for a thousand years;
entries.literal: The virtue of the osprey, for a thousand years lonely and still;

entries.zh: 牝雞之晨，殊邦接響。
entries.en: while the hen's crowing at dawn echoed from one foreign land to the next.
entries.literal: the hen's morning crowing, in distant states echo answered echo.

entries.zh: 窈窕淑女，靡有求於寤寐；
entries.en: Fair and gentle ladies were no longer sought in waking thought and in dreams;
entries.literal: Fair and gentle ladies—none sought in waking and sleep;

entries.zh: 鏗鏘環珮，鮮克嗣於徽音。
entries.en: and though jade pendants chimed at their belts, few could carry on the fame of worthy wives.
entries.literal: resounding pendants and rings—few could continue the excellent reputation.

entries.zh: 永念前修，歎深彤管。
entries.en: Ever mindful of the worthy women of old, I sigh deeply over the red brush that should have recorded their praise.
entries.literal: Ever mindful of former exemplars, I sigh deeply over the red tube.

entries.zh: 覽載籍於既往，考行事於當時，存亡得失之機，蓋亦多矣。
entries.en: In reviewing the records of the past and weighing conduct in the present, one finds that the turning points of survival and ruin, gain and loss, are many indeed.
entries.literal: Perusing the records of the past and examining conduct in the present, the springs of survival, extinction, gain, and loss are indeed many.

entries.zh: 故述皇后列傳，所以垂戒將來。
entries.en: That is why I compose this collective biography of empresses—to leave a warning for generations yet to come.
entries.literal: Therefore I set forth the collective biography of empresses, in order to leave a warning for those to come.

entries.zh: 頃之，熲國令上熲陰事，稱：「其子表仁謂熲曰：'司馬仲達初托疾不朝，遂有天下。
entries.en: Soon his estate steward denounced him, reporting, "His son Biaoren had said to him, 'Sima Yi feigned illness and stayed away from court — and in the end seized the realm.
entries.literal: Before long Jiong's estate steward reported Jiong's secret affairs, saying: "His son Biaoren said to Jiong: 'Sima Yi at first feigned illness and did not attend court, and in the end possessed all under Heaven.

entries.zh: 公今遇此，焉知非福！
entries.en: You are in the same position now — who is to say this is not a blessing in disguise?'
entries.literal: You now meet this — how do you know it is not fortune!'

entries.zh: '」於是上大怒，囚熲于內史省而鞫之。
entries.en: " The emperor was furious, imprisoned Jiong in the Ministry of the Interior, and put him on trial.
entries.literal: " Thereupon the sovereign was greatly enraged, imprisoned Jiong in the Ministry of the Interior, and interrogated him.

entries.zh: 憲司複奏熲他事，雲：「沙門真覺嘗謂熲雲：'明年國有大喪。
entries.en: The prosecutors added further charges, saying, "The monk Zhenjue had told Jiong, 'Next year the state will mourn a great death.'
entries.literal: The law officers again memorialized other matters concerning Jiong, saying: "The monk Zhenjue once told Jiong: 'Next year the state will have a great mourning.'

entries.zh: '尼令暉複雲：'十七、十八年，皇帝有大厄。
entries.en: The nun Linghui had also said, 'In the seventeenth and eighteenth years the emperor will face grave peril.
entries.literal: 'The nun Linghui again said: 'In the seventeenth and eighteenth years the emperor will suffer a great calamity.

entries.zh: 十九年不可過。
entries.en: He will not survive the nineteenth year.'
entries.literal: The nineteenth year cannot be passed.'

entries.zh: '」上聞而益怒，顧謂群臣曰：「帝王豈可力求！
entries.en: " The emperor, hearing this, turned to the court and exclaimed, "Does anyone think the throne can be seized by scheming!
entries.literal: " The sovereign heard and grew ever angrier, turned to the assembled ministers and said, "Can an emperor's throne be striven for by force!

entries.zh: 孔子以大聖之才，作法垂世，寧不欲大位邪？
entries.en: Confucius, for all his sagehood, laid down laws for the ages — would he not have wanted the throne?
entries.literal: Confucius, with the talent of the greatest sage, established law to last through the ages — would he not have desired the supreme position?

entries.zh: 天命不可耳。
entries.en: Only the Mandate of Heaven denied it to him.
entries.literal: It was only that the Mandate of Heaven did not allow it.

entries.zh: 熲與子言，自比晉帝，此何心乎？」
entries.en: Jiong spoke to his son and likened himself to an emperor of Jin — what treason is this?"
entries.literal: Jiong spoke with his son and compared himself to the Jin emperor — what sort of heart is this?"

entries.zh: 有司請斬熲。
entries.en: The judges asked that Jiong be executed.
entries.literal: The relevant offices requested Jiong be beheaded.

entries.zh: 上曰：「去年殺虞慶則，今茲斬王世積，如更誅熲，天下其謂我何？」
entries.en: The emperor said, "Last year I killed Yu Qingze, this year Wang Shiji — if I kill Jiong as well, what will the world say of me?"
entries.literal: The sovereign said: "Last year I killed Yu Qingze; this year I beheaded Wang Shiji — if I also execute Jiong, what will all under Heaven say of me?"

entries.zh: 於是除名為民。
entries.en: He was therefore stripped of rank and made a commoner.
entries.literal: Thereupon he was stripped of name and made a commoner.

entries.zh: 熲初為僕射，其母誡之曰：「汝富貴已極，但有一斫頭耳，爾宜慎之！」
entries.en: When Jiong first became vice director, his mother warned him, "You have risen as high as a man can — only the executioner's blade remains; take care!"
entries.literal: When Jiong first became Vice Director, his mother admonished him, saying: "Your wealth and honor have already reached the limit — there is only one thing left, a beheading — you should be careful!"

entries.zh: 熲由是常恐禍變。
entries.en: From that time he lived in constant fear of disaster.
entries.literal: Jiong thereby constantly feared calamity and change.

entries.zh: 及此，熲歡然無恨色，以為得免於禍。
entries.en: Now he accepted his punishment without bitterness, believing he had escaped with his life.
entries.literal: At this, Jiong was pleased and had no look of resentment, thinking he had escaped calamity.

entries.zh: 高熲，字昭玄，一名敏，自雲渤海蓚人也。
entries.en: Gao Jiong, whose courtesy name was Zhaoxuan and who was also known as Min, was a native of the Bohai frontier district, by his own account.
entries.literal: Gao Jiong — styled Zhaoxuan, also called Min, claimed by his own account to be from the Bohai border district of Zhuo.

entries.zh: 父賓，背齊歸周，大司馬獨孤信引為僚佐，賜姓獨孤氏。
entries.en: His father Bin had abandoned Northern Qi for Northern Zhou, where Grand Marshal Dugu Xin recruited him to his staff and bestowed the surname Dugu upon him.
entries.literal: His father Bin turned against Qi and submitted to Zhou; Grand Marshal Dugu Xin took him on as a staff officer and granted him the surname Dugu.

entries.zh: 及信被誅，妻子徙蜀。
entries.en: After Xin was put to death, his family was sent into exile in Shu.
entries.literal: When Xin was executed, his wife and children were banished to Shu.

entries.zh: 文獻皇后以賓父之故吏，每往來其家。
entries.en: Empress Wenxian — for Bin had once served under her father — was in the habit of visiting the Gao home.
entries.literal: Empress Wenxian, because Bin had been a former subordinate of her father, often came and went at his household.

entries.zh: 賓後官至鄀州刺史，及熲貴，贈禮部尚書、渤海公。
entries.en: Bin eventually rose to governor of Ezhou; once Jiong came to power, he was posthumously enfeoffed as Minister of Rites and Duke of Bohai.
entries.literal: Bin later reached the office of Governor of E Prefecture; when Jiong rose to eminence, Bin was posthumously made Minister of Rites and Duke of Bohai.

entries.zh: 河間王弘，字辟惡，高祖從祖弟也。
entries.en: Yang Hong, Prince of Hejian, courtesy name Bie'e, was a cousin of Emperor Wen on the paternal line.
entries.literal: Hejian Wang Hong, styled Bie'e, was a younger paternal-line cousin of Gaozu.

entries.zh: 祖愛敬，早卒。
entries.en: His grandfather Aijing died at an early age.
entries.literal: His grandfather Aijing died young.

entries.zh: 父元孫，少孤，隨母郭氏養于舅族。
entries.en: His father Yuansun lost his parents in childhood and was brought up by his mother, Lady Guo, among her maternal relatives.
entries.literal: His father Yuansun, orphaned in youth, was raised by his mother Lady Guo among her maternal clan.

entries.zh: 及武元皇帝與周太祖建義關中，元孫時在鄴下，懼為齊人所誅，因假外家姓為郭氏。
entries.en: When Emperor Wuyuan and the Zhou dynastic founder raised their banner in Guanzhong, Yuansun was still in Ye. Fearing the Northern Qi would put him to death, he assumed his maternal clan's surname and became Guo.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wuyuan and Zhou's founding emperor raised the banner of righteous rebellion in Guanzhong, Yuansun was then in Ye and, fearing execution by the people of Qi, took his maternal family's surname of Guo as his own.

entries.zh: 元孫死，齊為周所並，弘始入關，與高祖相得。
entries.en: After Yuansun died and Qi was overrun by Zhou, Hong finally entered Guanzhong, where he and the future Emperor Wen became close.
entries.literal: Yuansun died; when Qi was absorbed by Zhou, Hong first entered the passes and found favor with Gaozu.

entries.zh: 高祖哀之，為買田宅。
entries.en: Moved by his plight, Emperor Wen bought him land and a house.
entries.literal: Gaozu took pity on him and purchased fields and a residence for him.

entries.zh: 弘性明悟，有文武幹略。
entries.en: Hong was quick-witted by nature and possessed both literary and military ability.
entries.literal: Hong was bright and perceptive by nature, with both civil and military talent and resourcefulness.

entries.zh: 數從征伐，累遷開府儀同三司。
entries.en: He fought in several campaigns and rose in stages to the rank of Acting Third Rank Supervisor with the Opening of an Office.
entries.literal: He often followed on campaigns and was repeatedly promoted to Acting Third Rank Supervisor of the Imperial Retinue with the Opening of an Office.

entries.zh: 高祖為丞相，常置左右，委以心腹。
entries.en: While still serving as chancellor, Yang Jian kept Hong close at hand and treated him as one of his most trusted inner circle.
entries.literal: When Gaozu was chancellor, he was kept constantly at his side and entrusted as an intimate confidant.

entries.zh: 高祖詣周趙王宅，將及於難，弘時立於戶外，以衛高祖。
entries.en: On the occasion when Yang Jian visited the residence of Zhao, Prince of Zhou, and nearly came to harm, Hong stood guard outside the door to protect him.
entries.literal: When Gaozu went to the residence of Zhao, Prince of Zhou, and was about to meet with disaster, Hong stood outside the door at the time to guard Gaozu.

entries.zh: 尋加上開府，賜爵永康縣公。
entries.en: Before long he was also granted the privilege of opening his own office and given the title Marquis of Yongkang County.
