entries.en: He joined Yang Su against the Turks, won a victory, was promoted to Supreme Pillar of State, and was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Jiangdu commandery.
entries.literal: He followed Yang Su in striking the Turks and defeated them; he was promoted to Supreme Pillar of State and his enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Jiangdu commandery.

entries.zh: 煬帝即位，又改封新蔡郡公。
entries.en: When Emperor Yang came to the throne, his title was changed again to Duke of Xincai commandery.
entries.literal: When Emperor Yang acceded, his title was again changed to Duke of Xincai commandery.

entries.zh: 自是之後，不復任用。
entries.en: After that he was never again given office.
entries.literal: From then on he was no longer employed.

entries.zh: 大業五年，從幸太原。
entries.en: In the fifth year of Daye he accompanied the emperor to Taiyuan.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Daye he accompanied the imperial progress to Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 有京兆人達奚通妾王氏，能清歌，朝臣多相會觀之，僧壽亦豫焉，坐是除名。
entries.en: A concubine of Daxi Tong of Jingzhao named Wang was famed for her refined singing. Many ministers gathered to hear her, and Sengshou joined them; for that he was dismissed from office.
entries.literal: There was a concubine Wang of Daxi Tong of Jingzhao who could sing pure songs; many court ministers gathered to watch her, and Sengshou also took part—on this account he was struck from the rolls.

entries.zh: 尋令復位。
entries.en: He was soon restored to office.
entries.literal: Soon he was ordered restored to his post.

entries.zh: 八年，卒于京師，時年六十五。
entries.en: In the eighth year he died in the capital at the age of sixty-five.
entries.literal: In the eighth year he died in the capital, aged sixty-five.

entries.zh: 有子孝基。
entries.en: He left a son, Xiaoji.
entries.literal: He had a son Xiaoji.

entries.zh: 賀若弼，字輔伯，河南洛陽人也。
entries.en: He Ruo Bi, whose courtesy name was Fubo, came from Luoyang in Henan.
entries.literal: He Ruo Bi, courtesy name Fubo, was a native of Luoyang in Henan.

entries.zh: 父敦，以武烈知名，仕周為金州總管，宇文護忌而害之。
entries.en: His father Dun was renowned for martial prowess. He had served the Northern Zhou as Area Commander of Jinzhou until Yuwen Hu, envying him, had him put to death.
entries.literal: His father Dun was famed for martial valor; he served the Zhou as Area Commander of Jinzhou, but Yuwen Hu, envying him, had him killed.

entries.zh: 臨刑，呼弼謂之曰：「吾必欲平江南，然此心不果，汝當成吾志。
entries.en: At the execution block he called Bi to him and said, "I always meant to bring Jiangnan under control, but that ambition will die with me. You must finish what I began.
entries.literal: Facing execution, he called Bi and said to him, "I have always wished to pacify Jiangnan, yet this heart's aim will not be fulfilled—you must accomplish my aspiration.

entries.zh: 且吾以舌死，汝不可不思。」
entries.en: And I am dying for my own loose tongue. Do not forget that lesson."
entries.literal: Moreover, I die because of my tongue—you must not fail to reflect on this."

entries.zh: 因引錐刺弼舌出血，誡以慎口。
entries.en: He then drove an awl through Bi's tongue until it bled, warning him to guard every word he spoke.
entries.literal: Thereupon he took an awl and pierced Bi's tongue until it bled, admonishing him to be careful with his mouth.

entries.zh: 弼少慷慨有大志，驍勇便弓馬，解屬文，博涉書記，有重名於當世。
entries.en: In youth Bi was open-handed and ambitious, fierce in battle and expert with bow and horse, able to compose prose, widely read in the histories, and widely respected in his own day.
entries.literal: Bi in youth was magnanimous and possessed a great aspiration; he was fierce and brave, skilled with bow and horse, adept at composing literary pieces, broadly versed in written records, and had heavy renown in his age.

entries.zh: 周齊王憲聞而敬之，引為記室。
entries.en: Prince Xian of Northern Zhou heard of him, held him in esteem, and made him a secretariat secretary.
entries.literal: Prince Xian of Qi of Zhou heard of him and treated him with respect, bringing him in as a secretariat attendant.

entries.zh: 未幾，封當亭縣公，遷小內史。
entries.en: He was soon enfeoffed as Duke of Dangting county and promoted to Junior Inner Scribe.
entries.literal: Before long he was enfeoffed as Duke of Dangting county and transferred to Junior Inner Scribe.

entries.zh: 周武帝時，上柱國烏丸軌言於帝曰：「太子非帝王器，臣亦嘗與賀若弼論之。」
entries.en: During the reign of Northern Zhou's Emperor Wu, Supreme Pillar of State Wuwan Gui told the emperor, "The crown prince is no emperor's material. I have discussed this with He Ruo Bi as well."
entries.literal: In the time of Emperor Wu of Zhou, Supreme Pillar of State Wuwan Gui said to the emperor, "The crown prince is not material for an emperor; your subject has also once discussed this with He Ruo Bi."

entries.zh: 帝呼弼問之，弼知太子不可動搖，恐禍及己，詭對曰：「皇太子德業日新，未睹其闕。」
entries.en: The emperor summoned Bi and questioned him. Bi knew the crown prince's position could not be moved and feared for his own life, so he evasively answered, "The crown prince's virtue grows by the day. I have seen no flaw in him."
entries.literal: The emperor summoned Bi and questioned him; Bi knew the crown prince could not be shaken, feared calamity reaching himself, and deceitfully replied, "The crown prince's virtue and achievement renew themselves daily; I have not seen his failings."

entries.zh: 帝默然。
entries.en: The emperor said nothing.
entries.literal: The emperor was silent.

entries.zh: 弼既退，軌讓其背己，弼曰：「君不密則失臣，臣不密則失身，所以不敢輕議也。」
entries.en: After Bi withdrew, Gui reproached him for going back on their understanding. Bi said, "When a ruler is indiscreet he loses his minister; when a minister is indiscreet he loses his life. That is why I would not speak openly."
entries.literal: When Bi had withdrawn, Gui reproached him for betraying him; Bi said, "If the ruler is not discreet he loses his minister; if the minister is not discreet he loses his life—therefore I did not dare lightly discuss it."

entries.zh: 及宣帝嗣位，軌竟見誅，弼乃獲免。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan came to the throne, Gui was eventually executed—and Bi was spared.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xuan succeeded to the throne, Gui in the end was put to death, and Bi thereby escaped harm.

entries.zh: 尋與韋孝寬伐陳，攻拔數十城，弼計居多。
entries.en: He soon joined Wei Xiaokuan in the campaign against Chen, helped capture dozens of cities, and most of the plans behind those victories were Bi's.
entries.literal: Soon he joined Wei Xiaokuan in campaigning against Chen, stormed and took several tens of cities, and Bi's stratagems predominated in most cases.

entries.zh: 拜夀州刺史，改封襄邑縣公。
entries.en: He was appointed Inspector of Shouzhou and re-enfeoffed as Duke of Xiangyi county.
entries.literal: He was appointed Inspector of Shouzhou and his enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Xiangyi county.

entries.zh: 高祖為丞相，尉迥作亂鄴城，恐弼為變，遣長孫平馳驛代之。
entries.en: While Yang Jian was still Chancellor, Yu Chi rebelled at Yecheng. Fearing Bi might turn traitor, he sent Changsun Ping by fast relay to relieve him of command.
entries.literal: When the Founding Emperor was Chancellor, Yu Chi raised rebellion at Yecheng; fearing Bi might change sides, he sent Changsun Ping post-haste by relay stations to replace him.

entries.zh: 開皇初，高祖潛有吞併江南之志，以擒虎有文武才用，夙著聲名，於是拜為廬州總管，委以平陳之任，甚為敵人所憚。
entries.en: Early in the Kaihuang reign the emperor quietly set his sights on bringing the south under control. Qinhu was already famed for combining literary and military gifts, so he was made Area Commander of Luzhou and charged with conquering Chen—a commission that struck deep fear into the enemy.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, the Founding Emperor secretly harbored the aim of swallowing up the lands south of the Yangzi; because Qinhu possessed both civil and military talent and had long been famed, he was appointed Area Commander of Luzhou and entrusted with the task of pacifying Chen, and the enemy feared him greatly.

entries.zh: 及大舉伐陳，以擒虎為先鋒。
entries.en: When the full-scale invasion of Chen was launched, Qinhu was placed at the head of the army.
entries.literal: When a great campaign was launched against Chen, Qinhu was made vanguard.

entries.zh: 擒虎率五百人宵濟，襲採石，守者皆醉，擒虎遂取之。
entries.en: Qinhu led five hundred men across the river at night and stormed Caishi. The garrison was drunk, and he took the place without difficulty.
entries.literal: Qinhu led five hundred men across by night, struck Caishi, the defenders were all drunk, and Qinhu thereupon took it.

entries.zh: 進攻姑熟，半日而拔，次於新林。
entries.en: He pressed on to Gushu and captured it within half a day, then made camp at Xinlin.
entries.literal: He advanced to attack Gushu and took it in half a day, then encamped at Xinlin.

entries.zh: 江南父老素聞其威信，來謁軍門，晝夜不絕。
entries.en: The elders south of the Yangzi had long known his reputation for authority and fairness. They came to his camp in an unbroken stream, day and night.
entries.literal: The elders of the south of the Yangzi had long heard of his prestige and trustworthiness; they came to call at the camp gate day and night without cease.

entries.zh: 陳人大駭，其將樊巡、魯世真、田瑞等相繼降之。
entries.en: Chen forces were thrown into panic, and generals such as Fan Xun, Lu Shizhen, and Tian Rui surrendered to him in succession.
entries.literal: The Chen people were greatly alarmed; their generals Fan Xun, Lu Shizhen, Tian Rui, and others surrendered to him one after another.

entries.zh: 晉王廣上狀，高祖聞而大悅，宴賜群臣。
entries.en: Prince Jin Guang reported the news upstream. The emperor was delighted and held a feast to reward his ministers.
entries.literal: Prince of Jin Guang submitted a memorial; when the Founding Emperor heard it he was greatly pleased and held a feast to reward the court ministers.

entries.zh: 晉王遣行軍總管杜彥與擒虎合軍，步騎二萬，陳叔寶遣領軍蔡徵守朱雀航，聞擒虎將至，眾懼而潰。
entries.en: The Prince of Jin sent Campaign Commander Du Yan to join Qinhu with twenty thousand foot and horse. Chen Shubao ordered Palace Guard Director Cai Zheng to hold the Zhuque crossing, but at word that Qinhu was approaching the army panicked and broke.
entries.literal: The Prince of Jin sent Campaign Commander Du Yan to join forces with Qinhu—twenty thousand infantry and cavalry. Chen Shubao sent the Director of the Palace Guard Cai Zheng to hold the Zhuque crossing; when they heard Qinhu was coming, the troops were afraid and scattered in rout.

entries.zh: 任蠻奴為賀若弼所敗，棄軍降於擒虎。
entries.en: Ren Man'nu, already beaten by He Ruobi, abandoned his troops and surrendered to Qinhu.
entries.literal: Ren Man'nu had been defeated by He Ruobi; he abandoned his army and surrendered to Qinhu.

entries.zh: 擒虎以精騎五百，直入硃雀門。
entries.en: Qinhu rode through the Zhuque Gate at the head of five hundred elite cavalry.
entries.literal: Qinhu with five hundred picked horsemen entered straight through the Zhuque Gate.

entries.zh: 陳人欲戰，蠻奴捴之曰：「老夫尚降，諸君何事！」
entries.en: The Chen soldiers were ready to fight, but Man'nu shouted them down: "If even I, an old man, have surrendered, what are you still fighting for!"
entries.literal: The Chen troops wished to fight; Man'nu rebuked them, saying, "Even I, an old man, have submitted—what business have you!"

entries.zh: 眾皆散走。
entries.en: The men broke and fled in all directions.
entries.literal: The crowd all scattered and fled.

entries.zh: 遂平金陵，執陳主叔寶。
entries.en: He then took Jinling and captured Chen's ruler, Shubao.
entries.literal: Thereupon he pacified Jinling and seized Chen's ruler Shubao.

entries.zh: 時賀若弼亦有功。
entries.en: He Ruobi had won distinction as well.
entries.literal: At that time He Ruobi also had merit.

entries.zh: 乃下詔于晉王曰：「此二公者，深謀大略，東南逋寇，朕本委之，靜地恤民，悉如朕意。
entries.en: The emperor then issued an edict to the Prince of Jin: "These two commanders planned with foresight and executed on a grand scale. I entrusted the unruly southeast to them, and in calming the country and caring for the people they have done exactly as I intended.
entries.literal: Thereupon an edict was issued to the Prince of Jin, saying, "These two lords possess deep counsel and grand strategy. The fugitive bandits of the southeast—I originally entrusted them to them; in pacifying the land and showing compassion to the people, all has been as I wished.

entries.zh: 九州不一，已數百年，以名臣之功，成太平之業，天下盛事，何用過此！
entries.en: The realm had been divided for centuries; through the service of such renowned ministers the work of unification and peace has been achieved. What triumph under Heaven could be greater than this!
entries.literal: The Nine Provinces have not been united for several hundred years; through the achievement of famed ministers, the work of great peace has been accomplished—what event under Heaven could surpass this!

entries.zh: 聞以欣然，實深慶快。
entries.en: To hear this news fills me with joy; my satisfaction is profound.
entries.literal: On hearing it I am pleased with joy; truly my celebration and delight are deep.

entries.zh: 平定江表，二人之力也。」
entries.en: The pacification of the south is the work of these two men alone."
entries.literal: The pacification of the lands along the Yangzi is the achievement of these two men."

entries.zh: 賜物萬段。
entries.en: Each was rewarded with ten thousand bales of goods.
entries.literal: They were granted ten thousand bales of goods.

entries.zh: 又下優詔於擒虎、弼曰：「申國威于萬里，宣朝化於一隅，使東南之民俱出湯火，數百年寇旬日廓清，專是公之功也。
entries.en: A special edict went out to Qinhu and Bi: "You have carried our might across the realm and brought the court's civilizing rule to a distant quarter, lifting the people of the southeast out of misery. Centuries of disorder were swept away in days—and that is your doing alone.
entries.literal: A gracious edict was also issued to Qinhu and Bi, saying, "You have displayed the state's might for ten thousand li and spread the court's transforming influence in a corner of the realm, so that the people of the southeast all escaped boiling water and raging fire; banditry of several hundred years was cleared in the space of days—this achievement is yours alone.

entries.zh: 高名塞于宇宙，盛業光於天壤，逖聽前古，罕聞其匹。
entries.en: Your renown fills heaven and earth; your achievement outshines the land. Search the records of antiquity as you will—you will seldom find your equal.
entries.literal: Your lofty fame fills the cosmos; your splendid achievement shines between heaven and earth. Listening far back into antiquity, one rarely hears its equal.

entries.zh: 班師凱入，誠知非遠，相思之甚，寸陰若歲。」
entries.en: Your victorious return cannot be far away. I miss you so keenly that every moment drags like a year."
entries.literal: Your triumphant return with the army cannot, I know, be far off; my longing for you is so deep that each inch of shadow is like a year."

entries.zh: 及至京，弼與擒虎爭功於上前，弼曰：「臣在蔣山死戰，破其銳卒，擒其驍將，震揚威武，遂平陳國。
entries.en: After they reached the capital, Bi and Qinhu argued over credit before the emperor. Bi said, "I fought to the death on Mount Jiang, shattered their elite forces, captured their boldest generals, and by that display of force brought Chen to its knees.
entries.literal: When they reached the capital, Bi and Qinhu disputed merit before the throne. Bi said, "Your servant fought to the death on Mount Jiang, broke their crack troops, captured their fierce generals, displayed awe-inspiring might, and thereby pacified the state of Chen.

entries.zh: 韓擒虎略不交陣，豈臣之比！」
entries.en: Han Qinhu barely drew sword—how can he stand comparison with me!"
entries.literal: Han Qinhu scarcely crossed spears at all—how can he be compared with your servant!"

entries.zh: 擒虎曰：「本奉明旨，令臣與弼同時合勢，以取偽都。
entries.en: Qinhu replied, "I was under your explicit orders to coordinate with Bi and strike the rebel capital together.
entries.literal: Qinhu said, "I originally received your clear command that your servant and Bi should combine our strength at the same time to take the false capital.

entries.zh: 弼乃敢先期，逢賊遂戰，致令將士傷死甚多。
entries.en: Yet Bi rushed ahead on his own, met the enemy, and fought prematurely, costing us many dead and wounded.
entries.literal: Bi dared to move ahead of schedule; when he met the enemy he fought at once, causing many officers and soldiers to be wounded and killed.

entries.zh: 臣以輕騎五百，兵不血刃，直取金陵，降任蠻奴，執陳叔寶，據其府庫，傾其巢穴。
entries.en: I took five hundred light cavalry, entered Jinling without shedding blood, received Ren Man'nu's surrender, seized Chen Shubao, and occupied the treasuries and the heart of their power.
entries.literal: Your servant with five hundred light horsemen, blades unstained with blood, took Jinling straight off, made Ren Man'nu submit, seized Chen Shubao, occupied their treasuries, and overturned their nest.

entries.zh: 弼至夕，方扣北掖門，臣啟關而納之。
entries.en: Bi did not reach the North Side Gate until evening; I was the one who opened the gate and let him in.
entries.literal: Bi only in the evening came to knock at the North Side Gate; your servant opened the gate and admitted him.

entries.zh: 斯乃救罪不暇，安得與臣相比！」
entries.en: He was lucky to escape blame—how can he compare with me!"
entries.literal: He had barely time to beg off his offenses—how could he be compared with your servant!"

entries.zh: 上曰：「二將俱合上勳。」
entries.en: The emperor said, "Both of you have earned the highest credit."
entries.literal: The emperor said, "Both generals alike merit supreme merit."

entries.zh: 於是進位上柱國，賜物八千段。
entries.en: Qinhu was then promoted to Supreme Pillar of State and given eight thousand bales of goods.
entries.literal: Thereupon Qinhu was promoted to Supreme Pillar of State and granted eight thousand bales of goods.

entries.zh: 有司劾擒虎放縱士卒，淫汙陳宮，坐此不加爵邑。
entries.en: The authorities charged Qinhu with allowing his troops to run riot and desecrate the Chen palace, and for that reason he received no further titles or fiefs.
entries.literal: The responsible offices impeached Qinhu for letting his soldiers run wild and defiling the Chen palace; on this account he was not given additional enfeoffment or fief.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：夫天地未泰，聖哲啟其機；
entries.en: The historiographer writes: When heaven and earth are not yet at peace, sages and worthies seize the moment;
entries.literal: The historiographer says: When heaven and earth are not yet at peace, sages and worthies open the opportunity;

entries.zh: 疆埸尚梗，爪牙宣其力。
entries.en: when the frontiers remain blocked, warriors and champions bring their strength to bear.
entries.literal: when the frontiers are still obstructed, talons and fangs display their strength.

entries.zh: 周之方、邵，漢室韓、彭，代有其人，非一時也。
entries.en: Zhou had its Fang and Shao; the Han had its Han Xin and Peng Yue. Every age produces such men—it is never a matter of one moment alone.
entries.literal: The Fang and Shao of Zhou, the Han and Peng of the Han house—each age has had such men; it is not a matter of one time alone.

entries.zh: 自晉衰微，中原幅裂，區宇分隔，將三百年。
entries.en: From the decline of Jin the heartland was torn apart and the realm sundered—for nearly three hundred years.
entries.literal: From the decline of Jin, the central plains were torn apart and the realm divided—for nearly three hundred years.

entries.zh: 陳氏憑長江之地險，恃金陵之餘氣，以為天限南北，人莫能窺。
entries.en: The Chen court trusted in the Yangzi's natural defenses and Jinling's residual prestige, believing heaven itself had divided north from south and that no foe could cross.
entries.literal: The house of Chen relied on the Yangzi's strategic terrain and trusted in Jinling's lingering vigor, believing that heaven had set north and south apart and that no man could peer across.

entries.zh: 高祖爰應千齡，將一函夏。
entries.en: The Founding Emperor answered the summons of the age and set out to reunite the realm.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor then answered the call of a thousand years and was about to unify all within the four seas.

entries.zh: 賀若弼慷慨，申必取之長策，韓擒虎奮發，賈餘勇以爭先，勢甚疾雷，鋒逾駭電。
entries.en: He Ruobi, bold and high-spirited, laid out the strategy that would surely win; Han Qinhu threw himself into the fight and spent his last reserves of daring to lead the charge. Their momentum was like thunder, their blades swifter than lightning.
entries.literal: He Ruobi was open-handed and bold, setting forth the long strategy that must seize victory; Han Qinhu roused himself and sold his remaining courage to race ahead—their momentum like sudden thunder, their edge surpassing startling lightning.

entries.zh: 隋氏自此一戎，威加四海。
entries.en: With this single campaign the Sui made their might felt across the four seas.
entries.literal: From this one campaign the house of Sui made its authority felt across the four seas.

entries.zh: 稽諸天道，或時有廢興，考之人謀，實二臣之力。
entries.en: Measured against heaven's way, dynasties rise and fall in their season; measured by human design, the conquest was truly the work of these two ministers.
entries.literal: Examined against the way of heaven, rise and fall come in their seasons; examined in human counsel, it was truly the power of these two ministers.

entries.zh: 其俶儻英略，賀若居多，武毅威雄，韓擒虎稱重。
entries.en: In daring strategy and sweeping design, He Ruo had the edge; in martial resolve and commanding presence, Han Qinhu was the greater name.
entries.literal: In bold unconventionality and heroic strategy, He Ruo had the greater share; in martial resolve and awe-inspiring might, Han Qinhu was the weightier name.

entries.zh: 方于晉之王、杜，勳庸綽有餘地。
entries.en: Set beside the Wang and Du of Jin, their achievements would still have stood with room to spare.
entries.literal: Compared with Jin's Wang and Du, their achievements and merit still had room to spare.

entries.zh: 然賀若功成名立，矜伐不已，竟顛殞於非命，亦不密以失身。
entries.en: Yet He Ruo, once his fame was won, never stopped boasting of it and in the end died an untimely death—he had also failed to guard his tongue and paid with his life.
entries.literal: Yet He Ruo, his merit and fame established, never ceased boasting of his achievements; in the end he toppled and perished by an untimely death—he had also failed to keep counsel and so lost his life.

entries.zh: 若念父臨終之言，必不及於斯禍矣。
entries.en: Had he remembered his father's dying warning, he would never have come to such ruin.
entries.literal: Had he kept his father's dying words in mind, he would surely not have reached this calamity.

entries.zh: 韓擒虎累世將家，威聲動俗，敵國既破，名遂身全，幸也。
entries.en: Han Qinhu came from generations of military houses, and his reputation shook the realm. Once the enemy state fell, he won lasting fame and kept his life—a piece of good fortune.
entries.literal: Han Qinhu came from a family of generals for generations; his awesome reputation shook the age. Once the enemy state was broken, his fame was achieved and his person preserved—fortunate indeed.

entries.zh: 廣陵、甘棠，鹹有武藝，驍雄膽略，並為當時所推，赳赳干城，難兄難弟矣。
entries.en: The dukes of Guangling and Gantang were both skilled in arms; in boldness and resource they were admired alike—fierce bulwarks of the state, brothers each the equal of the other.
entries.literal: The lords of Guangling and Gantang both had martial arts; in fierce valor and daring stratagem they were alike commended in their day—stalwart defenders of the realm, brothers hard to match one against the other.

entries.zh: 洪字叔明，擒虎季弟也。
entries.en: Hong, whose courtesy name was Shuming, was Qinhu's youngest brother.
entries.literal: Hong, courtesy name Shuming, was Qinhu's youngest brother.

entries.zh: 少驍勇，善射，膂力過人。
entries.en: In his youth he was bold and fierce, an expert archer, and stronger than ordinary men.
entries.literal: In youth he was fierce and brave, skilled in archery, and his physical strength surpassed other men.

entries.zh: 仕周侍伯上士，後以軍功拜大都督。
entries.en: He served the Northern Zhou as Senior Gentleman of the Palace Guard and later became Grand Commander on the strength of his battlefield record.
entries.literal: He served the Zhou as Senior Gentleman of the Palace Guard; later, through military achievement, he was appointed Grand Commander.

entries.zh: 高祖為丞相，從韋孝寬破尉迥於相州，加上開府，甘棠縣侯，邑八百戶。
entries.en: While Yang Jian was still Chancellor, Hong followed Wei Xiaokuan in the defeat of Yu Chi at Xiangzhou, was granted the additional title of Opening the Mansion, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gantang county with eight hundred households.
entries.literal: When the Founding Emperor was Chancellor, Hong followed Wei Xiaokuan in defeating Yu Chi at Xiangzhou, was given the additional office of Opening the Mansion, and was made Marquis of Gantang county with a fief of eight hundred households.

entries.zh: 高祖受禪，進爵為公。
entries.en: When Yang Jian took the throne, Hong was promoted to duke.
entries.literal: When the Founding Emperor received the abdication, Hong was advanced in rank to duke.

entries.zh: 尋授驃騎將軍。
entries.en: He was soon appointed General of Valiant Cavalry.
entries.literal: Soon he was appointed General of Valiant Cavalry.

entries.zh: 開皇九年，平陳之役，授行軍總管。
entries.en: In the ninth year of Kaihuang, during the conquest of Chen, he was made Campaign Commander.
entries.literal: In the ninth year of Kaihuang, in the campaign to pacify Chen, he was appointed Campaign Commander.

entries.zh: 及陳平，晉王廣大獵于蔣山，有猛獸在圍中，眾皆懼。
entries.en: After Chen fell, Prince Jin Guang staged a grand hunt on Mount Jiang. A savage beast broke into the ring, and everyone was terrified.
entries.literal: When Chen was pacified, the Prince of Jin Guang held a great hunt on Mount Jiang; a fierce beast was within the encirclement, and all were afraid.

entries.zh: 洪馳馬射之，應弦而倒。
entries.en: Hong spurred his horse forward, loosed an arrow, and the beast dropped at the bow's report.
entries.literal: Hong galloped on horseback and shot it; at the twang of the bowstring it fell.

entries.zh: 陳氏諸將，列觀於側，莫不歎伏焉。
entries.en: Chen's former generals stood in a row to watch, every one of them sighing with admiration.
entries.literal: The various generals of the Chen clan lined up to watch from the side, and none failed to sigh in admiration and submit in awe.

entries.zh: 王大喜，賜縑百匹。
entries.en: The prince was delighted and rewarded him with a hundred bolts of silk.
entries.literal: The prince was greatly pleased and granted him one hundred bolts of silk.

entries.zh: 尋以功加柱國，拜蔣州刺史。
entries.en: Shortly afterward his battlefield record earned him the rank of Pillar of State and appointment as Inspector of Jiangzhou.
entries.literal: Soon, through achievement, he was given the additional rank of Pillar of State and appointed Inspector of Jiangzhou.

entries.zh: 數歲，轉廉州刺史。
entries.en: A few years later he was reassigned as Inspector of Lianzhou.
entries.literal: After several years he was transferred to Inspector of Lianzhou.

entries.zh: 時突厥屢為邊患，朝廷以洪驍勇，檢校朔州總管事。
entries.en: The Turks were raiding the frontier with growing frequency, and the court, trusting in Hong's martial prowess, put him in charge of Shuozhou as acting area commander.
entries.literal: At that time the Turks repeatedly became a border affliction; because Hong was fierce and brave, the court made him acting Area Commander of Shuozhou.

entries.zh: 尋拜代州總管。
entries.en: He was soon formally appointed Area Commander of Daizhou.
entries.literal: Soon he was appointed Area Commander of Daizhou.

entries.zh: 仁壽元年，突厥達頭可汗犯塞，洪率蔚州刺史劉隆、大將軍李藥王拒之。
entries.en: In the first year of Renshou, the Turk khan Datou broke through the border. Hong marched out with Liu Long, Inspector of Weizhou, and the great general Li Yaowang to meet him.
entries.literal: In the first year of Renshou, the Turkic khan Datou invaded the frontier passes; Hong led Liu Long, Inspector of Weizhou, and the great general Li Yaowang to resist him.

entries.zh: 遇虜于恆安，眾寡不敵，洪四面搏戰，身被重創，將士沮氣。
entries.en: At Heng'an they met the enemy badly outnumbered. Hong fought on every side, took grave wounds, and his troops' spirits sank.
entries.literal: They encountered the enemy at Heng'an; their numbers could not match the foe's; Hong fought on all four sides, his body suffered grave wounds, and officers and soldiers lost heart.

entries.zh: 虜悉眾圍之，矢下如雨。
entries.en: The Turks massed their full strength around them, and arrows came down like rain.
entries.literal: The enemy gathered their entire force to surround them; arrows fell like rain.

entries.zh: 洪偽與虜和，圍少解。
entries.en: Hong pretended to negotiate peace, and the ring of besiegers slackened slightly.
entries.literal: Hong feigned making peace with the enemy, and the encirclement loosened somewhat.

entries.zh: 洪率所領潰圍而出，死者大半，殺虜亦倍。
entries.en: Hong led his men in a desperate breakout. More than half his force was lost, but they killed twice as many of the enemy.
entries.literal: Hong led those under his command in breaking out of the encirclement; more than half died, yet those they killed among the enemy were twice as many.

entries.zh: 洪及藥王除名為民，隆竟坐死。
entries.en: Hong and Li Yaowang were stripped of rank and reduced to commoners; Liu Long was eventually sentenced to death.
entries.literal: Hong and Yaowang were stripped of rank and made commoners; Long in the end was condemned and executed.

entries.zh: 煬帝北巡，至恆安，見白骨被野，以問侍臣。
entries.en: On a northern tour Emperor Yang came to Heng'an, saw bleached bones strewn across the fields, and asked his attendants about them.
entries.literal: Emperor Yang toured the north; when he reached Heng'an and saw white bones covering the wilds, he questioned his attending ministers.

entries.zh: 侍臣曰：「往者韓洪與虜戰處也。」
entries.en: An attendant replied, "This is the ground where Han Hong once fought the Turks."
entries.literal: A minister attending him said, "This is where Han Hong fought the barbarians of old."

entries.zh: 帝憫然傷之，收葬骸骨，命五郡沙門為設佛供，拜洪隴西太守。
entries.en: Moved to pity, the emperor had the bones gathered and buried, ordered monks from five commanderies to perform Buddhist rites, and appointed Hong Administrator of Longxi.
entries.literal: The emperor sighed in pity and grief, gathered and buried the bones, ordered Buddhist monks of five commanderies to set out Buddhist offerings, and appointed Hong Administrator of Longxi.

entries.zh: 未幾，硃崖民王萬昌作亂，詔洪擊平之。
entries.en: Before long Wang Wanchang of Zhuyai raised a rebellion, and Hong was ordered to crush it.
entries.literal: Before long, Wang Wanchang of Zhuyai commandery raised rebellion; an edict ordered Hong to attack and pacify him.

entries.zh: 以功加位金紫光祿大夫，領郡如故。
entries.en: For this success he was promoted to Grand Master of Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon while retaining his prefectural post.
entries.literal: Through achievement his rank was raised to Grand Master of Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon, and he retained his commandery as before.

entries.zh: 俄而萬昌弟仲通複叛，又詔洪討平之。
entries.en: Soon Wanchang's brother Zhongtong rebelled as well, and Hong was again sent to put him down.
entries.literal: Soon Wanchang's younger brother Zhongtong rebelled again; again an edict ordered Hong to suppress and pacify him.

entries.zh: 師未旋，遇疾而卒，時年六十三。
entries.en: His army had not yet returned when illness took him. He was sixty-three.
entries.literal: Before the army returned, he fell ill and died, aged sixty-three at the time.

entries.zh: 高祖受禪，陰有並江南之志，訪可任者。
entries.en: After Yang Jian took the throne he quietly set his mind on unifying the south and asked whom he could trust with the task.
entries.literal: When the Founding Emperor received the abdication, he secretly harbored the aim of swallowing Jiangnan and sought one who could be entrusted with the task.

entries.zh: 高熲曰：「朝臣之內，文武才幹，無若賀若弼者。」
entries.en: Gao Jiong answered, "Among the ministers, no one matches He Ruo Bi in combined civil and military talent."
entries.literal: Gao Jiong said, "Among the court ministers, in civil and military talent and capacity, there is none like He Ruo Bi."

entries.zh: 高祖曰：「公得之矣。」
entries.en: The emperor said, "You have named the right man."
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor said, "You have got it exactly."

entries.zh: 於是拜弼為吳州總管，委以平陳之事，弼忻然以為己任。
entries.en: Bi was then made Area Commander of Wuzhou and charged with conquering Chen—a mission he accepted with evident satisfaction.
entries.literal: Thereupon Bi was appointed Area Commander of Wuzhou and entrusted with the matter of pacifying Chen; Bi gladly took it as his own charge.

entries.zh: 與壽州總管源雄並為重鎮。
entries.en: He and Yuan Xiong at Shouzhou together anchored the empire's southern front.
entries.literal: He and Yuan Xiong, Area Commander of Shouzhou, together formed a pair of great strongholds.

entries.zh: 弼遺雄詩曰：「交河驃騎幕，合浦伏波營，勿使騏驎上，無我二人名。」
entries.en: Bi sent Yuan Xiong a verse: "The flying-cavalry pavilion at Jiaohe, Fubo's camp at Hepu—when glory mounts the qilin's back, let not our two names be missing from the roll."
entries.literal: Bi sent Yuan Xiong a poem saying, "The camp of the Flying Cavalry at Jiaohe, the encampment of Fubo at Hepu—let not the qilin's back bear accolades without our two names upon it."

entries.zh: 獻取陳十策，上稱善，賜以寶刀。
entries.en: He submitted ten stratagems for the conquest of Chen. The emperor approved them and gave him a treasured sword.
entries.literal: He presented ten stratagems for taking Chen; the emperor praised them and granted him a precious blade.

entries.zh: 開皇九年，大舉伐陳，以弼為行軍總管。
entries.en: In the ninth year of Kaihuang the empire launched a full-scale invasion of Chen, with Bi as Campaign Commander.
entries.literal: In the ninth year of Kaihuang a great campaign was launched against Chen, with Bi as Campaign Commander.

entries.zh: 將渡江，酹酒而咒曰：「弼親承廟略，遠振國威，伐罪吊民，除凶翦暴，上天長江，鑒其若此。
entries.en: Before crossing the Yangzi he poured wine as an offering and swore an oath: "I take the court's grand design upon myself, carry our nation's might to distant shores, punish the guilty and succor the people, root out evil and end tyranny—Heaven and the Yangzi are my witnesses.
entries.literal: About to cross the river, he poured a libation and swore, saying, "Bi personally receives the court's grand strategy, bears the state's prestige to distant lands, punishes guilt and comforts the people, removes the vicious and cuts down the violent—Heaven above and the Yangzi bear witness to this.

entries.zh: 如便福善禍淫，大軍利涉；
entries.en: If Heaven truly rewards virtue and punishes wickedness, may this army cross in safety;
entries.literal: If indeed fortune attends the good and calamity the vicious, may the great army cross in ease;

entries.zh: 如事有乖違，得葬江魚腹中，死且不恨。」
entries.en: but if fate turns against us, let me lie in the bellies of the Yangzi's fish—I will die without regret."
entries.literal: if affairs go against this, let me be buried in the bellies of the river fish—I shall die without regret."

entries.zh: 先是，弼請緣江防人每交代之際，必集曆陽。
entries.en: Earlier Bi had arranged that whenever the Yangzi garrison forces rotated duty, they must muster at Liyang.
entries.literal: Before this, Bi had requested that each time the river-guard garrisons changed duty they must assemble at Liyang.

entries.zh: 於是大列旗幟，營幕被野。
entries.en: He then planted banners on a massive scale until tents and pennants covered the fields.
entries.literal: Thereupon he arrayed banners and flags on a great scale, and camp pavilions covered the wilds.

entries.zh: 陳人以為大兵至，悉發國中士馬。
entries.en: The Chen court believed a full invasion was at hand and mobilized every soldier and horse in the realm.
entries.literal: The Chen people thought a great army had arrived and mustered all the troops and horses in the realm.

entries.zh: 既知防人交代，其眾複散。
entries.en: Once they realized it was only a routine rotation, the armies dispersed again.
entries.literal: When they learned it was only the garrison changing duty, their masses again dispersed.

entries.zh: 後以為常，不復設備。
entries.en: After that they treated such alarms as routine and stopped preparing defenses.
entries.literal: Later this was taken as routine, and they no longer made preparations.

entries.zh: 及此，弼以大軍濟江，陳人弗之覺也。
entries.en: This time Bi crossed the Yangzi with his full army, and the Chen never noticed.
entries.literal: On this occasion Bi led the great army across the river, and the Chen people did not perceive it.

entries.zh: 襲陳南徐州，拔之，執其刺史黃恪。
entries.en: He struck Southern Xuzhou by surprise, took the city, and captured its inspector, Huang Ke.
entries.literal: He surprised Chen's Southern Xuzhou, stormed it, and seized its Inspector Huang Ke.

entries.zh: 軍令嚴肅，秋毫不犯。
entries.en: Discipline in his army was iron—not even a stalk of grain was touched.
entries.literal: Military discipline was severe; not even an autumn hair was violated.

entries.zh: 有軍士于民間沽酒者，弼立斬之。
entries.en: When a soldier was caught buying wine in town, Bi had him executed on the spot.
entries.literal: When a soldier bought wine among the people, Bi at once had him beheaded.

entries.zh: 進屯蔣山之白土岡，陳將魯達、周智安、任蠻奴、田瑞、樊毅、孔范、蕭摩訶等以勁兵拒戰。
entries.en: He advanced to Baitu Hill on Mount Jiang, where Chen's generals Lu Da, Zhou Zhi'an, Ren Man'nu, Tian Rui, Fan Yi, Kong Fan, Xiao Mohe, and others barred his path with elite troops.
entries.literal: Advancing, he encamped at Baitu Hill on Mount Jiang; the Chen generals Lu Da, Zhou Zhi'an, Ren Man'nu, Tian Rui, Fan Yi, Kong Fan, Xiao Mohe, and others met him with crack troops in battle.

entries.zh: 田瑞先犯弼軍，弼擊走之。
entries.en: Tian Rui attacked first; Bi drove him off.
entries.literal: Tian Rui first attacked Bi's army; Bi struck and put him to flight.

entries.zh: 魯達等相繼遞進，弼軍屢卻。
entries.en: Lu Da and the rest pressed forward one after another, and Bi's line gave ground again and again.
entries.literal: Lu Da and the others in succession advanced wave upon wave, and Bi's army repeatedly fell back.

entries.zh: 弼揣知其驕，士卒且惰，於是督厲將士，殊死戰，遂大破之。
entries.en: Bi judged the enemy overconfident and his own men growing slack. He rallied his officers and men to a fight to the death and broke the Chen army completely.
entries.literal: Bi surmised that they were arrogant and his own troops were growing slack; thereupon he spurred and exhorted officers and soldiers to fight a battle unto death, and in the end routed them utterly.

entries.zh: 麾下開府員明擒摩訶至，弼命左右牽斬之。
entries.en: His officer Yuan Ming, holder of the title Opening the Mansion, brought Xiao Mohe as a captive. Bi ordered his guards to drag him out for execution.
entries.literal: His subordinate Kaifu Yuan Ming captured Mohe and brought him; Bi ordered those at his side to drag him forth and behead him.

entries.zh: 摩訶顏色自若，弼釋而禮之。
entries.en: Mohe's face never changed. Bi released him and received him with full courtesy.
entries.literal: Mohe's countenance remained as calm as before; Bi released him and treated him with ceremony.

entries.zh: 從北掖門而入。
entries.en: He entered the city through the North Side Gate.
entries.literal: He entered by the North Side Gate.

entries.zh: 時韓擒虎已執陳叔寶，弼至，呼叔寶視之。
entries.en: By then Han Qinhu had already taken Chen Shubao prisoner. When Bi arrived he summoned Shubao to face him.
entries.literal: At that time Han Qinhu had already seized Chen Shubao; when Bi arrived he called Shubao forth to look at him.

entries.zh: 叔寶惶懼流汗，股慄再拜。
entries.en: Shubao broke out in a cold sweat, his legs trembling as he kowtowed again and again.
entries.literal: Shubao was fearful and alarmed, sweating; his legs trembling, he bowed twice.

entries.zh: 弼謂之曰：「小國之君，當大國卿，拜，禮也。
entries.en: Bi told him, "A ruler of a lesser state greeting an officer of a greater one—that bow is proper etiquette.
entries.literal: Bi said to him, "The ruler of a small state meeting a minister of a great state—bowing is proper ritual.

entries.zh: 入朝不失作歸命侯，無勞恐懼。」
entries.en: When you appear at court you will still be made Marquis Who Surrenders. There is nothing to fear."
entries.literal: When you enter court you will not lose the making of a Marquis Who Submits to Fate—there is no need for fear."

entries.zh: 既而弼恚恨不獲叔寶，功在韓擒虎之後，於是與擒虎相詢，挺刃而出。
entries.en: Afterward Bi brooded over having missed capturing Shubao himself and taking second place to Han Qinhu. He quarreled with Qinhu and went for his blade.
entries.literal: Soon afterward Bi resented and regretted that he had not captured Shubao himself, that his merit stood after Han Qinhu's; thereupon he exchanged words with Qinhu and, drawing a blade, came forth.

entries.zh: 上聞弼有功，大悅，下詔褒揚，語在《韓擒虎傳》。
entries.en: When the emperor heard of Bi's success he was delighted and issued an edict of praise; the full account appears in the biography of Han Qinhu.
entries.literal: The emperor heard that Bi had merit, was greatly pleased, and issued an edict praising and commending him—the account is in the "Biography of Han Qinhu."

entries.zh: 晉王以弼先期決戰，違軍命，於是以弼屬吏。
entries.en: Prince Jin Guang, angry that Bi had forced a decisive battle ahead of schedule in defiance of orders, handed him over to the military judges.
entries.literal: The Prince of Jin, because Bi had decided the battle ahead of schedule in violation of military orders, thereupon turned Bi over to the legal officers.

entries.zh: 上驛召之，及見，迎勞曰：「克定三吳，公之功也。
entries.en: The emperor summoned him by fast courier. When they met, he welcomed him with praise: "Pacifying the Three Wu was your doing.
entries.literal: The emperor summoned him by post relay; when he arrived and was received, the emperor greeted him with praise, saying, "The pacification of Sanwu is your achievement.

entries.zh: 命登禦坐，賜物八千段，加位上柱國，進爵宋國公，真食襄邑三千戶，加以寶劍、寶帶、金甕、金盤各一，並雉尾扇、曲蓋，雜彩二千段，女樂二部，又賜陳叔寶妹為妾。」
entries.en: Have him take a seat beside the throne and shower him with rewards: eight thousand bales of goods, promotion to Supreme Pillar of State, elevation to Duke of Song, a fief of three thousand households at Xiangyi, a precious sword, belt, golden jar, and golden platter, pheasant-tail fans and curved canopies, two thousand bales of colored silk, two bands of palace musicians, and Chen Shubao's younger sister as concubine."
entries.literal: He ordered him to ascend the imperial seat, granted eight thousand bales of goods, promoted him to Supreme Pillar of State, advanced his noble rank to Duke of Song state, granted a fief income of three thousand households at Xiangyi, and further gave him each one of a precious sword, precious belt, golden jar, and golden platter, along with pheasant-tail fans, curved canopies, two thousand bales of mixed silks, two troupes of female musicians, and also granted him Chen Shubao's younger sister as concubine."

entries.zh: 拜右領軍大將軍，尋轉右武候大將軍。
entries.en: He was made General of the Right Army of the Guard, then transferred to General of the Right Military Guard.
entries.literal: He was appointed General of the Right Army of the Guard; soon he was transferred to General of the Right Military Guard.

entries.zh: 弼時貴盛，位望隆重，其兄隆為武都郡公，弟東為萬榮郡公，並刺史、列將。
entries.en: Bi was then at the height of power and prestige. His elder brother Long was Duke of Wudu and his younger brother Dong Duke of Wanrong; all held prefectures and field commands.
entries.literal: At that time Bi was illustrious and flourishing, his position and repute weighty and solemn; his elder brother Long was Duke of Wudu commandery, his younger brother Dong Duke of Wanrong commandery—all were prefectural governors and ranked generals.

entries.zh: 弼家珍玩不可勝計，婢妾曳綺羅者數百，時人榮之。
entries.en: Bi's household overflowed with treasures, and hundreds of maidservants and concubines dressed in silks; contemporaries regarded his station as the summit of honor.
entries.literal: The precious curios in Bi's household were beyond counting; serving girls and concubines trailing gauze and silk numbered in the hundreds, and men of the time envied him for it.

entries.zh: 弼自謂功名出朝臣之右，每以宰相自許。
entries.en: Bi believed his achievements outranked every minister at court and openly expected to be made chancellor.
entries.literal: Bi considered his merit and fame to stand above the court ministers, and often reckoned himself fit for the chancellorship.

entries.zh: 既而楊素為右僕射，弼仍為將軍，甚不平，形於言色，由是免官，弼怨望愈甚。
entries.en: When Yang Su became Right Vice Director while Bi remained only a general, Bi's displeasure showed plainly in words and face. He was stripped of office, and his resentment only deepened.
entries.literal: Before long Yang Su became Right Vice Director; Bi remained a general, was very displeased, and it showed in word and countenance; on this account he was dismissed from office, and Bi's resentment grew ever deeper.

entries.zh: 後數年，下弼獄，上謂之曰：「我以高熲、楊素為宰相，汝每倡言，雲此二人惟堪啖飯耳，是何意也？」
entries.en: A few years later Bi was thrown into prison. The emperor confronted him: "I made Gao Jiong and Yang Su my chancellors, yet you kept saying they were fit for nothing but filling their bowls. What did you mean by that?"
entries.literal: Several years later Bi was cast into prison; the emperor said to him, "I made Gao Jiong and Yang Su chancellors, yet you repeatedly spread word saying these two men are fit only for eating rice—what is the meaning of this?"

entries.zh: 弼曰：「熲，臣之故人，素，臣之舅子，臣並知其為人，誠有此語。」
entries.en: Bi replied, "Jiong is an old friend of mine, and Su is my nephew by marriage. I know both men well, and I did say it."
entries.literal: Bi said, "Jiong is an old acquaintance of your subject; Su is my nephew by marriage—I know both their characters, and I truly did speak such words."

entries.zh: 公卿奏弼怨望，罪當死。
entries.en: The officials reported that Bi's resentful talk amounted to a capital crime.
entries.literal: The dukes and ministers memorialized that Bi harbored resentment, and his offense deserved death.

entries.zh: 上惜其功，於是除名為民。
entries.en: The emperor valued his past service, however, and reduced him to commoner status instead of executing him.
entries.literal: The emperor prized his achievements, and thereupon stripped him of rank and made him a commoner.

entries.zh: 歲餘，複其爵位。
entries.en: After a year his titles were restored.
entries.literal: After more than a year his noble rank and position were restored.

entries.zh: 上亦忌之，不復任使，然每宴賜，遇之甚厚。
entries.en: The emperor still mistrusted him and gave him no further appointments, yet at every banquet and grant he treated Bi with unusual generosity.
entries.literal: The emperor also feared him and no longer appointed or employed him, yet whenever there were feasts and grants he treated him with great munificence.

entries.zh: 開皇十九年，上幸仁壽宮，宴王公，詔弼為五言詩，詞意憤怨，帝覽而容之。
entries.en: In the nineteenth year of Kaihuang the emperor feasted the princes at Renshou Palace and ordered Bi to compose a pentasyllabic poem. The verses were bitter and resentful, but the emperor let them pass.
entries.literal: In the nineteenth year of Kaihuang the emperor visited Renshou Palace, feasted the princes and dukes, and ordered Bi to compose a five-character poem; the words and intent were resentful and bitter, yet when the emperor read it he tolerated it.

entries.zh: 嘗遇突厥入朝，上賜之射，突厥一發中的。
entries.en: On one occasion when Turks came to court, the emperor arranged an archery display. A Turk hit the target on his first shot.
entries.literal: Once when Turks came to court, the emperor granted them an archery contest; a Turk hit the target with one shot.

entries.zh: 上曰：「非賀若弼無能當此。」
entries.en: The emperor said, "Only He Ruo Bi can answer this."
entries.literal: The emperor said, "None but He Ruo Bi can meet this challenge."

entries.zh: 於是命弼。
entries.en: He then summoned Bi.
entries.literal: Thereupon he ordered Bi.

entries.zh: 弼再拜祝曰：「臣若赤誠奉國者，當一發破的。
entries.en: Bi bowed twice and prayed aloud: "If I serve the state with a loyal heart, let my first arrow find the mark.
entries.literal: Bi twice bowed and prayed, saying, "If your subject is one who serves the state with pure loyalty, let one shot pierce the target.

entries.zh: 如其不然，發不中也。」
entries.en: If not, let the arrow miss."
entries.literal: If it is not so, the shot will not hit."

entries.zh: 既射，一發而中。
entries.en: He loosed one arrow—and hit.
entries.literal: Having shot, with one release he hit.

entries.zh: 上大悅，顧謂突厥曰：「此人天賜我也！」
entries.en: The emperor was delighted and said to the Turks, "Heaven gave me this man!"
entries.literal: The emperor was greatly pleased and, turning to the Turks, said, "This man Heaven has given to me!"

entries.zh: 煬帝之在東宮，嘗謂弼曰：「楊素、韓擒虎、史萬歲三人，俱稱良將，優劣如何？」
entries.en: While he was still crown prince, Emperor Yang once asked Bi, "Yang Su, Han Qinhu, and Shi Wansui are all called great generals—how do they rank against one another?"
entries.literal: When Emperor Yang was in the Eastern Palace, he once said to Bi, "Yang Su, Han Qinhu, and Shi Wansui—the three are all called fine generals; how do they compare in superiority and inferiority?"

entries.zh: 弼曰：「楊素是猛將，非謀將；
entries.en: Bi answered, "Yang Su is a fierce fighter, not a strategist;
entries.literal: Bi said, "Yang Su is a fierce general, not a stratagem general;

entries.zh: 韓擒虎是鬥將，非領將；
entries.en: Han Qinhu is a duelist, not a commander;
entries.literal: Han Qinhu is a combat general, not a command general;

entries.zh: 史萬歲是騎將，非大將。」
entries.en: Shi Wansui is a cavalryman, not a supreme commander."
entries.literal: Shi Wansui is a cavalry general, not a great general."

entries.zh: 太子曰：「然則大將誰也？」
entries.en: The crown prince asked, "Then who is the supreme commander?"
entries.literal: The crown prince said, "Then who is the great general?"

entries.zh: 弼拜曰：「唯殿下所擇。」
entries.en: Bi bowed and said, "That is for Your Highness to decide."
entries.literal: Bi bowed and said, "Whomever Your Highness selects."

entries.zh: 弼意自許為大將。
entries.en: In his own mind, Bi was already the supreme commander.
entries.literal: In his mind Bi took himself to be the great general.

entries.zh: 及煬帝嗣位，尤被疏忌。
entries.en: Once Emperor Yang took the throne, Bi was kept at an even greater distance and watched with suspicion.
entries.literal: When Emperor Yang succeeded to the throne, Bi was especially kept at a distance and regarded with suspicion.

entries.zh: 大業三年，從駕北巡，至榆林。
entries.en: In the third year of Daye he joined the emperor's northern tour as far as Yulin.
entries.literal: In the third year of Daye he accompanied the imperial progress on the northern tour as far as Yulin.

entries.zh: 帝時為大帳，其下可坐數千人，召突厥啟民可汗饗之。
entries.en: The emperor pitched an enormous tent that could seat thousands and summoned Qimin Qaghan of the Turks to a feast beneath it.
entries.literal: The emperor had at that time a great tent under which several thousand men could be seated; he summoned Qimin Qaghan of the Turks to feast there.

entries.zh: 弼以為大侈，與高熲、宇文弼等私議得失，為人所奏，竟坐誅，時年六十四。
entries.en: Bi considered the display outrageously lavish and privately debated its folly with Gao Jiong, Yuwen Bi, and others. Someone informed on them, and Bi was executed at the age of sixty-four.
entries.literal: Bi regarded this as gross extravagance and privately discussed its right and wrong with Gao Jiong, Yuwen Bi, and others; someone reported them, and in the end Bi was executed on the charge, aged sixty-four.

entries.zh: 妻子為官奴婢，群從徙邊。
entries.en: His wife and children were enslaved to the state, and his kinsmen were exiled to the borderlands.
entries.literal: His wife and children were made government slave-servants, and his clansmen were banished to the frontier.

entries.zh: 隋書卷五十二列傳第十七
entries.en: Book of Sui, Volume 52, Biographies 17.
entries.literal: Book of Sui, Volume 52, Biographies 17.

entries.zh: 達奚長儒字富仁，代人也．祖俟，魏定州刺史．父慶，驃騎大將軍、儀同三司．長儒少懷節操，膽烈過人．十五，襲爵樂安公．魏大統中，起家奉車都尉．周太祖引為親信，以質直恭勤，授子都督．數有戰功，假輔國將軍，累遷使持節、撫軍將軍、通直散騎常侍．平蜀之役，恒為先鋒，攻城野戰，所當必破之．除車騎大將軍、儀同三司，增邑三百戶．天和中，除渭南郡守，遷驃騎大將軍、開府儀同三司．從武帝平齊，遷上開府，進爵成安郡公，邑千二百戶，別封一子縣公．宣政元年，除左前軍勇猛中大夫．後與烏丸軌圍陳將吳明徹於呂梁，陳遣驍將劉景率勁勇七千來為聲援，軌令長儒逆拒之．長儒於是取車輪數百，繫以大石，沉之清水，連轂相次，以待景軍．景至，船艦礙輪不得進．長儒乃縱奇兵，水陸俱發，大破之，俘數千人．及獲吳明徹，以功進位大將軍．尋授行軍總管，北巡沙塞，卒與虜遇，接戰，大破之．
entries.en: Daxi Changru, styled Furen, came from Dai. His grandfather Si had been Wei’s inspector of Dingzhou; his father Qing held the ranks of general of agile cavalry and director of the three departments with equal standing. Even as a young man Changru was known for moral resolve and a daring that outstripped ordinary men. At fifteen he succeeded to the dukedom of Le’an. Under the Great Unity reign of Wei he entered service as commandant of the imperial carriages. Emperor Taizu of Zhou took him into his personal trust, and for his plainspoken loyalty and tireless diligence he received a sub-commandant’s commission. Battle honors followed in number; he was acting general who supports the state, then rose through commissioner bearing the staff, general who pacifies the army, and regular attendant-in-ordinary of the scattered cavalry. In the conquest of Shu he was always in the van—whether in siege or in the field, whatever he struck gave way. He was made general of chariots and cavalry and director of the three departments with equal standing, with three hundred added households in his fief. In the Tianhe period he became administrator of Weinan commandery, then general of agile cavalry and director of a bureau with equal standing. He followed Emperor Wu in the pacification of Qi, was promoted to superior director of the bureau, advanced to duke of Cheng’an with twelve hundred households, and had one son enfeoffed separately as a county duke. In the first year of Xuanzheng he was appointed valiant grand master of the left forward army. Later, with Wuwan Gui, he besieged the Chen commander Wu Mingche at Lüliang. Chen dispatched the fierce general Liu Jing with seven thousand elite troops in relief; Gui ordered Changru to intercept them. Changru took hundreds of cartwheels, lashed heavy stones to them, and sank them in the clear current so that hub followed hub in a barrier across the river. When Jing arrived, his fleet fouled on the wheels and could not pass. Changru then loosed his strike force by land and water together and broke the enemy, taking several thousand prisoners. After Wu Mingche fell into their hands, Changru was promoted to grand general for his achievement. He was soon made commander on campaign and patrolled the northern sands; he suddenly met the barbarians in battle and crushed them.
entries.literal: Daxi Changru, courtesy name Furen, was a native of Dai. His grandfather Si served as Regional Inspector of Dingzhou under Wei. His father Qing was General of Agile Cavalry and Director of the Three Departments with Equal Standing. From youth Changru cherished integrity of character and courage that surpassed other men. At fifteen he inherited the title Duke of Le'an. In the Great Unity era of Wei he first took office as Commandant of the Imperial Carriages. Emperor Taizu of Zhou drew him into his inner circle; for his straightforward, respectful diligence he was made a sub-commandant. He won battle honors repeatedly, was provisionally made General Who Supports the State, and was promoted in succession to Commissioner Bearing the Staff, General Who Pacifies the Army, and Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Scattered Cavalry. In the campaign to pacify Shu he was constantly in the vanguard; whether storming cities or fighting in the field, wherever he went he invariably broke the enemy. He was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Director of the Three Departments with Equal Standing, with three hundred additional households in his fief. In the Tianhe era he was made Administrator of Weinan Commandery, then promoted to General of Agile Cavalry and Director of the Bureau with Equal Standing. When he followed Emperor Wu in pacifying Qi he was promoted to Superior Director of the Bureau, advanced to Duke of Cheng'an Commandery with a fief of twelve hundred households, and one son was separately enfeoffed as a county duke. In the first year of Xuanzheng he was appointed Valiant Grand Master of the Left Forward Army. Later, together with Wuwan Gui, he besieged the Chen general Wu Mingche at Lüliang. Chen sent the fierce general Liu Jing at the head of seven thousand picked troops as a relief force. Gui ordered Changru to meet and repel them. Changru then took several hundred cart wheels, bound great stones to them, and sank them in the clear water in a continuous chain of hubs to await Jing's army. When Jing arrived, his ships struck the wheels and could not advance. Changru then unleashed his special troops, attacking by land and water together, and routed them completely, taking several thousand prisoners. When Wu Mingche was captured, Changru was promoted to Grand General for his merit. Soon afterward he was appointed Commander on Campaign and patrolled the northern desert frontier; he suddenly encountered the barbarians, joined battle, and defeated them utterly.

entries.zh: 賀婁子幹字萬壽，本代人也．隨魏氏南遷，世居關右．祖道成，魏侍中、太子太傅．父景賢，右衛大將軍．子幹少以驍武知名．周武帝時，釋褐司水上士，稱為強濟．累遷小司水，以勤勞，封思安縣子．俄授使持節、儀同大將軍．大象初，領軍器監，尋除秦州刺史，進爵為伯．
entries.en: Helou Zigan, styled Wanshou, was originally from Dai. When the Wei moved south his family settled for generations west of the Pass. His grandfather Daocheng had been Wei’s attendant-in-chief and grand tutor of the heir apparent; his father Jingxian was general of the right guard. From youth Zigan was known for martial daring. Under Emperor Wu of Zhou he entered service as master of waters in the waterways office and was praised as forceful and capable. He rose to junior director of waterways and, for diligent service, was enfeoffed as viscount of Si’an county. He was soon made commissioner bearing the staff and general with equal standing. At the start of the Daxiang era he headed the directorate of armaments, then became governor of Qinzhou and was advanced to earl.
entries.literal: Helou Zigan, courtesy name Wanshou, was originally a native of Dai. When the Wei moved south his family settled for generations in the lands west of the Pass. His grandfather Daocheng was Attendant-in-Chief and Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent under Wei. His father Jingxian was General of the Right Guard. Zigan was known from youth for fierce martial prowess. Under Emperor Wu of Zhou he first took office as Master of Waters of the Department of Waterways and was praised as forceful and capable. He rose in succession to Junior Director of Waterways; for diligent service he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Si'an County. Soon he was made Commissioner Bearing the Staff and General with Equal Standing. At the start of the Daxiang era he headed the Directorate of Armaments, then was appointed Governor of Qinzhou and advanced to the rank of Earl.

entries.zh: 史萬歲，京兆杜陵人也．父靜，周滄州刺史．萬歲少英武，善騎射，驍捷若飛．好讀兵書，兼精占候．年十五，值周、齊戰於芒山，萬歲時從父入軍，旗鼓正相望，萬歲令左右趣治裝急去．俄而周師大敗，其父由是奇之．武帝時，釋褐侍伯上士．及平齊之役，其父戰沒，萬歲以忠臣子，拜開府儀同三司，襲爵太平縣公．
entries.en: Shi Wansui came from Duling in Jingzhao. His father Jing had been Zhou’s governor of Cangzhou. From youth Wansui was bold and martial, skilled in riding and archery, swift as if he could fly. He loved military texts and was also expert in divination and celestial signs. At fifteen, when Zhou and Qi fought at Mount Mang, he was with his father in the army. The two hosts were just facing each other when Wansui told his attendants to pack up and leave at once. Soon the Zhou army was routed, and his father marveled at him. Under Emperor Wu he entered service as senior attendant of the guard. In the pacification of Qi his father died in battle; as a loyal minister’s son, Wansui was made director of the bureau with equal standing and inherited the dukedom of Taiping county.
entries.literal: Shi Wansui was a native of Duling in Jingzhao. His father Jing was Governor of Cangzhou under Zhou. Wansui from youth was heroic and martial, skilled in horsemanship and archery, swift and agile as if flying. He loved to read books of war and was also expert in divination and observation of the heavens. At fifteen, when Zhou and Qi fought at Mount Mang, Wansui was following his father into the army. The banners and drums of the two sides were just facing one another when Wansui ordered his attendants to pack up quickly and leave at once. Soon the Zhou army was utterly defeated, and his father marveled at him for this. Under Emperor Wu he first took office as Senior Attendant of the Guard. In the campaign to pacify Qi his father fell in battle; as the son of a loyal minister, Wansui was appointed Director of the Bureau with Equal Standing and inherited the title Duke of Taiping County.

entries.zh: 高祖作相，王謙舉兵於蜀，沙氐上柱國楊永安扇動利、興、武、文、沙、龍等六州以應謙，詔長儒擊破之．謙二子自京師亡歸其父，長儒並捕斬之．高祖受禪，進位上大將軍，封蘄春郡公，邑二千五百戶．
entries.en: While Emperor Gaozu was still regent, Wang Qian rebelled in Shu. Yang Yong'an of the Shadi Di, a pillar of state of the first rank, roused the six prefectures of Li, Xing, Wu, Wen, Sha, and Long in support of Qian, and an edict sent Changru to break them. Qian’s two sons escaped the capital to join their father; Changru seized and executed them both. When Gaozu took the throne, Changru was promoted to grand general of the first rank and enfeoffed as duke of Qichun commandery with twenty-five hundred households.
entries.literal: When Emperor Gaozu served as Chancellor, Wang Qian raised troops in Shu. Yang Yong'an of the Shadi, a pillar of state of the first rank, stirred up the six prefectures of Li, Xing, Wu, Wen, Sha, and Long to respond to Qian. An edict ordered Changru to defeat them. Qian's two sons fled the capital to rejoin their father; Changru captured and executed them both. When Gaozu received the abdication, Changru was promoted to Grand General of the First Rank and enfeoffed as Duke of Qichun Commandery with a fief of twenty-five hundred households.

entries.zh: 開皇二年，突厥沙鉢略可汗並弟葉護及潘那可汗眾十餘萬，寇掠而南，詔以長儒為行軍總管，率眾二千擊之．遇於周槃，眾寡不敵，軍中大懼，長儒慷慨，神色愈烈．為虜所衝突，散而復聚，且戰且行，轉鬥三日，五兵咸盡，士卒以拳毆之，手皆見骨，殺傷萬計，虜氣稍奪，於是解去．長儒身被五創，通中者二；
entries.en: In the second year of Kaihuang, Shabolue Khan of the Turks, together with his younger brother, the yabghu, and Panna Khan, led a horde of more than a hundred thousand south in plunder. Changru was made commander on campaign and sent against them with two thousand men. They met at Zhoupan. Outnumbered, the army was seized with dread—but Changru only grew more fervent, his face fiercer than before. The barbarians broke his line again and again; his men scattered, re-formed, and fought on as they marched, wheeling through the hills for three days until every weapon was spent. Then they struck the enemy with bare fists until bone showed through their hands. Tens of thousands fell on both sides; the Turks’ spirit finally broke, and they drew off. Changru himself took five wounds, two of them grave.
entries.literal: In the second year of Kaihuang, Shabolue Khan of the Turks, together with his younger brother, the yabghu, and Panna Khan, led more than a hundred thousand men in a southern raid. An edict appointed Changru Commander on Campaign and ordered him to strike them with two thousand troops. They met at Zhoupan. His force was few and could not match the enemy; fear spread through the army. Changru grew all the more ardent in spirit, his bearing fiercer than before. The barbarians charged and broke his ranks, yet the men scattered and re-formed, fighting as they marched for three days across the hills. Every weapon was exhausted; the soldiers beat the enemy with their fists until bone showed through their hands. Casualties on both sides numbered in the tens of thousands. The enemy's momentum gradually waned, and they then withdrew. Changru himself received five wounds, two of them deep.

entries.zh: 其戰士死傷者十八九．突厥本欲大掠秦、隴，既逢長儒，兵皆力戰，虜意大沮，明日，於戰處焚屍慟哭而去．高祖下詔曰：「突厥猖狂，輒犯邊塞，犬羊之眾，彌亙山原．而長儒受任北鄙，式遏寇賊，所部之內，少將百倍．以晝通宵，四面抗敵，凡十有四戰，所向必摧．兇徒就戮，過半不反，鋒刃之餘，亡魂竄跡．自非英威奮發，奉國情深，撫御有方，士卒用命，豈能以少破眾，若斯之偉？
entries.en: Eight or nine tenths of his fighting men were killed or wounded. The Turks had meant to ravage Qin and Long on a grand scale; meeting Changru, they found every man resisting to the limit, and their spirit collapsed. The next day they burned their dead on the field, wailed over them, and withdrew. Gaozu issued an edict: “The Turks are reckless, ever raiding the frontier; their dog-and-goat hordes blanket hill and plain. Yet Changru, posted to the northern marches, held the raiders at bay though his command held scarcely one man for every hundred of theirs. From dawn through the night he fought on every side in fourteen engagements and broke whatever he met. The enemy were cut down; more than half never returned; the survivors fled the blades in terror to the wilds. Without heroic fire, deep loyalty to the state, skilled command, and soldiers who gave their all, who could have shattered such a host with so few—a feat as great as this?
entries.literal: Of his fighting men, eight or nine in ten were killed or wounded. The Turks had originally intended to plunder Qin and Long on a great scale, but having met Changru, every man fought to the utmost; the barbarians' hearts were deeply cast down. The next day they burned the corpses on the field, wailed in grief, and departed. Emperor Gaozu issued an edict saying: 'The Turks are insolent and repeatedly violate the border. Their dog-and-goat hordes cover mountains and plains. Yet Changru, charged with the northern marches, checked the raiders though his command held scarcely one man for every hundred of the foe. From daylight through the night he resisted on every side in fourteen engagements, and wherever he turned he shattered the enemy. The wicked were slain; more than half never returned; those who escaped the blades fled in terror to the wilds. Had he not roused heroic might, borne deep loyalty to the state, governed his men with skill, and won their willing obedience, how could he have broken such a multitude with so few—an achievement so magnificent as this?

entries.zh: 言念勳庸，宜隆名器，可上柱國，餘勳迴授一子．其戰亡將士，皆贈官三轉，子孫襲之．」
entries.en: When I consider his service, he deserves the highest honors: let him be pillar of state of the first rank, and let his remaining honors pass to one son. Every officer and soldier who fell in this fight shall receive three posthumous promotions, inheritable by their descendants.”
entries.literal: Considering his merit, it is fitting to elevate his titles: he is approved as Pillar of State of the First Rank, and his remaining honors are conferred on one son. All officers and soldiers who died in battle are posthumously promoted three ranks, to be inherited by their descendants.'

entries.zh: 其年，授寧州刺史，尋轉鄜州刺史，母憂去職．長儒性至孝，水漿不入口五日，毀悴過禮，殆將滅性，天子嘉歎．起為夏州總管三州六鎮都將事，匈奴憚之，不敢窺塞．以病免．又除襄州總管，在職二年，轉蘭州總管．高祖遣涼州總管獨孤羅、原州總管元褒、靈州總管賀若誼等發卒備胡，皆受長儒節度．長儒率眾出祁連山北，西至蒲類海，無虜而還．復轉荊州總管三十六州諸軍事，高祖謂之曰：「江陵要害，國之南門，今以委公，朕無慮也．」歲餘，卒官．諡曰威．子暠大業時，官至太僕少卿．
entries.en: That year he became governor of Ningzhou, then of Binzhou, and left office when his mother died. Deeply filial by nature, he took neither food nor drink for five days; his mourning exceeded the rites and nearly cost him his life, and the emperor marveled at it. Recalled as commander of Xiazhou with authority over three prefectures and six garrisons, he so awed the Xiongnu that they dared not test the border. Illness forced his retirement. He was made commander of Xiangzhou, served two years, then transferred to Lanzhou. Gaozu sent the commanders of Liangzhou, Yuanzhou, and Lingzhou—Dugu Luo, Yuan Bao, and Heruo Yi—to raise troops against the barbarians, all under Changru’s orders. Changru led his men north of the Qilian range as far west as Lake Pulei and returned without meeting the enemy. He was then made commander of Jingzhou with military authority over thirty-six prefectures. Gaozu told him, “Jiangling is the realm’s southern gate; with you there, I need not worry.” A little over a year later he died in office. His posthumous name was Wei. His son Gao, in the Daye reign, rose to vice director of the imperial stud.
entries.literal: That same year he was made Governor of Ningzhou, then transferred to Governor of Binzhou. He left office on his mother's death. Changru was profoundly filial by nature: for five days he took neither water nor food, and his grief exceeded the rites, nearly costing him his life. The Son of Heaven praised and sighed over him. He was recalled as Commander of Xiazhou with authority over three prefectures and six garrisons; the Xiongnu feared him and dared not peer at the border. He was dismissed because of illness. He was again appointed Commander of Xiangzhou; after two years in office he was transferred to Commander of Lanzhou. Gaozu sent the commanders of Liangzhou, Yuanzhou, and Lingzhou—Dugu Luo, Yuan Bao, and Heruo Yi—to raise troops against the barbarians, all under Changru's command. Changru led his force north of the Qilian Mountains as far west as Lake Pulei and returned without encountering the enemy. He was again made Commander of Jingzhou with military authority over thirty-six prefectures. Gaozu told him: 'Jiangling is a strategic point, the southern gate of the realm; now that I entrust it to you, I have no worries.' After a little more than a year he died in office. His posthumous title was Wei. His son Gao, in the Daye era, reached the post of Vice Director of the Imperial Stud.

entries.zh: 及尉迥作亂，子幹與宇文司錄從韋孝寬討之．遇賊圍懷州，子幹與宇文述等擊破之．高祖大悅，手書曰：「逆賊尉迥，敢遣蟻眾，作寇懷州．公受命誅討，應機蕩滌，聞以嗟贊，不易可言．丈夫富貴之秋，正在今日，善建功名，以副朝望也．」其後每戰先登，及破鄴城，與崔弘度逐迥至樓上．進位上開府，封武川縣公，邑三千戶，以思安縣伯別封子皎．
entries.en: When Yuchi Jiong rebelled, Zigan and the registrar Yuwen Shu followed Wei Xiaokuan to suppress him. When the rebels besieged Huaizhou, Zigan and Yuwen Shu and others broke the siege. Gaozu was delighted and wrote in his own hand: “The traitor Yuchi Jiong dared send an ant-like swarm against Huaizhou. You took command and swept them away as the moment required—I can hardly find words for my admiration. A man’s season of wealth and honor is now; build your merit to answer the court’s hopes.” After that he was first over the wall in every fight. When Ye fell, he and Cui Hongdu chased Jiong to the top of a tower. He was promoted to superior director of the bureau, enfeoffed as duke of Wuchuan with three thousand households, and his son Jiao was separately given the earldom of Si’an.
entries.literal: When Yuchi Jiong rebelled, Zigan and Yuwen Shu, the registrar, followed Wei Xiaokuan in the campaign. When the rebels besieged Huaizhou, Zigan and Yuwen Shu and others broke the siege. Gaozu was greatly pleased and wrote in his own hand: 'The traitor Yuchi Jiong dared send an ant-like horde to raid Huaizhou. You received the command to punish him and swept the enemy away as the moment required; hearing of it I sigh with admiration—words can scarcely express it. The season of a man's wealth and honor is today; build your merit well to answer the court's hopes.' Thereafter he was first to charge in every battle. When Ye City was taken, he and Cui Hongdu pursued Jiong to the tower top. He was promoted to Superior Director of the Bureau, enfeoffed as Duke of Wuchuan County with a fief of three thousand households, and his son Jiao was separately enfeoffed with the earldom of Si'an.

entries.zh: 開皇元年，進爵鉅鹿郡公．其年，吐谷渾寇涼州，子幹以行軍總管從上柱國元諧擊之，功最優，詔褒美．高祖慮邊塞未安，即令子幹鎮涼州．明年，突厥寇蘭州，子幹率眾拒之，至可洛峐山，與賊相遇．賊眾甚盛，子幹阻川為營，賊軍不得水數日，人馬甚敝，縱擊，大破之．於是冊授子幹為上大將軍曰：「於戲！
entries.en: In the first year of Kaihuang he was advanced to duke of Julu commandery. That year the Tuyuhun raided Liangzhou; Zigan, as commander on campaign under the pillar of state Yuan Xie, won the highest distinction, and an edict praised him. Fearing the frontier was still unsettled, Gaozu immediately posted Zigan to garrison Liangzhou. The next year the Turks raided Lanzhou; Zigan led troops to meet them at Mount Keluoqi. The enemy force was overwhelming. Zigan dammed the stream and encamped; for days the enemy could not reach water, and men and horses wore out. He then struck and broke them utterly. An investiture document appointed him grand general of the first rank, reading: “Ah!
entries.literal: In the first year of Kaihuang he was advanced to Duke of Julu Commandery. That year the Tuyuhun raided Liangzhou; Zigan, as Commander on Campaign, followed the Pillar of State Yuan Xie in the attack and won the highest merit. An edict praised him. Gaozu, fearing the frontier was not yet secure, immediately ordered Zigan to garrison Liangzhou. The next year the Turks raided Lanzhou; Zigan led troops to resist them. At Mount Keluoqi he met the enemy. The rebel force was very strong. Zigan blocked the stream and made camp; for several days the enemy army could not reach water, and men and horses grew exhausted. He then launched an attack and routed them completely. Thereupon an investiture document appointed Zigan Grand General of the First Rank, saying: 'Ah!

entries.zh: 敬聽朕命．唯爾器量閑明，志情強果，任經武將，勤績有聞．往歲凶醜未寧，屢驚疆埸，拓土靜亂，殊有厥勞．是用崇茲賞典，加此車服，往欽哉！
entries.en: Hear and heed Our command. Your capacity is broad and your judgment clear; your will is firm and resolute; you are fit to bear a commander’s duties, and your diligent achievements are well known. In years past the wicked were not yet pacified and the borders were repeatedly alarmed; in extending the realm and quieting disorder you have shown outstanding merit. Therefore We raise you with this reward and add these chariots and robes—go and revere them!
entries.literal: Hear and heed Our command. You alone are broad in capacity and clear in judgment, firm and resolute in will and feeling, fit to bear the duties of a military commander, and your diligent achievements are well known. In years past the wicked were not yet pacified and the borders were repeatedly alarmed; in extending the realm and quieting disorder you have shown outstanding merit. Therefore We raise you with this reward and add these chariots and robes—go and revere them!

entries.zh: 祗承榮冊，可不慎歟！」
entries.en: Reverently receive this glorious patent—will you not be careful?”
entries.literal: Reverently receive this glorious patent—can you not be careful?'

entries.zh: 徵授營新都副監，尋拜工部尚書．其年，突厥復犯塞，以行軍總管從竇榮定擊之．子幹別路破賊，斬首千餘級，高祖嘉之，遣通事舍人曹威齎優詔勞勉之．子幹請入朝，詔令馳驛奉見．吐谷渾復寇邊，西方多被其害，命子幹討之．馳驛至河西，發五州兵，入掠其國，殺男女萬餘口，二旬而還．高祖以隴西頻被寇掠，甚患之．彼俗不設村塢，敕子幹勒民為堡，營田積穀，以備不虞．子幹上書曰：「比者兇寇侵擾，蕩滅之期，匪朝伊夕．伏願聖慮，勿以為懷．今臣在此，觀機而作，不得準詔行事．且隴西、河右，土曠民稀，邊境未寧，不可廣為田種．比見屯田之所，獲少費多，虛役人功，卒逢踐暴．屯田疏遠者，請皆廢省．但隴右之民以畜牧為事，若更屯聚，彌不獲安．只可嚴謹斥候，豈容集人聚畜．請要路之所，加其防守．但使鎮戍連接，烽候相望，民雖散居，必謂無慮．」高祖從之．俄而虜寇岷、洮二州，子幹勒兵赴之，賊聞而遁去．
entries.en: He was summoned as deputy supervisor of the new capital works, then made minister of works. That year the Turks again raided the frontier; as commander on campaign he followed Dou Rongding. Zigan took a separate route, routed the enemy, and took more than a thousand heads. Gaozu commended him and sent the attendant of affairs Cao Wei with a favoring edict of consolation. Zigan asked to attend court and was ordered to come post-haste by relay. The Tuyuhun raided again and ravaged the west; Zigan was sent against them. He galloped to Hexi, raised troops from five prefectures, invaded their lands, and killed more than ten thousand men and women, returning within twenty days. Gaozu was deeply troubled that Longxi was repeatedly plundered. The people there did not build walled villages; he ordered Zigan to compel them to fortify, open military farms, and store grain against emergencies. Zigan memorialized: “The raiders have been harassing us lately, but their destruction is not far off—I pray Your Majesty not to worry. Here I watch for the moment to act and cannot always follow the statutes to the letter. Longxi and the lands west of the River are wide and thinly peopled; the border is not yet secure, and broad farming is impossible. I have seen that military colonies yield little for great cost, wasting labor only to be overrun. I ask that distant colonies be abolished. The people of Longyou live by herding; if we herd them into colonies they will be still less secure. Strict scouting is enough—we cannot mass people and livestock together. Strengthen the defenses on the main routes; if garrisons link and beacons face one another, the people may live scattered and still be safe.” Gaozu agreed. Soon the barbarians raided Min and Tao; Zigan marched to meet them and they fled at the news.
entries.literal: He was summoned and appointed Deputy Supervisor of the New Capital Construction, then made Minister of Works. That year the Turks again violated the border; as Commander on Campaign he followed Dou Rongding in the attack. Zigan took a separate route, defeated the enemy, and took more than a thousand heads. Gaozu commended him and sent the Attendant of Affairs Cao Wei with an edict of favor to console and encourage him. Zigan requested an audience at court and was ordered to come post-haste by relay. The Tuyuhun again raided the frontier and did great harm in the west; Zigan was ordered to punish them. He rode post-haste to Hexi, raised troops from five prefectures, invaded their country, and killed more than ten thousand men and women, returning within twenty days. Gaozu was deeply troubled that Longxi was repeatedly raided. The local custom did not provide for walled villages; he ordered Zigan to compel the people to build forts, open military farms, and store grain against emergencies. Zigan memorialized: 'Recently the fierce raiders have been harassing us, but the day of their destruction is not far off. I humbly pray Your Sacred Mind not to be troubled. Now that I am here I watch for the moment to act and cannot follow the statutes to the letter. Moreover, in Longxi and west of the River the land is broad and the people sparse; the border is not yet secure and extensive farming cannot be undertaken. I have seen that in the military colonies the harvest is small and the cost great, wasting human labor only to suffer sudden raids. I ask that distant colonies all be abolished. The people of Longyou live by herding; if they are gathered into colonies they will be still less at ease. It is enough to keep scouts strict—how can we mass people and herds together? I ask that key routes receive added defense. If garrisons link together and beacon fires face one another, though the people live scattered they will surely be secure.' Gaozu agreed. Soon the barbarians raided Min and Tao prefectures; Zigan led troops to the rescue and the enemy fled on hearing of his approach.

entries.zh: 高祖以子幹曉習邊事，授榆關總管十鎮諸軍事．歲餘，拜雲州刺史，甚為虜所憚．後數年，突厥雍虞閭遣使請降，並獻羊馬．詔以子幹為行軍總管，出西北道應接之．還拜雲州總管，以突厥所獻馬百匹、羊千口以賜之，乃下書曰：「自公守北門，風塵不警．突厥所獻，還以賜公．」母憂去職．朝廷以榆關重鎮，非子幹不可，尋起視事．十四年，以病卒官，時年六十．高祖傷惜者久之，賻縑千匹，米麥千斛，贈懷、魏等四州刺史，諡曰懷．子善柱嗣，官至黔安太守．
entries.en: Because Zigan knew the frontier well, Gaozu made him commander of Yuguan with military authority over ten garrisons. A year later he became governor of Yunzhou and was greatly feared by the barbarians. Some years later Yongyulü of the Turks sent envoys to surrender and presented sheep and horses. Zigan was made commander on campaign to go out by the northwest route to receive them. On his return he was commander of Yunzhou; the hundred horses and thousand sheep the Turks had presented were given to him, with an imperial letter: “Since you have guarded the northern gate, the frontier has been quiet. What the Turks presented We return to you.” He left office when his mother died, but the court held that Yuguan could not do without him and soon recalled him. In the fourteenth year he died in office of illness at sixty. Gaozu mourned him long, granted a thousand bolts of silk and a thousand hu of grain and millet, posthumously made him governor of Huai, Wei, and two other prefectures, and gave him the posthumous name Huai. His son Shanzhu succeeded him and rose to administrator of Qian’an.
entries.literal: Gaozu, because Zigan understood frontier affairs well, appointed him Commander of Yuguan with military authority over ten garrisons. After a year he was made Governor of Yunzhou and was greatly feared by the barbarians. Several years later Yongyulü of the Turks sent envoys to request surrender and presented sheep and horses. An edict made Zigan Commander on Campaign to go out by the northwest route to receive them. On his return he was appointed Commander of Yunzhou; the hundred horses and thousand sheep presented by the Turks were given to him as a gift, and an imperial letter said: 'Since you have guarded the northern gate, the dust of war has not been raised. What the Turks presented We return and bestow upon you.' He left office on his mother's death. The court held that the strategic post of Yuguan could not do without Zigan, and he was soon recalled to duty. In the fourteenth year he died in office of illness at the age of sixty. Gaozu mourned him for a long time, granted a thousand bolts of silk and a thousand hu of grain and millet in funeral gifts, posthumously made him Governor of the four prefectures of Huai, Wei, and others, and gave the posthumous title Huai. His son Shanzhu succeeded him and reached the post of Administrator of Qian'an.
