entries.zh: 及高智慧等作亂江南，以行軍總管從楊素擊之．萬歲率眾二千，自東陽別道而進，踰嶺越海，攻陷溪洞不可勝數．前後七百餘戰，轉鬥千餘里，寂無聲問者十旬，遠近皆以萬歲為沒．萬歲以水陸阻絕，信使不通，乃置書竹筒中，浮之於水．汲者得之，以言於素．素大悅，上其事．高祖嗟歎，賜其家錢十萬，還拜左領軍將軍．
entries.en: When Gao Zhihui and others rebelled in the south, Wansui followed Yang Su as commander on campaign. With two thousand men he advanced by a separate route from Dongyang, crossed mountains and sea, and took ravine strongholds beyond count. In more than seven hundred fights over a thousand li of hills, for a hundred days no word came from him; everyone thought Wansui was dead. Cut off by land and water, he sealed a letter in a bamboo tube and set it adrift. Someone who drew water found it and told Su. Su was delighted and reported upward. Gaozu marveled and gave his family one hundred thousand cash; on his return Wansui was made general of the left forward army.
entries.literal: When Gao Zhihui and others rebelled in the south, Wansui, as Commander on Campaign, followed Yang Su in the attack. Wansui led two thousand men by a separate route from Dongyang, crossed ranges and seas, and stormed ravine strongholds beyond counting. In more than seven hundred battles over a thousand li of marching hills, for a hundred days there was no word from him; near and far all thought Wansui had perished. Because land and water routes were cut off and messengers could not pass, he placed a letter in a bamboo tube and floated it on the water. One who drew water found it and reported to Su. Su was greatly pleased and submitted the matter to the throne. Gaozu sighed in admiration, granted his family one hundred thousand cash, and on his return appointed him General of the Left Forward Army.

entries.zh: 先是，南寧夷爨翫來降，拜昆州刺史，既而復叛．遂以萬歲為行軍總管，率眾擊之．入自蜻蛉川，經弄凍，次小勃弄、大勃弄，至于南中．賊前後屯據要害，萬歲皆擊破之．行數百里，見諸葛亮紀功碑，銘其背曰：「萬歲之後，勝我者過此．」萬歲令左右倒其碑而進．渡西二河，入渠濫川，行千餘里，破其三十餘部，虜獲男女二萬餘口．諸夷大懼，遣使請降，獻明珠徑寸．於是勒石頌美隋德．萬歲遣使馳奏，請將翫入朝，詔許之．爨翫陰有二心，不欲詣闕，因賂萬歲以金寶，萬歲於是捨翫而還．蜀王時在益州，知其受賂，遣使將索之．萬歲聞而悉以所得金寶沉之於江，索無所獲．以功進位柱國．晉王廣虛衿敬之，待以交友之禮．上知為所善，令萬歲督晉府軍事．明年，爨翫復反，蜀王秀奏萬歲受賂縱賊，致生邊患，無大臣節．上令窮治其事，事皆驗，罪當死．上數之曰：「受金放賊，重勞士馬．朕念將士暴露，寢不安席，食不甘味，卿豈社稷臣也？」
entries.en: Earlier, Cuan Wan of the Ningnan Yi had surrendered and been made governor of Kunzhou, then rebelled again. Wansui was sent as commander on campaign against him. He entered by the Qingling River, passed Nongdong, and halted at Lesser and Greater Bonong before reaching the southern heartland. The rebels held every strong point; Wansui broke them all. After several hundred li he came upon Zhuge Liang’s victory stele, inscribed on the back: “After ten thousand years, whoever surpasses me will pass this place.” Wansui had his men overturn it and march on. He crossed the two western rivers, entered the Quluan River, marched more than a thousand li, and shattered more than thirty tribes, taking more than twenty thousand captives. The Yi were terrified, sent envoys to surrender, and presented a pearl an inch across. He carved a stone praising Sui virtue. Wansui sent a swift report asking that Wan be brought to court; the edict agreed. Wan secretly had no wish to come to the capital and bribed Wansui with gold and jewels; Wansui then left him and returned. The prince of Shu was in Yizhou; learning of the bribe, he sent men to seize the goods. Wansui heard of it and sank everything he had received in the river, and nothing was found. For his merit he was made pillar of state. Prince Jin Guang treated him with open respect as a friend. The emperor, knowing Guang favored him, put Wansui in charge of the prince of Jin’s military affairs. The next year Cuan Wan rebelled again. Prince Xiu of Shu reported that Wansui had taken bribes and released the rebel, bringing border trouble and failing the integrity of a great minister. A full investigation confirmed everything; the crime merited death. The emperor recounted his offenses: “You took gold and let the rebel go, wasting soldiers and horses. When I think of men exposed in the field I cannot sleep or eat with ease—are you a minister of the altars of state?”
entries.literal: Earlier, Cuan Wan of the Ningnan Yi had come to surrender and was appointed Governor of Kunzhou, but soon rebelled again. Wansui was therefore made Commander on Campaign and led troops to attack him. He entered by the Qingling River, passed through Nongdong, halted at Lesser Bonong and Greater Bonong, and reached the southern center. The rebels held key points before and behind; Wansui defeated them all. After marching several hundred li he saw Zhuge Liang's stele commemorating merit, inscribed on the reverse: 'After ten thousand years, whoever surpasses me will pass this place.' Wansui ordered his attendants to overturn the stele and advance. He crossed the two western rivers, entered the Quluan River, marched more than a thousand li, and broke more than thirty tribes, capturing more than twenty thousand men and women. The various Yi were greatly afraid, sent envoys to surrender, and presented a pearl an inch across. He then carved a stone praising Sui virtue. Wansui sent a messenger post-haste to report and request that Wan be brought to court; the edict approved. Wan secretly had other intentions and did not wish to go to the capital; he therefore bribed Wansui with gold and jewels, and Wansui thereupon left Wan and returned. The Prince of Shu was then in Yizhou; learning of the bribe, he sent men to seize the goods. When Wansui heard of it he sank all the gold and jewels he had received in the river, and nothing could be found. For his merit he was promoted to Pillar of State. Prince Jin Guang treated him with open respect and the courtesy due a friend. The Emperor, knowing Guang favored him, ordered Wansui to supervise the military affairs of the Prince of Jin's establishment. The next year Cuan Wan rebelled again. Prince Xiu of Shu memorialized that Wansui had taken bribes and released the rebel, causing border trouble and lacking the integrity of a great minister. The Emperor ordered a full investigation; the facts were all verified and the crime merited death. The Emperor counted his offenses, saying: 'You took gold and released the rebel, greatly wasting soldiers and horses. When I think of the troops exposed in the field I cannot sleep peacefully or eat with pleasure—are you a minister of the altars of state?'

entries.zh: 萬歲曰：「臣留爨翫者，恐其州有變，留以鎮撫．臣還至瀘水，詔書方到，由是不將入朝，實不受賂．」上以萬歲心有欺隱，大怒曰：「朕以卿為好人，何乃官高祿重，翻為國賊也？」
entries.en: Wansui said, “I left Cuan Wan because I feared unrest in his prefecture and kept him to pacify the region. When I reached the Lu River your edict had only just arrived, so I did not bring him in. I truly took no bribe.” The emperor, believing he was deceitful, raged: “I thought you a good man—how, with high rank and rich pay, have you become a traitor to the state?”
entries.literal: Wansui said: 'Your servant left Cuan Wan because I feared trouble in his prefecture and kept him to pacify and reassure the region. When I returned to the Lu River the edict had only just arrived; therefore I did not bring him to court. I truly did not accept a bribe.' The Emperor, believing Wansui harbored deceit in his heart, was greatly angered and said: 'I took you for a good man—how is it that with high office and heavy emolument you have turned into a traitor to the state?'

entries.zh: 顧有司曰：「明日將斬之．」萬歲懼而服罪，頓首請命．左僕射高熲、左衛大將軍元旻等進曰：「史萬歲雄略過人，每行兵用師之處，未嘗不身先士卒，尤善撫御，將士樂為致力，雖古名將未能過也．」上意少解，於是除名為民．歲餘，復官爵．尋拜河州刺史，復領行軍總管以備胡．
entries.en: He turned to the officials: “Tomorrow he dies.” Wansui, terrified, confessed and begged for his life. The left vice director Gao Jiong, the general of the left guard Yuan Min, and others said, “Shi Wansui’s strategy surpasses other men; in every campaign he leads from the front. He is especially skilled at winning his men, who gladly give their all—even famous generals of old could not match him.” The emperor’s anger eased somewhat; Wansui was stripped of rank and made a commoner. After a year his titles were restored. He was soon governor of Hezhou and again commander on campaign against the barbarians.
entries.literal: He turned to the officials and said: 'Tomorrow he shall be beheaded.' Wansui in fear confessed guilt and knocked his head on the ground begging for his life. The Left Vice Director Gao Jiong, the General of the Left Guard Yuan Min, and others advanced and said: 'Shi Wansui's heroic strategy surpasses other men; wherever he leads troops in campaign he has never failed to go before the soldiers in person. He is especially skilled in comforting and controlling them, and officers and men gladly exert themselves for him—even famous generals of old could not surpass him.' The Emperor's mind softened somewhat, and Wansui was therefore stripped of rank and made a commoner. After more than a year his office and titles were restored. Soon he was appointed Governor of Hezhou and again made Commander on Campaign to guard against the barbarians.

entries.zh: 開皇末，突厥達頭可汗犯塞，上令晉王廣及楊素出靈武道，漢王諒與萬歲出馬邑道．[一]萬歲率柱國張定和、大將軍李藥王、楊義臣等出塞，至大斤山，與虜相遇．達頭遣使問曰：「隋將為誰？」
entries.en: At the end of Kaihuang the Turk khan Tatou raided the frontier. The emperor sent Prince Jin Guang and Yang Su by the Lingwu route, and Prince Han Liang and Wansui by the Mayi route. [1] Wansui led the pillars of state Zhang Dinghe and the grand generals Li Yaowang, Yang Yichen, and others beyond the border. At Mount Dajin they met the enemy. Tatou sent a messenger to ask, “Who is the Sui general?”
entries.literal: At the end of Kaihuang the Turk Khan Tatou violated the border. The Emperor ordered Prince Jin Guang and Yang Su to go out by the Lingwu route, and Prince Han Liang and Wansui by the Mayi route. [1] Wansui led the Pillars of State Zhang Dinghe, the Grand Generals Li Yaowang, Yang Yichen, and others beyond the border. At Mount Dajin they met the barbarians. Tatou sent a messenger to ask: 'Who is the Sui general?'

entries.zh: 候騎報「史萬歲也」．突厥復問曰：「得非敦煌戍卒乎？」
entries.en: The scouts answered, “Shi Wansui.” The Turks asked again, “Is he not the garrison soldier from Dunhuang?”
entries.literal: The scouts reported, 'It is Shi Wansui.' The Turks asked again: 'Can it be the garrison soldier from Dunhuang?'

entries.zh: 候騎曰：「是也．」達頭聞之，懼而引去．萬歲馳追百餘里乃及，擊大破之，斬數千級，逐北入磧數百里，虜遁逃而還．楊素害其功，因譖萬歲云：「突厥本降，初不為寇，來於塞上畜牧耳．」遂寢其功．萬歲數抗表陳狀，上未之悟．會上從仁壽宮初還京師，廢皇太子，窮東宮黨與．上問萬歲所在，萬歲實在朝堂，楊素見上方怒，因曰：「萬歲謁東宮矣．」以激怒上．上謂為信然，令召萬歲．時所將士卒在朝稱冤者數百人，萬歲謂之曰：「吾今日為汝極言於上，事當決矣．」既見上，言將士有功，為朝廷所抑，詞氣憤厲，忤於上．上大怒，令左右摧殺之．既而悔，追之不及，因下詔罪萬歲曰：「柱國、太平公萬歲，拔擢委任，每總戎機．往以南寧逆亂，令其出討．而昆州刺史爨翫包藏逆心，為民興患．朕備有成敕，令將入朝．萬歲乃多受金銀，違敕令住，致爨翫尋為反逆，更勞師旅，方始平定．所司檢校，罪合極刑，捨過念功，恕其性命，年月未久，即復本官．近復總戎，進討蕃裔．突厥達頭可汗領其兇眾，欲相拒抗，既見軍威，便即奔退，兵不血刃，賊徒瓦解．如此稱捷，國家盛事，朕欲成其勳庸，復加褒賞．而萬歲、定和通簿之日，乃懷姦詐，妄稱逆面交兵，不以實陳，懷反覆之方，弄國家之法．若竭誠立節，心無虛罔者，乃為良將，至如萬歲，懷詐要功，便是國賊，朝憲難虧，不可再捨．」死之日，天下士庶聞者，識與不識，莫不冤惜．
entries.en: The scouts said, “It is he.” When Tatou heard this he withdrew in fear. Wansui galloped after them for more than a hundred li, overtook them, and broke them utterly, taking several thousand heads. He drove the fugitives north into the desert for hundreds of li before they escaped and he returned. Yang Su, jealous of his glory, slandered him: “The Turks had already surrendered and were only pasturing livestock at the border—they were not raiding.” His merit was buried. Wansui memorialized again and again; the emperor would not see it. When the emperor returned from Renshou Palace to the capital, deposed the crown prince, and hunted the eastern palace faction, he asked where Wansui was. Wansui was in fact at court, but Yang Su, seeing his anger, said, “Wansui has gone to the eastern palace,” to inflame him further. The emperor believed it and summoned Wansui. Several hundred soldiers he had commanded were at court petitioning that they had been wronged. Wansui told them, “Today I will speak out for you before the emperor—the matter will be settled.” Before the emperor he spoke of his men’s merit and how the court had suppressed them; his tone was fierce and he gave offense. The emperor raged and ordered his attendants to kill him on the spot. He soon regretted it but could not undo the deed, and issued an edict condemning Wansui: “The pillar of state and duke of Taiping, Wansui, was raised and entrusted with every campaign. When the south rebelled he was sent to punish them. Cuan Wan of Kunzhou harbored treachery and harmed the people. We had made full plans to bring him to court. Wansui took much gold and silver, disobeyed Our plan by leaving him, and Cuan Wan soon rebelled again, costing fresh armies before order returned. The crime merited death; remembering his merit We spared him and soon restored his rank. Recently he commanded the advance against the frontier tribes. Tatou led his fierce horde to resist; at sight of our might they fled—blades unstained, the enemy dissolved. Such a victory is the state’s glory; We meant to crown his merit with new rewards. Yet on the day the registers were filed he and Dinghe lied, claiming they had met the enemy in battle when they had not, mocking the laws of the state. Only one who serves with full loyalty and no deceit is a true general; Wansui, who sought merit by fraud, is a traitor. The statutes cannot bend—we will not spare him again.” On the day he died, all who heard, whether they knew him or not, mourned him.
entries.literal: The scouts said: 'It is he.' When Tatou heard this he was afraid and withdrew. Wansui galloped in pursuit for more than a hundred li before overtaking them, struck a great defeat, and took several thousand heads. He drove the fleeing enemy north into the desert for several hundred li, then the barbarians escaped and he returned. Yang Su, jealous of his merit, slandered Wansui, saying: 'The Turks had originally surrendered and were not raiding at all—they had only come to pasture livestock at the border.' His merit was therefore suppressed. Wansui repeatedly submitted memorials stating the facts, but the Emperor did not understand. When the Emperor had just returned from Renshou Palace to the capital, deposed the Crown Prince, and pursued the Eastern Palace faction, he asked where Wansui was. Wansui was in fact at court, but Yang Su, seeing the Emperor's anger, said: 'Wansui has gone to visit the Eastern Palace'—to inflame him further. The Emperor believed it and ordered Wansui summoned. Several hundred soldiers he had commanded were at court petitioning that they had been wronged. Wansui told them: 'Today I shall speak out fully for you before the Emperor—the matter will be settled.' When he saw the Emperor he spoke of the troops' merit and how the court had suppressed them; his tone was fierce and he offended the Emperor. The Emperor was greatly angered and ordered his attendants to kill him on the spot. He soon regretted it but could not overtake the deed, and therefore issued an edict condemning Wansui: 'The Pillar of State and Duke of Taiping, Wansui, was raised and entrusted with command of the army on every campaign. Formerly, when the south rebelled, he was sent to punish them. The Governor of Kunzhou, Cuan Wan, harbored treacherous intent and brought harm to the people. We had made full plans and ordered Wan brought to court. Wansui accepted much gold and silver, disobeyed the plan by keeping him, and caused Cuan Wan soon to rebel again, costing further armies before it was pacified. The authorities investigated; the crime merited extreme punishment, but We pardoned his life remembering his merit, and within a short time restored his office. Recently he again commanded the army in advance against the frontier tribes. The Turk Khan Tatou led his fierce horde intending to resist; once they saw our military might they fled at once—blades unstained, the rebels dissolved. Such a victory is a glory of the state; We wished to complete his merit and reward him again. Yet on the day the registers were submitted, Wansui and Dinghe harbored treachery, falsely claiming they had met the rebels in battle face to face and did not report the truth, cherishing schemes of reversal and mocking the laws of the state. Only one who serves with full loyalty and upright conduct, without deceit in his heart, is a good general; as for Wansui, who sought merit by fraud, he is a traitor to the state. The statutes of the court cannot be bent—we cannot spare him again.' On the day of his death, all gentlemen and commoners who heard of it, whether they knew him or not, none failed to mourn him.

entries.zh: 劉方，京兆長安人也．性剛決，有膽氣．仕周承御上士，尋以戰功，拜上儀同．高祖為丞相，方從韋孝寬破尉迥於相州，以功加開府，賜爵河陰縣侯，邑八百戶．高祖受禪，進爵為公．開皇三年，從衛王爽破突厥於白道，進位大將軍．其後歷甘、瓜二州刺史，尚未知名．
entries.en: Liu Fang came from Chang’an in Jingzhao. Firm and resolute by nature, he had real courage. Under Zhou he was senior attendant of the imperial carriage and soon, for battle merit, director with equal standing of the first rank. When Gaozu was chancellor, Fang followed Wei Xiaokuan in defeating Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou, was given the rank of director of the bureau, and enfeoffed as marquis of Heyin with eight hundred households. When Gaozu took the throne he was advanced to duke. In the third year of Kaihuang he followed Prince Shuang of Wei in defeating the Turks at Baidao and was promoted to grand general. He later served as governor of Gan and Gua but was not yet widely known.
entries.literal: Liu Fang was a native of Chang'an in Jingzhao. By nature he was firm and resolute and possessed courage. He served Zhou as Senior Attendant of the Imperial Carriage and soon, for battle merit, was made Director with Equal Standing of the First Rank. When Gaozu was Chancellor, Fang followed Wei Xiaokuan in defeating Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou; for his merit he was given the rank of Director of the Bureau and enfeoffed as Marquis of Heyin County with a fief of eight hundred households. When Gaozu received the abdication he was advanced to Duke. In the third year of Kaihuang he followed Prince of Wei Shuang in defeating the Turks at Baidao and was promoted to Grand General. Thereafter he served in succession as Governor of Gan and Gua prefectures and was not yet widely known.

entries.zh: 仁壽中，會交州俚人李佛子作亂，據越王故城，遣其兄子大權據龍編城，其別帥李普鼎據烏延城．左僕射楊素言方有將帥之略，上於是詔方為交州道行軍總管，以度支侍郎敬德亮為長史，統二十七營而進．方法令嚴肅，軍容齊整，有犯禁者，造次斬之，然仁而愛士，有疾病者，親自撫養．長史敬德亮從軍至尹州，疾甚，不能進，留之州館．分別之際，方哀其危篤，流涕嗚咽，感動行路．其有威惠如此，論者稱為良將．至都隆嶺，遇賊二千餘人來犯官軍，方遣營主宋纂、何貴、嚴願等擊破之．進兵臨佛子，先令人諭以禍褔，佛子懼而降，送於京師．其有桀黠者，恐於後為亂，皆斬之．
entries.en: In the Renshou era the Li chieftain Li Fozi of Jiaozhou rebelled, seized the old city of the King of Yue, sent his nephew Daquan to hold Longbian, and his lieutenant Li Puding to hold Wuyan. The left vice director Yang Su said Fang had a commander’s gifts, and the emperor made him commander on the Jiaozhou route with Jing Deliang of the revenue office as chief clerk, advancing with twenty-seven battalions. Fang’s discipline was severe and his ranks orderly; violators were beheaded on the spot, yet he was kind to his men and nursed the sick himself. Chief clerk Jing Deliang fell gravely ill at Yinzhou and could not continue; Fang left him at the prefectural lodge and wept at their parting so that passersby were moved. With such authority and kindness together, men called him a fine general. At Dulong Ridge more than two thousand rebels attacked; Fang sent the battalion commanders Song Zuan, He Gui, and Yan Yuan to break them. Advancing on Fozi, he first sent men to explain fortune and disaster; Fozi surrendered in fear and was sent to the capital. The stubborn and cunning, lest they rebel again, were all executed.
entries.literal: In the Renshou era the Li chieftain Li Fozi of Jiaozhou rebelled, seized the old city of the King of Yue, sent his elder brother's son Daquan to hold Longbian City, and his lieutenant Li Puding to hold Wuyan City. The Left Vice Director Yang Su said Fang had the strategy of a commander, and the Emperor thereupon appointed Fang Commander on Campaign of the Jiaozhou Route, with the Vice Director of Revenue Jing Deliang as Chief Clerk, advancing with twenty-seven battalions. Fang's laws and orders were stern; his army's appearance was orderly. Whoever violated the prohibitions was beheaded on the spot, yet he was benevolent and loved his men, and when any were ill he nursed them himself. Chief Clerk Jing Deliang accompanied the army to Yinzhou, grew gravely ill, and could not continue; he was left at the prefectural lodge. At their parting Fang grieved for his critical condition, wept and sobbed, and moved all who passed on the road. With such authority and kindness combined, commentators called him a fine general. At Dulong Ridge he met more than two thousand rebels coming to attack the government army; Fang sent the battalion commanders Song Zuan, He Gui, Yan Yuan, and others to defeat them. Advancing against Fozi, he first sent men to explain fortune and disaster; Fozi in fear surrendered and was sent to the capital. Those who were stubborn and cunning, fearing future disorder, were all executed.

entries.zh: 尋授驩州道行軍總管，以尚書右丞李綱為司馬，經略林邑．方遣欽州刺史甯長真、驩州刺史李暈、上開府秦雄以步騎出越常，方親率大將軍張愻、司馬李綱舟師趣比景．高祖崩，煬帝即位，大業元年正月，軍至海口．林邑王梵志遣兵守險，方擊走之．師次闍黎江，賊據南岸立柵，方盛陳旗幟，擊金鼓，賊懼而潰．既渡江，行三十里，賊乘巨象，四面而至．方以弩射象，象中創，卻蹂其陣，王師力戰，賊奔於柵，因攻破之，俘馘萬計．於是濟區粟，度六里，前後逢賊，每戰必擒．進至大緣江，賊據險為柵，又擊破之．逕馬援銅柱，南行八日，至其國都．林邑王梵志棄城奔海，獲其廟主金人，污其宮室，刻石紀功而還．士卒腳腫，死者十四五．方在道遇患而卒，帝甚傷惜之，乃下詔曰：「方肅承廟略，恭行天討，飲冰遄邁，視險若夷．摧鋒直指，出其不意，鯨鯢盡殪，巢穴咸傾，役不再勞，肅清海外．致身王事，誠績可嘉，可贈上柱國、盧國公．」子通仁嗣．
entries.en: He was soon made commander on the Huanzhou route with Li Gang of the state affairs office as chief of staff to pacify Linyi. Fang sent Ning Changzhen, governor of Qinzhou, Li Yun, governor of Huanzhou, and the superior director Qin Xiong with infantry and cavalry by Yuechang, while he himself led Zhang Xun and Li Gang with the fleet toward Bijing. Gaozu died and Emperor Yang succeeded; in the first month of Daye year one the army reached Haikou. King Fan Zhi of Linyi sent troops to hold the passes; Fang drove them off. At the Zhanli River the enemy held the south bank behind palisades. Fang displayed his banners and beat drums and gongs; the enemy broke in fear. After crossing they marched thirty li when the enemy came on great elephants from every side. Fang shot the elephants with crossbows; wounded, they trampled their own ranks. The imperial army fought hard; the enemy fled to their palisades and were stormed, with tens of thousands taken. They crossed the Qulu and the Six Li, met the enemy again and again, and captured them in every fight. At the Dayuan River the enemy held the passes once more and were broken again. Passing Ma Yuan’s bronze pillar, they marched south eight days to the capital. King Fan Zhi abandoned the city and fled to the sea. They seized the temple’s golden image, defiled the palaces, carved a stone of victory, and returned. The soldiers had swollen feet; four or five in ten died. Fang fell ill on the road and died. The emperor mourned him deeply and issued an edict: “Fang reverently carried out the state’s strategy and Heaven’s punishment, drinking ice as he hastened on, treating peril as level ground. He crushed the vanguard and struck unawares; the enemy were destroyed and their nests overturned; the work was not done twice and the southern sea was cleared. He gave his life to the throne with true merit—let him be posthumously pillar of state of the first rank and duke of Lu.” His son Tongren succeeded him.
entries.literal: Soon he was appointed Commander on Campaign of the Huanzhou Route, with the Right Director of the Department of State Affairs Li Gang as Chief of Staff, to pacify Linyi. Fang sent the Governor of Qinzhou Ning Changzhen, the Governor of Huanzhou Li Yun, and the Superior Director of the Bureau Qin Xiong with infantry and cavalry out by Yuechang, while he personally led the Grand General Zhang Xun and Chief of Staff Li Gang with the fleet toward Bijing. Gaozu died and Emperor Yang succeeded; in the first month of the first year of Daye the army reached Haikou. King Fan Zhi of Linyi sent troops to guard the passes; Fang drove them off. The army halted at the Zhanli River; the rebels held the south bank and built palisades. Fang arrayed his banners in full display and beat gongs and drums; the enemy in fear broke and fled. After crossing the river they marched thirty li when the rebels came on great elephants from every side. Fang shot the elephants with crossbows; wounded, they trampled their own ranks. The imperial army fought hard; the rebels fled to their palisades and were stormed and broken, with captives and heads numbering in the tens of thousands. They then crossed the Qulu, passed the Six Li, met the enemy repeatedly before and behind, and captured them in every battle. Advancing to the Dayuan River, the rebels again held the passes with palisades and were again defeated. Passing Ma Yuan's bronze pillar, they marched south eight days to the enemy capital. King Fan Zhi of Linyi abandoned the city and fled to the sea. They seized the golden image of the temple lord, defiled the palaces, carved a stone commemorating merit, and returned. The soldiers suffered swollen feet; four or five in ten died. Fang fell ill on the road and died. The Emperor mourned him deeply and issued an edict: 'Fang reverently carried out the temple strategy and respectfully executed Heaven's punishment, drinking ice as he hastened forward, treating perils as level ground. Crushing the vanguard and striking straight, he took the enemy unawares; whales and krakens were all destroyed and nests overturned; the task was not labored twice and the lands beyond the sea were pacified. He gave his person to the king's service with merit truly praiseworthy; he is posthumously approved as Pillar of State of the First Rank and Duke of Lu.' His son Tongren succeeded him.

entries.zh: 開皇時，有馮昱、王𢶏、李充、楊武通、陳永貴、房兆，俱為邊將，名顯當時．昱、𢶏，並不知何許人也．昱多權略，有武藝．高祖初為丞相，以行軍總管與王誼、李威等討叛蠻，平之，拜柱國．開皇初，又以行軍總管屯乙弗泊以備胡．突厥數萬騎來掩之，昱力戰累日，眾寡不敵，竟為虜所敗，亡失數千人，殺虜亦過當．其後備邊數年，每戰常大克捷．𢶏驍勇善射，高祖以其有將帥才，每以行軍總管屯兵江北，禦陳寇．數有戰功，為陳人所憚．伐陳之役，及高智慧反，攻討皆有殊績．官至柱國、白水郡公．充，隴西成紀人也．少慷慨，有英略．開皇中，頻以行軍總管擊突厥有功，官至上柱國、武陽郡公，拜朔州總管，甚有威名，為虜所憚．後有人譖其謀反，徵還京師，上譴怒之．充性素剛，遂憂憤而卒．武通，弘農華陰人，性果烈，善馳射．數以行軍總管討西南夷，每有功，封白水郡公，拜左武衛大將軍．時党項羌屢為邊患，朝廷以其有威名，歷岷、蘭二州總管以鎮之．後與周法尚討嘉州叛獠，法尚軍初不利，武通率數千人，為賊斷其歸路．武通於是束馬懸車，出賊不意，頻戰破之．賊知其孤軍無援，傾部落而至．武通轉鬥數百里，為賊所拒，四面路絕．武通輕騎接戰，墜馬，為賊所執，殺而噉之．永貴，隴右胡人也，本姓白氏，以勇烈知名．高祖甚親愛之，數以行軍總管鎮邊，每戰必單騎陷陣．官至柱國、蘭利二州總管，封北陳郡公．兆，代人也，本姓屋引氏，剛毅有武略．頻為行軍總管擊胡，以功官至柱國、徐州總管．並史失其事．
entries.en: In the Kaihuang era Feng Yu, Wang Biao, Li Chong, Yang Wutong, Chen Yonggui, and Fang Zhao were all frontier generals famous in their day. Yu and Biao’s origins are unknown. Yu was full of stratagems and martial skill. When Gaozu was first chancellor he was commander on campaign with Wang Yi and Li Wei against rebellious tribes and was made pillar of state. At the start of Kaihuang he garrisoned Yifu Po against the barbarians. Tens of thousands of Turk horsemen surprised him; he fought for days but was outnumbered, was defeated, and lost several thousand men—though the enemy dead were equally great. He guarded the frontier for years afterward and won great victories in every fight. Biao was fierce and skilled in archery; Gaozu saw commander’s talent in him and repeatedly posted him north of the River against Chen raiders. He won repeated honors and was feared by Chen. In the conquest of Chen and the suppression of Gao Zhihui he won outstanding merit, rising to pillar of state and duke of Baishui. Chong came from Chengji in Longxi; from youth he was generous and strategically minded. In Kaihuang he repeatedly struck the Turks with merit, rose to pillar of state of the first rank and duke of Wuyang, and commanded Shuozhou with a name the barbarians feared. Later someone accused him of treason; summoned to the capital, he was rebuked by the emperor. Stubborn by nature, he died of grief and anger. Wutong came from Huayin in Hongnong, resolute and skilled at mounted archery. He repeatedly campaigned against the southwestern Yi with merit, was duke of Baishui, and general of the left martial guard. The Tangut Qiang troubled the border; the court posted him to Min and Lan for his renown. With Zhou Fashang he attacked rebel Liao of Jiazhou. Fashang’s army faltered; Wutong led several thousand men cut off from retreat. He bound the horses and lowered the carts, took the enemy unawares, and broke them repeatedly. Knowing his isolated force had no relief, the enemy brought their whole tribes against him. Wutong marched for hundreds of li among the hills until every road was cut. He fought on light horse, fell, was seized, killed, and eaten. Yonggui was a Hu man of Longyou, originally surnamed Bai, famed for courage. Gaozu favored him and repeatedly posted him to the frontier; in every battle he charged alone. He rose to pillar of state, commander of Lan and Li, and duke of Beichen. Zhao came from Dai, originally of the Wuyin clan, firm and strategically minded. He repeatedly campaigned against the barbarians and rose to pillar of state and commander of Xuzhou. For all of them the history has lost the details.
entries.literal: In the Kaihuang era there were Feng Yu, Wang Biao, Li Chong, Yang Wutong, Chen Yonggui, and Fang Zhao, all frontier generals famous in their day. For Yu and Biao it is not known where they came from. Yu was full of stratagems and possessed martial skill. When Gaozu was first Chancellor he was made Commander on Campaign with Wang Yi, Li Wei, and others to suppress rebellious barbarians and pacify them; he was appointed Pillar of State. At the start of Kaihuang he was again Commander on Campaign, garrisoning Yifu Po to guard against the barbarians. Several tens of thousands of Turk horsemen came to surprise him; Yu fought fiercely for many days but his force was few and could not match them; he was finally defeated by the barbarians, losing several thousand men, though the barbarians killed were also more than equal. Thereafter he guarded the frontier for several years and won great victories in every battle. Biao was fierce and brave and skilled in archery; Gaozu, seeing his talent as a commander, repeatedly made him Commander on Campaign to station troops north of the River against Chen raiders. He won battle honors repeatedly and was feared by the Chen. In the campaign against Chen and when Gao Zhihui rebelled, his attacks all won outstanding merit. He reached the rank of Pillar of State and Duke of Baishui Commandery. Chong was a native of Chengji in Longxi. From youth he was generous and possessed heroic strategy. In Kaihuang he repeatedly served as Commander on Campaign against the Turks with merit, rose to Pillar of State of the First Rank and Duke of Wuyang Commandery, and was appointed Commander of Shuozhou with great renown, feared by the barbarians. Later someone slandered him for plotting rebellion; he was summoned back to the capital and the Emperor rebuked him in anger. Chong was by nature stubborn and died of grief and indignation. Wutong was a native of Huayin in Hongnong, resolute and fierce by nature, skilled in mounted archery. He repeatedly served as Commander on Campaign against the southwestern Yi and won merit each time; he was enfeoffed as Duke of Baishui Commandery and appointed General of the Left Martial Guard. At the time the Tangut Qiang repeatedly troubled the border; the court, because of his renown, made him in succession Commander of Min and Lan prefectures to pacify them. Later, with Zhou Fashang, he attacked the rebel Liao of Jiazhou. Fashang's army was at first unsuccessful; Wutong led several thousand men whose retreat was cut off by the enemy. Wutong then bound the horses and lowered the carts, took the enemy unawares, and defeated them repeatedly in battle. The enemy, knowing his isolated army had no relief, brought their whole tribes against him. Wutong marched for several hundred li among the hills, was blocked by the enemy, and found every road cut off. Wutong fought on light horse, fell from his mount, was seized by the enemy, killed, and eaten. Yonggui was a Hu man of Longyou, originally surnamed Bai, renowned for fierce courage. Gaozu was very fond of him and repeatedly made him Commander on Campaign to guard the frontier; in every battle he charged the lines alone on horseback. He reached Pillar of State and Commander of the two prefectures of Lan and Li, and was enfeoffed as Duke of Beichen Commandery. Zhao was a native of Dai, originally of the Wuyin clan, firm and resolute with military strategy. He repeatedly served as Commander on Campaign against the barbarians and for merit reached Pillar of State and Commander of Xuzhou. For all of them the history has lost the details of their deeds.

entries.zh: 達奚長儒
entries.en: Daxi Changru
entries.literal: Daxi Changru

entries.zh: 王長述，京兆霸城人也。
entries.en: Wang Changshu came from Bacheng in Jingzhao.
entries.literal: Wang Changshu was a native of Bacheng in Jingzhao.

entries.zh: 祖羆，魏太尉。
entries.en: His grandfather Pi had been Wei's Grand Commandant.
entries.literal: His grandfather Pi was Grand Commandant of Wei.

entries.zh: 父慶遠，周淮州刺史。
entries.en: His father Qingyuan was Zhou’s governor of Huaizhou.
entries.literal: His father Qingyuan was Governor of Huaizhou under Zhou.

entries.zh: 長述幼有儀範，年八歲，周太祖見而異之，曰：「王公有此孫，足為不朽。」
entries.en: Changshu had dignified bearing even as a child. At eight, Zhou Taizu saw him and marveled, saying, "Duke Wang has this grandson—that alone is enough to make his line immortal."
entries.literal: From childhood Changshu had dignified bearing. At eight years of age, Zhou Taizu saw him and was struck by him, saying: "The Duke Wang has this grandson; that is enough for immortality."

entries.zh: 解褐員外散騎侍郎，封長安縣伯。
entries.en: He left commoner status for attendant-in-ordinary of the scattered cavalry and was enfeoffed as earl of Chang'an county.
entries.literal: He was released from commoner status and made Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Scattered Cavalry, enfeoffed as Earl of Chang'an County.

entries.zh: 累遷撫軍將軍、銀青光祿大夫、太子舍人。
entries.en: He rose in turn to general who pacifies the army, grand master for splendid happiness with the silver seal, and aide to the crown prince.
entries.literal: He was promoted in succession to General Who Pacifies the Army, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness with the Silver Seal, and Aide to the Crown Prince.

entries.zh: 長述早孤，少為祖羆所養，及羆薨，居喪過禮，有詔褒異之。
entries.en: Orphaned young, he was raised by his grandfather Pi; when Pi died his mourning exceeded the rites and an edict singled him out for praise.
entries.literal: Changshu was orphaned early and was raised by his grandfather Pi. When Pi died, his mourning exceeded the rites, and an edict praised him for it.

entries.zh: 免喪，襲封扶風郡公，邑三千戶。
entries.en: When mourning ended he inherited the dukedom of Fufeng with three thousand households.
entries.literal: When mourning ended he inherited the title Duke of Fufeng Commandery with a fief of three thousand households.

entries.zh: 除中書舍人，修起居注，改封龍門郡公。
entries.en: Appointed secretariat aide and charged with compiling the diurnal records, he was re-enfeoffed as duke of Longmen commandery.
entries.literal: He was appointed Secretariat Aide and compiled the Diurnal Records, and his fief was changed to Duke of Longmen Commandery.

entries.zh: 從于謹平江陵有功，增邑五百戶。
entries.en: He followed Yu Jin in pacifying Jiangling and, for his merit, received an additional five hundred households in his fief.
entries.literal: For merit in following Yu Jin in pacifying Jiangling, his fief was increased by five hundred households.

entries.zh: 周受禪，又增邑通前四千七百戶。
entries.en: When the Zhou dynasty was founded, his fief grew further to a total of four thousand seven hundred households.
entries.literal: When Zhou received the abdication, his fief was again increased, reaching four thousand seven hundred households in all with previous additions.

entries.zh: 拜賓部大夫。
entries.en: He was made grand master of the guest department.
entries.literal: He was appointed Grand Master of the Guest Department.

entries.zh: 出為晉州刺史，轉玉壁總管長史。
entries.en: He served as governor of Jizhou, then became chief clerk under the area commander at Yubi.
entries.literal: He went out as Governor of Jizhou and was transferred to Chief Clerk of the Area Commander of Yubi.

entries.zh: 尋授司憲大夫，出拜廣州刺史。
entries.en: Soon appointed grand master for law, he went out to serve as governor of Guangzhou.
entries.literal: Shortly he was appointed Grand Master for Law and went out as Governor of Guangzhou.

entries.zh: 甚有威惠，吏人懷之，在任數年，蠻夷歸之者三萬餘戶。
entries.en: He combined stern authority with kindness, winning the loyalty of officials and commoners alike; within a few years more than thirty thousand barbarian households came over to his rule.
entries.literal: He had great authority and grace; officials and people cherished him. In several years in office, more than thirty thousand households of barbarians submitted to him.

entries.zh: 朝議嘉之，就拜大將軍。
entries.en: When the court commended his record, he was promoted on the spot to grand general.
entries.literal: The court assembly praised this, and he was appointed on the spot as Grand General.

entries.zh: 後曆襄、仁二州總管，並有能名。
entries.en: He later held area commands in Xiang and Ren, earning a name for competence in both posts.
entries.literal: Later he served successively as Area Commander of Xiang and Ren prefectures, and in both gained a reputation for capability.

entries.zh: 及高祖為丞相，授信州總管，部內夷、獠猶有未賓，長述討平之，進位上大將軍。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen was still chancellor, he was made area commander of Xinzhou; Changshu pacified the unsubmissive Yi and Liao within his district and was promoted to grand general-in-chief.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen became Chancellor, he was entrusted as Area Commander of Xinzhou. Within his jurisdiction some Yi and Liao tribes had not yet submitted, and Changshu suppressed and pacified them, advancing in rank to Grand General-in-Chief.

entries.zh: 王謙作亂益州，遣使致書於長述，因執其使，上其書，又陳取謙之策。
entries.en: When Wang Qian rose in rebellion in Yizhou, he sent a messenger with a letter to Changshu; Changshu seized the envoy, forwarded the letter to the throne, and submitted a plan for taking Qian.
entries.literal: When Wang Qian rebelled in Yizhou, he sent a messenger with a letter to Changshu. Changshu thereupon seized the messenger, submitted the letter, and also set forth a plan to capture Qian.

entries.zh: 上大悅，前後賜黃金五百兩，授行軍總管，率眾討謙。
entries.en: The emperor was delighted, rewarded him with five hundred taels of gold in all, and made him campaign commander to lead forces against Qian.
entries.literal: The Emperor was greatly pleased and in succession granted five hundred taels of gold, appointing him Campaign Commander to lead troops to punish Qian.

entries.zh: 以功進位柱國。
entries.en: For his achievements he was raised to pillar of the state.
entries.literal: For merit he was promoted to Pillar of the State.

entries.zh: 開皇初，復獻平陳之計，修營戰艦，爲上流之師。
entries.en: Early in the Kaihuang era he again submitted a plan to conquer Chen, built a fleet of war-ships, and commanded the upstream forces.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Kaihuang, he again presented a plan to pacify Chen, built and outfitted war-ships, and served as the force of the upper Yangtze.

entries.zh: 上善其能，頻加賞勞，下書曰：「毎覽髙策，深相嘉歎，命將之日，當以公爲元帥也。」
entries.en: The emperor approved his talents, showered him with rewards, and wrote: "Your bold plans always win my admiration; when the day comes to appoint a commander-in-chief, it will be you."
entries.literal: The Emperor approved of his ability and repeatedly added rewards and commendations, issuing a letter saying: "Whenever I read your lofty plans I deeply admire and praise them. When the day comes to appoint a commander, you shall be made supreme commander."

entries.zh: 後數歳，以行軍總管撃南寧，未至，道病卒。
entries.en: A few years later, while leading a campaign against Nanning as campaign commander, he fell ill on the road and died before reaching his destination.
entries.literal: Several years later, as Campaign Commander he attacked Nanning but died of illness on the road before arriving.

entries.zh: 上甚傷惜之，令使者弔祭，贈上柱國、冀州刺史，諡曰莊。
entries.en: The emperor mourned him deeply, sent envoys to perform rites of condolence, and posthumously invested him as senior pillar of the state and governor of Jizhou with the posthumous name Zhuang.
entries.literal: The Emperor was deeply grieved and ordered an emissary to offer mourning sacrifices; posthumously he was granted Senior Pillar of the State and Governor of Jizhou, with the posthumous title Zhuang.

entries.zh: 子謨嗣。
entries.en: His son Mo succeeded him.
entries.literal: His son Mo succeeded.

entries.zh: 謨弟軌，大業末，東郡通守。
entries.en: Mo's younger brother Gui served as prefect of Dong commandery at the end of the Daye era.
entries.literal: Mo's younger brother Gui, at the end of the Daye era, was Prefect of Dongjun.

entries.zh: 少子文楷，起部郎。
entries.en: His youngest son Wenkai was a gentleman in the ministry of rites.
entries.literal: His youngest son Wenkai was a Gentleman of the Ministry of Ceremonies.

entries.zh: 李衍，字拔豆，遼東襄平人也。
entries.en: Li Yan, styled Badou, came from Xiangping in Liaodong.
entries.literal: Li Yan, courtesy name Badou, was a native of Xiangping in Liaodong.

entries.zh: 父弼，周太師。
entries.en: His father Bi had been Zhou's grand preceptor.
entries.literal: His father Bi was Grand Preceptor of Zhou.

entries.zh: 衍少專武藝，慷慨有志略。
entries.en: From youth Yan devoted himself to martial arts; generous and ambitious, he had both drive and strategic sense.
entries.literal: Yan in youth devoted himself to martial arts, was generous of spirit, and had ambition and stratagem.

entries.zh: 周太祖時，釋褐千牛備身，封懷仁縣公。
entries.en: Under Zhou Taizu he entered service as a thousand-ox guard attendant and was enfeoffed as duke of Huairen county.
entries.literal: In the time of Zhou Taizu, he left commoner status as Thousand-Ox Guard Attendant and was enfeoffed as Duke of Huairen County.

entries.zh: 加開府，改封普寧縣公，遷義州刺史。
entries.en: Granted an opened government office, re-enfeoffed as duke of Puning county, he became governor of Yizhou.
entries.literal: He was granted the Opening of a Government Office, his fief was changed to Duke of Puning County, and he was transferred to Governor of Yizhou.

entries.zh: 尋從韋孝寬鎮玉壁城，數與賊戰，敵人憚之。
entries.en: He soon followed Wei Xiaokuan in holding Yubi fortress; after many battles with the enemy they came to fear him.
entries.literal: Soon he followed Wei Xiaokuan in garrisoning Yubi fortress, fought the enemy many times, and the enemy feared him.

entries.zh: 及平齊，以軍功進授大將軍，改封真鄉郡公，拜左宮伯，賜雜彩三百匹，奴婢二十口，賜子仲威爵浮陽郡公。
entries.en: After the conquest of Qi he was promoted to grand general on account of his military merit, re-enfeoffed as duke of Zhenxiang commandery, and made left palace guard; he received three hundred bolts of colored silk, twenty slaves, and his son Zhongwei was enfeoffed as duke of Fuyang commandery.
entries.literal: When Qi was pacified, for military merit he was promoted and appointed Grand General, his fief changed to Duke of Zhenxiang Commandery; he was appointed Left Palace Guard and granted three hundred lengths of mixed silks, twenty slaves and maidservants, and his son Zhongwei was granted the title Duke of Fuyang Commandery.

entries.zh: 後曆定、鄜二州刺史。
entries.en: He later served as governor of Ding and Fu prefectures in succession.
entries.literal: Later he served successively as Governor of Ding and Fu prefectures.

entries.zh: 及王謙作亂，高祖以衍為行軍總管，從梁睿擊平之。
entries.en: When Wang Qian rebelled, Emperor Wen made Yan campaign commander and he followed Liang Rui to put down the revolt.
entries.literal: When Wang Qian rebelled, Emperor Wen appointed Yan as Campaign Commander; he followed Liang Rui in attacking and pacifying him.

entries.zh: 進位上大將軍，賜縑二千匹。
entries.en: He was promoted to grand general-in-chief and given two thousand bolts of fine silk.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Grand General-in-Chief and granted two thousand bolts of fine silk.

entries.zh: 開皇元年，又以行軍總管討叛蠻，平之。
entries.en: In the first year of Kaihuang, again as campaign commander, he suppressed rebellious tribes and pacified them.
entries.literal: In the first year of Kaihuang, again as Campaign Commander he punished rebellious barbarians and pacified them.

entries.zh: 進位柱國，賜帛二千匹。
entries.en: He was raised to pillar of the state and given two thousand bolts of silk.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Pillar of the State and granted two thousand bolts of silk.

entries.zh: 尋檢校利州總管事。
entries.en: He was soon put in charge of the area command of Lizhou.
entries.literal: Soon he was appointed to inspect and manage the affairs of the Area Commander of Lizhou.

entries.zh: 明年，突厥犯塞，以行軍總管率眾討之，不見虜而還。
entries.en: The following year, when the Turks raided the border, he led a punitive campaign as campaign commander but found no enemy and returned.
entries.literal: The next year the Turks raided the frontier; as Campaign Commander he led troops to attack them but returned without encountering the enemy.

entries.zh: 轉介州刺史。
entries.en: He was transferred to governor of Jiezhou.
entries.literal: He was transferred to Governor of Jiezhou.

entries.zh: 後數年，朝廷將有事江南，詔衍於襄州道營戰船。
entries.en: Some years later, as the court prepared for action in the south, Yan was ordered to build warships along the Xiangzhou route.
entries.literal: Several years later, when the court planned action against the Jiangnan region, Yan was ordered to build war-ships on the Xiangzhou route.

entries.zh: 及大舉伐陳，授行軍總管，從秦王俊出襄陽道，以功賜帛三千匹，米六百石。
entries.en: During the great invasion of Chen he was made campaign commander and marched with Prince Qin Jun via the Xiangyang route; for his achievements he received three thousand bolts of silk and six hundred shi of grain.
entries.literal: When a great campaign was launched against Chen, he was appointed Campaign Commander and followed Prince Qin Jun out by the Xiangyang route; for merit he was granted three thousand bolts of silk and six hundred shi of grain.

entries.zh: 拜安州總管，頗有惠政，歲餘，以疾還京師，卒于家，時年五十七。
entries.en: Appointed area commander of Anzhou, he governed with notable benevolence; a little over a year later illness forced him back to the capital, where he died at home at fifty-seven.
entries.literal: He was appointed Area Commander of Anzhou, had benevolent policies, and after a little more than a year returned to the capital due to illness and died at home, aged fifty-seven.

entries.zh: 子仲威嗣。
entries.en: His son Zhongwei succeeded him.
entries.literal: His son Zhongwei succeeded.

entries.zh: 衍弟子長雅，尚高祖女襄國公主，襲父綸爵，為河陽郡公。
entries.en: Yan's younger kinsman Changya married Emperor Wen's daughter Princess Xiangguo, inherited his father Lun's title, and held the dukedom of Heyang.
entries.literal: Yan's younger clansman Changya married the Emperor's daughter Princess Xiangguo, inherited his father Lun's title, and was Duke of Heyang Commandery.

entries.zh: 開皇初，拜將軍、散騎常侍，曆內史侍郎、河州刺史、檢校秦州總管。
entries.en: Early in Kaihuang he became general and regular attendant of the scattered cavalry, later serving as vice minister of the secretariat, governor of Hezhou, and supervisor of the Qinzhou area command.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Kaihuang he was appointed General and Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry, and successively served as Vice Minister of the Secretariat, Governor of Hezhou, and Inspector managing the Area Commander of Qinzhou.

entries.zh: 伊婁謙，字彥恭，本鮮卑人也。
entries.en: Yi Louqian, styled Yangong, was a Xianbei by origin.
entries.literal: Yi Louqian, courtesy name Yangong, was originally of Xianbei ethnicity.

entries.zh: 其先代為酋長，隨魏南遷。
entries.en: His forebears had served for generations as tribal chieftains and moved south with the Wei court.
entries.literal: His ancestors for generations were chieftains and migrated south with Wei.

entries.zh: 祖信，中部太守。
entries.en: His grandfather Xin was administrator of Zhongbu commandery.
entries.literal: His grandfather Xin was Administrator of Zhongbu.

entries.zh: 父靈，相、隆二州刺史。
entries.en: His father Ling had been governor of Xiang and Long prefectures.
entries.literal: His father Ling was Governor of Xiang and Long prefectures.

entries.zh: 謙性忠直，善辭令。
entries.en: Qian was loyal and forthright by nature and gifted with eloquence.
entries.literal: Qian was by nature loyal and upright and skilled in eloquence and discourse.

entries.zh: 仕魏為直閣將軍。
entries.en: Under the Wei he served as a direct gate general.
entries.literal: He served Wei as Direct Gate General.

entries.zh: 周受禪，累遷宣納上士，使持節、車騎大將軍。
entries.en: After the Zhou dynasty was established he rose through the ranks to senior clerk for proclamations and reception, and held the title general of chariots and cavalry with imperial credentials.
entries.literal: When Zhou received the abdication, he was promoted in succession to Senior Clerk for Proclamations and Reception, Bearing the Staff of Authority as General of Chariots and Cavalry.

entries.zh: 武帝將伐齊，引入內殿，從容謂曰：「朕將有事戎馬，何者為先？」
entries.en: When Emperor Wu prepared to attack Qi, he summoned Qian to the inner hall and asked casually, "I am about to take the field—where should I strike first?"
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu was about to attack Qi, he summoned Qian into the inner hall and said at ease: "I am about to take up arms. Where should I strike first?"

entries.zh: 謙對曰：「愚臣誠不足以知大事，但偽齊僭擅，跋扈不恭，沈溺倡優，耽昏曲蘖。
entries.en: Qian answered, "Your humble servant is hardly fit to counsel on great affairs, but the usurping Qi court is arrogant and insolent, lost in actors and wine and debauchery.
entries.literal: Qian replied: "Your foolish subject truly is not enough to know great affairs, but the false Qi usurps and is overbearing and insolent, drowning in actors and singers and sunk in debauchery and wine.

entries.zh: 其折衝之將斛律明月已斃，讒人之口，上下離心，道路仄目。
entries.en: Their finest warrior, Hulu Yue, is dead; slander fills the court, rulers and subjects are estranged, and common folk watch the roads in fear.
entries.literal: Its general who breaks enemy ranks, Hulu Yue, is already dead; slanderers are active and superiors and subordinates are divided in heart; people on the roads narrow their eyes in fear.

entries.zh: 若命六師，臣之願也。」
entries.en: If you send the six armies, that would be this subject's dearest wish."
entries.literal: If Your Majesty commands the Six Armies, that is this subject's wish."

entries.zh: 帝大笑，因使謙與小司寇拓拔偉聘齊觀釁。
entries.en: The emperor laughed aloud and sent Qian with junior minister of justice Tuoba Wei as envoys to Qi to spy out its condition.
entries.literal: The Emperor laughed heartily and thereupon sent Qian with Junior Minister of Justice Tuoba Wei as envoys to Qi to observe signs of strife.

entries.zh: 帝尋發兵。
entries.en: The emperor soon launched his armies.
entries.literal: The Emperor soon mobilized troops.

entries.zh: 齊主知之，令其僕射陽休之責謙曰：「貴朝盛夏徵兵，馬首何向？」
entries.en: When the Qi ruler learned of this, his vice premier Yang Xiuzhi challenged Qian: "Your court is mobilizing in high summer—where are your armies heading?"
entries.literal: The Qi ruler learned of this and had his Vice Premier Yang Xiuzhi reproach Qian, saying: "Your noble court is mobilizing troops in midsummer—where are your horses' heads turned?"

entries.zh: 謙答曰：「僕憑式之始，未聞興師。
entries.en: Qian replied, "Since I assumed my post I have heard nothing of any mobilization.
entries.literal: Qian replied: "From the time I took my post I have not heard of mobilizing armies.

entries.zh: 設複西增白帝之城，東益巴丘之戍，人情恆理，豈足怪哉！」
entries.en: If you strengthened White Emperor City in the west and added garrisons at Baqiu in the east, that would be ordinary human prudence—what is strange about that!"
entries.literal: Even if the west again strengthened the walls of White Emperor City and the east added garrisons at Baqiu, that would be the constant reasoning of human affairs—why should it be surprising!"

entries.zh: 謙參軍高遵以情輸于齊，遂拘留謙不遣。
entries.en: Qian's aide Gao Zun betrayed their secrets to Qi, and the Qi court detained Qian and refused to release him.
entries.literal: Qian's staff officer Gao Zun divulged the situation to Qi, whereupon they detained Qian and did not send him back.

entries.zh: 帝克并州，召謙勞之曰：「朕之舉兵，本俟卿還；
entries.en: After the emperor took Bingzhou he summoned Qian and consoled him: "I had meant to wait until you returned before marching;
entries.literal: When the Emperor captured Bingzhou, he summoned Qian to console him, saying: "My mobilizing of armies was originally waiting for your return;

entries.zh: 不圖高遵中為叛逆，乖朕宿心，遵之罪也。」
entries.en: I never imagined Gao Zun would betray us mid-course, thwarting my long-held plan—the fault is Zun's alone."
entries.literal: I did not expect that Gao Zun in the middle would prove traitorous, contrary to my long-held intent—the fault is Zun's."

entries.zh: 乃執遵付謙，任令報復。
entries.en: He had Zun seized and handed over to Qian, leaving revenge entirely to his discretion.
entries.literal: Thereupon he seized Zun and handed him to Qian, leaving revenge entirely to his discretion.

entries.zh: 謙頓首請赦之，帝曰：「卿可聚眾唾面，令知愧也。」
entries.en: Qian prostrated himself and begged pardon for Zun. The emperor said, "Gather the men and let them spit in his face—that should teach him shame."
entries.literal: Qian prostrated himself and begged pardon for him. The Emperor said: "You may gather the crowd to spit in his face and let him know shame."

entries.zh: 謙跪曰：「以遵之罪，又非唾面之責。」
entries.en: Qian knelt and said, "Zun's crime does not warrant such a punishment as spitting in the face."
entries.literal: Qian knelt and said: "For Zun's crime, spitting in the face is not the appropriate punishment."

entries.zh: 帝善其言而止。
entries.en: The emperor approved and let the matter drop.
entries.literal: The Emperor approved his words and desisted.

entries.zh: 謙竟待遵如初。
entries.en: Qian continued to treat Zun exactly as before.
entries.literal: Qian in the end treated Zun as before.

entries.zh: 其寬厚仁恕，皆此類也。
entries.en: His magnanimity and kindness were characteristic in just this way.
entries.literal: His magnanimity, kindness, and forbearance were all of this kind.

entries.zh: 尋賜爵濟陽縣伯，累遷前驅中大夫。
entries.en: He was soon enfeoffed as earl of Jiyang county and rose to grand master of the vanguard.
entries.literal: Soon he was granted the title Earl of Jiyang County and was promoted in succession to Grand Master of the Vanguard.

entries.zh: 大象中，進爵爲侯，加位開府。
entries.en: During the Daxiang reign he was raised to marquis and granted an opened government office.
entries.literal: In the Daxiang era, he was advanced to Marquis and granted the Opening of a Government Office.

entries.zh: 髙祖作相，授亳州總管，俄征還京。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen was chancellor he was made area commander of Bozhou, then soon recalled to the capital.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen became Chancellor, he was appointed Area Commander of Bozhou and was soon recalled to the capital.

entries.zh: 旣平王謙，謙恥與逆人同名，因爾稱字。
entries.en: After Wang Qian's rebellion was crushed, Louqian was ashamed to share a name with the traitor and henceforth used his courtesy name.
entries.literal: After Wang Qian was pacified, Louqian was ashamed to share a name with the rebel and therefore used his courtesy name.

entries.zh: 髙祖受禪，以彦恭爲左武候將軍，俄拜大將軍，進爵爲公。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen ascended the throne he made Yangong left commander of the martial guard, soon promoted him to grand general and raised him to duke.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen accepted the abdication, he appointed Yangong as Left Commander of the Martial Guard; soon he was appointed Grand General and advanced to Duke.

entries.zh: 數年，出爲澤州刺史，淸約自處，甚得人和。
entries.en: After several years he was posted as governor of Zezhou; frugal and self-restrained, he won the people's affection.
entries.literal: After several years he went out as Governor of Zezhou, was frugal and restrained in his conduct, and greatly won human harmony.

entries.zh: 以疾去職，吏人攀戀，行數百里不絶。
entries.en: When illness forced him to retire, officials and townspeople lined the road for hundreds of li to bid him farewell.
entries.literal: He resigned on account of illness; officials and people clung to him in farewell, stretching for several hundred li without ceasing.

entries.zh: 數歳，卒於家，時年七十。
entries.en: A few years later he died at home at the age of seventy.
entries.literal: After several years he died at home, aged seventy.

entries.zh: 子傑嗣。
entries.en: His son Jie succeeded him.
entries.literal: His son Jie succeeded.

entries.zh: 田仁恭，字長貴，平涼長城人也。
entries.en: Tian Rengong, styled Changgui, came from Changcheng in Pingliang.
entries.literal: Tian Rengong, courtesy name Changgui, was a native of Changcheng in Pingliang.

entries.zh: 父弘，周大司空。
entries.en: His father Hong had been Zhou's grand minister of works.
entries.literal: His father Hong was Grand Minister of Works of Zhou.

entries.zh: 仁恭性寬仁，有局度。
entries.en: Rengong was magnanimous and humane by nature, with breadth of vision.
entries.literal: Rengong was by nature magnanimous and humane and had breadth of vision.

entries.zh: 在周以明經為掌式中士。
entries.en: Under the Zhou he passed the classics examination and became senior clerk for ritual forms.
entries.literal: Under Zhou, through mastery of the Classics he became Senior Clerk for Ritual Forms.

entries.zh: 後以父軍功賜爵鶉陰子。
entries.en: He later received the viscounty of Chunyin in recognition of his father's military achievements.
entries.literal: Later for his father's military merit he was granted the title Viscount of Chunyin.

entries.zh: 大塚宰宇文護引為中外兵曹。
entries.en: Grand Steward of the Tomb Yuwen Hu brought him in as clerk of central and external military affairs.
entries.literal: Grand Steward of the Tomb Yuwen Hu recruited him as Clerk of Central and External Military Affairs.

entries.zh: 後數載，複以父功拜開府儀同三司，遷中外府掾。
entries.en: Some years later, again on his father's account, he was made grand master with an opened office of equal honor to the three excellencies and transferred to a clerkship in the central and external offices.
entries.literal: Several years later, again for his father's merit he was appointed Grand Master with the Opening of a Government Office with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies and was transferred to Clerk of the Central and External Offices.

entries.zh: 從護征伐，數有戰功，改封襄武縣公，邑五百戶。
entries.en: He followed Hu on campaign and won repeated distinction; he was re-enfeoffed as duke of Xiangwu county with a fief of five hundred households.
entries.literal: Following Hu on campaigns, he had military merit many times; his fief was changed to Duke of Xiangwu County with a domain of five hundred households.

entries.zh: 從武帝平齊，加授上開府，進封淅陽郡公，增邑二千戶，拜幽州總管。
entries.en: He followed Emperor Wu in the conquest of Qi and was granted senior opened office, raised to duke of Xiyang commandery with an additional two thousand households, and made area commander of Youzhou.
entries.literal: Following Emperor Wu in pacifying Qi, he was additionally granted Senior Opening of a Government Office, advanced to Duke of Xiyang Commandery with an increased fief of two thousand households, and appointed Area Commander of Youzhou.

entries.zh: 宣帝時，進爵雁門郡公。
entries.en: Under Emperor Xuan he was raised to duke of Yanmen commandery.
entries.literal: In the time of Emperor Xuan, he was advanced to Duke of Yanmen Commandery.

entries.zh: 高祖為丞相，征拜小司馬，進位大將軍。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen was chancellor he was summoned as junior vice minister of war and promoted to grand general.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen became Chancellor, he was summoned and appointed Junior Vice Minister of War and advanced to Grand General.

entries.zh: 從韋孝寬破尉遲迥于相州，拜柱國。
entries.en: He followed Wei Xiaokuan in defeating Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou and was made pillar of the state.
entries.literal: Following Wei Xiaokuan, he defeated Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou and was appointed Pillar of the State.

entries.zh: 高祖受禪，進上柱國，拜太子太師，甚見親重，嘗幸其第，宴飲極歡，禮賜殊厚。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen ascended the throne, he was raised to senior pillar of the state and made grand preceptor to the crown prince; greatly favored, he received imperial visits, lavish feasts, and exceptional gifts.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen accepted the abdication, he was promoted to Senior Pillar of the State and appointed Grand Preceptor to the Crown Prince; he was greatly favored and trusted, and the Emperor once visited his residence, feasting with the utmost joy and granting him exceptionally generous gifts.

entries.zh: 奉詔營廟社，進爵觀國公，增邑通前五千戶。
entries.en: Ordered to oversee construction of the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain, he was raised to duke of Guan state with a total fief of five thousand households.
entries.literal: By imperial order he oversaw construction of the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain, was advanced to Duke of Guan State, and his fief was increased to five thousand households in all with previous additions.

entries.zh: 未幾，拜右武衛大將軍。
entries.en: Before long he was made grand general of the right martial guard.
entries.literal: Before long he was appointed Grand General of the Right Martial Guard.

entries.zh: 歲餘，卒官，時年四十七。
entries.en: A little over a year later he died in office at the age of forty-seven.
entries.literal: After a little more than a year he died in office, aged forty-seven.

entries.zh: 贈司空，諡曰敬。
entries.en: He was posthumously invested as minister of works with the posthumous name Jing.
entries.literal: Posthumously he was granted Minister of Works, with the posthumous title Jing.

entries.zh: 子世師嗣。
entries.en: His son Shishi succeeded him.
entries.literal: His son Shishi succeeded.

entries.zh: 次子德懋，在《孝義傳》。
entries.en: His second son Demao appears in the Biography of Filial Devotion and Righteousness.
entries.literal: His second son Demao is treated in the Biography of Filial Devotion and Righteousness.

entries.zh: 時有任城郡公王景、鮮虞縣公謝慶恩，並官至上柱國。
entries.en: At the time Wang Jing, duke of Rencheng, and Xie Qing'en, duke of Xianyu, both held the rank of senior pillar of the state.
entries.literal: At the time Duke of Rencheng Wang Jing and Duke of Xianyu Xie Qing'en both held office as Senior Pillars of the State.

entries.zh: 大義公辛遵及其弟韶，並官至柱國。
entries.en: Xin Zun, duke of Dayi, and his younger brother Shao both rose to pillar of the state.
entries.literal: Duke of Dayi Xin Zun and his younger brother Shao both reached office as Pillars of the State.

entries.zh: 高祖以其俱佐命功臣，特加崇貴，親禮與仁恭等。
entries.en: Because they had all aided his rise as founding ministers, Emperor Wen specially honored them and received them with the same personal courtesy as Rengong and the others.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen, because they were all founding ministers who had aided his rise, specially honored them and treated them with personal courtesy like Rengong and the others.

entries.zh: 事皆亡失雲。
entries.en: The records of their careers have all been lost.
entries.literal: Their affairs have all been lost.

entries.zh: 元亨，字德良，一名孝才，河南洛陽人也。
entries.en: Yuan Heng, styled Deliang and also known as Xiaocai, came from Luoyang in Henan.
entries.literal: Yuan Heng, courtesy name Deliang, also named Xiaocai, was a native of Luoyang in Henan.

entries.zh: 父季海，魏司徒、馮翊王，遇周、齊分隔，季海遂仕長安。
entries.en: His father Jihai had been Wei's minister of education and king of Fengyi; when Zhou and Qi split the realm, Jihai entered service in Chang'an.
entries.literal: His father Jihai was Minister of Education and King of Fengyi under Wei; when Zhou and Qi were divided, Jihai took office in Chang'an.

entries.zh: 亨時年數歲，與母李氏在洛陽。
entries.en: Heng was then only a few years old and stayed in Luoyang with his mother, Lady Li.
entries.literal: Heng was then only a few years old and remained in Luoyang with his mother, Lady Li.

entries.zh: 齊神武帝以亨父在關西，禁錮之。
entries.en: Because Heng's father was in the west, Emperor Shenwu of Qi had mother and son placed under confinement.
entries.literal: Emperor Shenwu of Qi, because Heng's father was in the west, had them placed under confinement.

entries.zh: 其母則魏司空李沖之女也，素有智謀，遂詐稱凍餒，請就食于滎陽。
entries.en: His mother, a daughter of Wei's minister of works Li Chong, was shrewd by nature; she feigned hunger and cold and asked permission to go to Xingyang for food.
entries.literal: His mother was the daughter of Wei Minister of Works Li Chong and was by nature resourceful; she therefore feigned hunger and cold and asked to go to Xingyang for food.

entries.zh: 齊人以其去關西尚遠，老婦弱子，不以為疑，遂許之。
entries.en: The Qi authorities, seeing only an old woman and a small boy still far from the western frontier, suspected nothing and granted permission.
entries.literal: The Qi people, thinking them still far from the western frontier and only an old woman with a weak child, suspected nothing and granted permission.

entries.zh: 李氏陰托大豪李長壽，攜亨及孤侄八人，潛行草間，得至長安。
entries.en: Lady Li secretly enlisted the great magnate Li Changshou, took Heng and eight orphaned nephews, and traveled by hidden paths until they reached Chang'an.
entries.literal: Lady Li secretly entrusted herself to the great magnate Li Changshou, took Heng and eight orphaned nephews, and traveled hidden among the grasslands until they reached Chang'an.

entries.zh: 周太祖見而大悅，以亨功臣子，甚優禮之。
entries.en: Zhou Taizu was delighted to see them and, because Heng was the son of a founding minister, treated him with exceptional favor.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu saw them and was greatly pleased; because Heng was the son of a founding minister, he treated him with exceptional courtesy.

entries.zh: 亨年十二，魏恭帝在儲宮，引為交友。
entries.en: At twelve, when Emperor Gong of Wei was crown prince, Heng was taken into his circle of companions.
entries.literal: When Heng was twelve, Emperor Gong of Wei was crown prince and took him as a companion.

entries.zh: 釋褐千牛備身。
entries.en: He entered service as a thousand-ox guard attendant.
entries.literal: He left commoner status as Thousand-Ox Guard Attendant.

entries.zh: 大統末，襲爵馮翊王，邑千戶。
entries.en: At the end of the Datong era he inherited the kingship of Fenyang with a fief of one thousand households.
entries.literal: At the end of Datong he inherited the title King of Fenyang with a fief of one thousand households.

entries.zh: 授拜之日，悲慟不能自勝。
entries.en: On the day he received the appointment he was overcome with grief and could not contain himself.
entries.literal: On the day he received the appointment he was overcome with grief and could not contain himself.

entries.zh: 俄遷通直散騎常侍，曆武衛將軍、勳州刺史，改封平涼王。
entries.en: He was soon made regular attendant of the scattered cavalry with direct transmission, later serving as general of the martial guard and governor of Xunzhou before being re-enfeoffed as king of Pingliang.
entries.literal: Soon he was transferred to Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry with Direct Transmission, and successively served as General of the Martial Guard and Governor of Xunzhou; his title was changed to King of Pingliang.

entries.zh: 周閔帝受禪，例降為公。
entries.en: When Emperor Min of Zhou ascended the throne, by precedent his title was reduced to duke.
entries.literal: When Emperor Min of Zhou accepted the abdication, by precedent his rank was reduced to duke.

entries.zh: 明、武時，曆隴州刺史、禦正大夫、小司馬。
entries.en: Under Emperors Ming and Wu he served in succession as governor of Longzhou, grand master for rectification, and junior vice minister of war.
entries.literal: Under Emperors Ming and Wu he successively served as Governor of Longzhou, Grand Master for Rectification, and Junior Vice Minister of War.

entries.zh: 宣帝時，為洛州刺史。
entries.en: Under Emperor Xuan he was governor of Luozhou.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Xuan he was Governor of Luozhou.

entries.zh: 高祖為丞相，遇尉遲迥作亂，洛陽人梁康、邢流水等舉兵應迥。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen was chancellor, Yuchi Jiong rebelled; Liang Kang, Xing Liushui, and other men of Luoyang raised troops in support of him.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen became Chancellor, Yuchi Jiong rebelled; the men of Luoyang Liang Kang, Xing Liushui, and others raised troops in response to Jiong.

entries.zh: 旬日之間，眾至萬餘。
entries.en: Within ten days their force swelled to more than ten thousand men.
entries.literal: Within ten days their force reached more than ten thousand.

entries.zh: 州治中王文舒潛與梁康相結，將圖亨。
entries.en: The prefectural aide Wang Wenshu secretly colluded with Liang Kang and plotted against Heng.
entries.literal: The prefectural aide Wang Wenshu secretly joined with Liang Kang and planned to seize Heng.

entries.zh: 亨陰知其謀，乃選關中兵，得二千人為左右，執文舒斬之，以兵襲擊梁康、邢流水，皆破之。
entries.en: Learning of the plot in secret, Heng selected two thousand Guanzhong troops as his guard, seized Wenshu and executed him, then attacked Liang Kang and Xing Liushui and routed them both.
entries.literal: Heng secretly learned of the plot, selected two thousand troops from Guanzhong as his personal guard, seized Wenshu and executed him, then attacked Liang Kang and Xing Liushui and defeated them both.

entries.zh: 高祖受禪，征拜太常卿，增邑七百戶。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen ascended the throne, Heng was summoned as minister of ceremonies and his fief was increased by seven hundred households.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen accepted the abdication, Heng was summoned and appointed Minister of Ceremonies, and his fief was increased by seven hundred households.

entries.zh: 尋出為衛州刺史，加大將軍。
entries.en: He was soon posted as governor of Weizhou and promoted to grand general.
entries.literal: Soon he went out as Governor of Weizhou and was promoted to Grand General.

entries.zh: 衛土俗薄，亨以威嚴鎮之，在職八年，風化大洽。
entries.en: The people of Wei were morally lax; Heng governed with stern authority, and in eight years local customs were thoroughly reformed.
entries.literal: The people of Wei were shallow in custom; Heng governed them with stern authority, and in eight years in office local customs were greatly transformed.

entries.zh: 後以老病，表乞骸骨，吏人詣闕上表，請留臥治，上嗟歎者久之。
entries.en: Later, afflicted by age and illness, he requested retirement; officials and townspeople petitioned the throne to let him remain and govern from his bed, and the emperor sighed over this at length.
entries.literal: Later, due to age and illness, he submitted a memorial requesting retirement; officials and people went to the palace to submit memorials asking that he remain and govern from his bed, and the Emperor sighed over this for a long time.

entries.zh: 其年，亨以篤疾，重請還京，上令使者致醫藥，問動靜，相望於道。
entries.en: That year, as his illness grew grave, he again asked to return to the capital; the emperor sent envoys with medicine and inquiries in an unbroken stream along the road.
entries.literal: That year, as Heng's illness grew grave, he again asked to return to the capital; the Emperor sent envoys with medicine and inquiries, one after another along the road.

entries.zh: 歲餘，卒于家，時年六十九。
entries.en: A little over a year later he died at home at the age of sixty-nine.
entries.literal: After a little more than a year he died at home, aged sixty-nine.

entries.zh: 諡曰宣。
entries.en: He was given the posthumous name Xuan.
entries.literal: His posthumous title was Xuan.

entries.zh: 杜整，字皇育，京兆杜陵人也。
entries.en: Du Zheng, styled Huangyu, came from Duling in Jingzhao.
entries.literal: Du Zheng, courtesy name Huangyu, was a native of Duling in Jingzhao.

entries.zh: 祖盛，魏直閣將軍、潁川太守。
entries.en: His grandfather Sheng had been a direct gate general and administrator of Yingchuan under Wei.
entries.literal: His grandfather Sheng was Direct Gate General and Administrator of Yingchuan under Wei.

entries.zh: 父辟，渭州刺史。
entries.en: His father Pi had been governor of Weizhou.
entries.literal: His father Pi was Governor of Weizhou.

entries.zh: 整少有風概，九歲丁父憂，哀毀骨立，事母以孝聞。
entries.en: From youth Zheng had force of character; at nine he mourned his father until his frame was wasted away, and he was known for filial devotion to his mother.
entries.literal: Zheng from youth had force of character; at nine he entered mourning for his father, grieving until his bones showed, and was known for filial service to his mother.

entries.zh: 及長，驍勇有膂力，好讀孫、吳《兵法》。
entries.en: When grown he was bold and physically powerful and loved to read the military treatises of Sunzi and Wuzi.
entries.literal: When grown he was bold and brave with great physical strength and loved to read the military treatises of Sunzi and Wuzi.

entries.zh: 魏大統末，襲爵武鄉侯。
entries.en: At the end of the Wei Datong era he inherited the marquisate of Wuxiang.
entries.literal: At the end of Datong under Wei he inherited the title Marquis of Wuxiang.

entries.zh: 周太祖引為親信。
entries.en: Zhou Taizu brought him in as a trusted intimate.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu recruited him as a trusted intimate.

entries.zh: 後事宇文護子中山公訓，甚被親遇。
entries.en: He later served Yuwen Hu's son, Duke of Zhongshan Xun, and was greatly favored.
entries.literal: Later he served Yuwen Hu's son Duke of Zhongshan Xun and was greatly favored.

entries.zh: 俄授都督。
entries.en: He was soon appointed colonel.
entries.literal: Soon he was appointed Colonel.

entries.zh: 明帝時，為內侍上士，累遷儀同三司，拜武州刺史。
entries.en: Under Emperor Ming he was senior attendant of the inner service, rose to grand master with equal honor to the three excellencies, and was made governor of Wuzhou.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Ming he was Senior Attendant of the Inner Service and was promoted in succession to Grand Master with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies, then appointed Governor of Wuzhou.

entries.zh: 從武帝平齊，加上儀同，進爵平原縣公，邑千戶，入為勳曹中大夫。
entries.en: He followed Emperor Wu in pacifying Qi, was granted senior equal honor, raised to duke of Pingyuan county with a fief of one thousand households, and entered the capital as grand master of the bureau of merits.
entries.literal: Following Emperor Wu in pacifying Qi, he was granted Senior Equal Honor, advanced to Duke of Pingyuan County with a fief of one thousand households, and entered service as Grand Master of the Bureau of Merits.

entries.zh: 高祖為丞相，進位開府。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen was chancellor he was granted an opened government office.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen became Chancellor, he was promoted to the Opening of a Government Office.

entries.zh: 及受禪，加上開府，進封長廣郡公，俄拜左武衛將軍。
entries.en: When the throne changed hands he was granted senior opened office, raised to duke of Changguang commandery, and soon made general of the left martial guard.
entries.literal: When the abdication was accepted he was granted Senior Opening, advanced to Duke of Changguang Commandery, and soon appointed General of the Left Martial Guard.

entries.zh: 在職數年，以母憂去職，起令視事。
entries.en: After several years in office he resigned to mourn his mother but was recalled and ordered to resume his duties.
entries.literal: After several years in office he resigned on account of mourning for his mother but was recalled and ordered to resume duties.

entries.zh: 開皇六年，突厥犯塞，詔遣衛王爽總戎北伐，以整為行軍總管兼元帥長史。
entries.en: In the sixth year of Kaihuang, when the Turks raided the frontier, Prince Wei Shuang was ordered to command the northern campaign and Zheng was made campaign commander and chief of staff to the supreme commander.
entries.literal: In the sixth year of Kaihuang the Turks raided the frontier; an edict dispatched Prince Wei Shuang to command the northern campaign, with Zheng as Campaign Commander and chief of staff to the supreme commander.

entries.zh: 至合川，無虜而還。
entries.en: They reached Hechuan, found no enemy, and returned.
entries.literal: Reaching Hechuan, they found no enemy and returned.

entries.zh: 整密進取陳之策，上善之，於是以行軍總管鎮襄陽。
entries.en: Zheng secretly submitted a plan to conquer Chen; the emperor approved it and made him campaign commander at Xiangyang.
entries.literal: Zheng secretly submitted a plan to capture Chen; the Emperor approved it and thereupon appointed him Campaign Commander to garrison Xiangyang.

entries.zh: 尋病卒，時年五十五。
entries.en: He soon died of illness at the age of fifty-five.
entries.literal: Soon he died of illness, aged fifty-five.

entries.zh: 高祖聞而傷之，贈帛四百匹，米四百石，諡曰襄。
entries.en: The emperor was grieved at the news, granted four hundred bolts of silk and four hundred shi of grain, and gave him the posthumous name Xiang.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen heard of it he was grieved and granted four hundred bolts of silk and four hundred shi of grain; his posthumous title was Xiang.

entries.zh: 子楷嗣。
entries.en: His son Kai succeeded him.
entries.literal: His son Kai succeeded.

entries.zh: 官至開府。
entries.en: He rose to grand master with an opened government office.
entries.literal: He reached office as Grand Master with the Opening of a Government Office.

entries.zh: 李徹，字廣達，朔方岩綠人也。
entries.en: Li Che, styled Guangda, came from Yanlü in Shuofang.
entries.literal: Li Che, courtesy name Guangda, was a native of Yanlü in Shuofang.

entries.zh: 父和，開皇初為柱國。
entries.en: His father He became pillar of the state at the beginning of Kaihuang.
entries.literal: His father He became Pillar of the State at the beginning of Kaihuang.

entries.zh: 徹性剛毅，有器幹，偉容儀，多武藝。
entries.en: Che was resolute and firm by nature, capable and imposing in bearing, and skilled in many martial arts.
entries.literal: Che was by nature resolute and firm, had capacity and ability, possessed an imposing appearance, and was skilled in many martial arts.

entries.zh: 大塚宰宇文護引為親信，尋拜殿中司馬，累遷奉車都尉。
entries.en: Grand Steward of the Tomb Yuwen Hu brought him in as a trusted intimate; he was soon made palace attendant major and rose to commandant of the imperial carriages.
entries.literal: Grand Steward of the Tomb Yuwen Hu recruited him as a trusted intimate; soon he was appointed Palace Attendant Major and was promoted in succession to Commandant of the Imperial Carriages.

entries.zh: 護以徹謹厚有才具，甚禮之。
entries.en: Because Che was careful, honest, and talented, Hu treated him with great courtesy.
entries.literal: Hu, because Che was careful, honest, and talented, treated him with great courtesy.

entries.zh: 護子中山公訓為蒲州刺史，護令徹以本官從焉。
entries.en: Hu's son, Duke of Zhongshan Xun, was governor of Puzhou, and Hu ordered Che to accompany him in his existing office.
entries.literal: Hu's son Duke of Zhongshan Xun was Governor of Puzhou, and Hu ordered Che to accompany him in his original office.

entries.zh: 未幾，拜車騎大將軍、儀同三司。
entries.en: Before long he was made general of chariots and cavalry with equal honor to the three excellencies.
entries.literal: Before long he was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Grand Master with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies.

entries.zh: 武帝時，從皇太子西征吐谷渾，以功賜爵同昌縣男，邑三百戶。
entries.en: Under Emperor Wu he followed the crown prince on the western campaign against Tuyuhun and for his merit was enfeoffed as viscount of Tongchang county with three hundred households.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Wu he followed the Crown Prince on the western campaign against Tuyuhun and for merit was granted the title Viscount of Tongchang County with a fief of three hundred households.

entries.zh: 後從帝拔晉州。
entries.en: He later followed the emperor in capturing Jizhou.
entries.literal: Later he followed the Emperor in capturing Jizhou.

entries.zh: 及帝班師，徹與齊王憲屯雞棲原。
entries.en: When the emperor withdrew, Che and Prince of Qi Xian encamped at Jiqiyuan.
entries.literal: When the Emperor withdrew the army, Che and Prince of Qi Xian encamped at Jiqiyuan.

entries.zh: 齊主高緯以大軍至，憲引兵西上，以避其鋒。
entries.en: The Qi ruler Gao Wei arrived with a great army; Xian led his troops westward to avoid their spearhead.
entries.literal: The Qi ruler Gao Wei arrived with a great army; Xian led his troops westward to avoid their spearhead.

entries.zh: 緯遣其驍將賀蘭豹子率勁騎躡憲，戰于晉州城北。
entries.en: Wei sent his fierce general Helan Baozi with crack cavalry to pursue Xian, and they fought north of Jizhou city.
entries.literal: Wei sent his fierce general Helan Baozi with crack cavalry to pursue Xian; they fought north of Jizhou city.

entries.zh: 憲師敗，徹與楊素、宇文慶等力戰，憲軍賴以獲全。
entries.en: Xian's army was defeated; Che, Yang Su, Yuwen Qing, and others fought fiercely and preserved Xian's army intact.
entries.literal: Xian's army was defeated; Che, Yang Su, Yuwen Qing, and others fought fiercely, and Xian's army was preserved intact thanks to them.

entries.zh: 復從帝破齊師於汾北，乘勝下髙壁，拔晉陽，擒髙湝於冀州，倶有力焉。
entries.en: He again followed the emperor in defeating Qi forces north of the Fen River, pressed the victory to take Gaobi and Jinyang, and helped capture Gao Jie at Jizhou.
